World.title: Mexican mayor found alive after hours-long abduction
World.content:
Rio Bravo mayor freed by captors after being abducted in Zacatecas state, known for violence linked to cartel activity.

The mayor of the Mexican border town of Rio Bravo has been found alive after being abducted in the violence-ridden Zacatecas state in northern Mexico.

Federal officials said Miguel Angel Almaraz was released by his captors on Sunday, hours after being taken to the city of Zacatecas.

He was abducted while travelling with family and friends in a region that straddles the states of Zacatecas and San Luis Potosi on Saturday, when his car was intercepted by armed men, who let the others go.

Almaraz’s relatives were able to reach a town in San Luis Potosi, where they alerted authorities about the incident, according to the state’s Security Department.

Almaraz is the mayor of Rio Bravo, a municipality of about 110,000 people in Tamaulipas state, 11km (7 miles) from Mexico’s border with Texas, United States.

He was acquitted of money laundering charges in 2015, after being imprisoned for six years.

He is a member of the conservative National Action Party, but was previously associated with the left-wing Party of the Democratic Revolution.

It is unclear why Almaraz was taken. Authorities say they are investigating the case, including who might be involved in the abduction.

Zacatecas state is known for activity involving the Jalisco New Generation Cartel and the Sinaloa Cartel, both accused of attacking civilians and politicians.



A car bomb exploded outside a municipal police headquarters in Ojo Caliente, Zacatecas state, in August, injuring 11 people and damaging about 30 homes. Officials said the attack may have been retaliation by an organised crime group after a recent arrest.

In June 2021, police discovered the bullet-ridden bodies of 18 men after an apparent gun battle between suspected drug cartels in Zacatecas state.

World.title: Chancellor Merz to nominate Aigner as Germany’s first woman president
World.content:
Ilse Aigner, speaker of the Bavarian state parliament, belongs to the Christian Social Union in Bavaria (CSU) party.

Share Chancellor Merz to nominate Aigner as Germany’s first woman president on social media

German Chancellor Friedrich Merz will nominate Bavarian politician Ilse Aigner for Germany’s next president, which would make her the country’s first female head of state.

Merz made the announcement at a dinner for leaders of his centre-right Christian Democratic Union (CDU) party on Sunday.

Aigner, speaker of the Bavarian state parliament, belongs to the Christian Social Union (CSU), the Bavarian sister party of the CDU.

If her nomination is confirmed at a CDU and CSU meeting on Monday, she would almost certainly be formally elected.

According to German political practice, coalition parties must agree on a common candidate. The governing coalition is made up of the CDU, the CSU and the Social Democratic Party (SPD).

The SPD has frequently voiced its support for Aigner as president.

The German president is elected by the Federal Convention, convened solely to choose the president. It will decide on incumbent Frank-Walter Steinmeier’s successor on January 30.

Steinmeier, a Social Democrat, took office in 2017, and will reach the limit of two five-year terms in March 2027.

Germany’s president holds a largely ceremonial position, signing legislation into law and formally appointing ministers.

But the president can play the role of a neutral arbiter, above party politics, and acts as a symbol of national unity.

The CSU put forward Aigner’s name earlier this year, but the CDU held back from endorsing her while Merz considered alternatives, straining relations between the parties.

Aigner, 61, began her political career in local politics before being elected to federal parliament in 1998.



She served as agriculture minister under former Chancellor Angela Merkel before returning to her home state of Bavaria, where she became speaker of the state parliament in 2018.

World.title: Lopez double fires Barcelona to win at Atletico Madrid
World.content:
Fermin Lopez brace has Barcelona come from behind to win 2-1 at Atletico Madrid to go three points clear in La Liga.

Share Barcelona turn it around at Atletico Madrid to win 2-1 on social media

Fermin Lopez scored twice as Barcelona overcame an early deficit at Atletico Madrid to win 2-1 and go three points clear at the top of La Liga.

Barca’s win takes them three points clear of second-placed Real Madrid and five ahead of Atletico, in third, after 12 games.

Giuliano Simeone opened the scoring in the 10th minute for the home side, turning home a close range volley from Julian Alvarez’s cross from the left.

The home side had a series of early chances as they sought to register an eighth straight win, but Fermin swept in an equaliser on the cusp of halftime after a ball broke to him in the box.

Lamine Yamal set up Fermin’s second goal in the 66th minute with an incisive pass, and Lopez fired past Jan Oblak with a first-time finish to silence the Metropolitano and secure a fifth straight away league win over Atleti for the first time.

“It was a very difficult match. The first half was tough, but we managed to come from behind and secure the win,” Barcelona midfielder Lopez told La Liga TV after the match.

“I think we were not being clinical enough. After the goal, we gained more confidence.

“Lamine [Yamal] has been very good. His pass for the second goal was half the goal itself. I’m very happy,” Lopez said.

“We wanted to go into the break as league leaders and get three points. The equaliser lifted a weight off our shoulders, and we had more control.



“We knew at halftime that we had to continue playing the way we finished the first half. I think the team produced an incredible second half, both defensively and offensively. We’re very happy.”

World.title: Surgeon having lunch near Krakow shooting undoubtedly saved officer's life, colleague says
World.content:
One of two surgeons who treated victims on the streets in the aftermath of a mass shooting in Krakow, Poland said his colleague "undoubtedly" saved the life of a gravely injured police officer.

The pair were eating near the city's Main Market Square on Saturday when a gunman began firing at random, killing six people and injuring 15.

The doctors raced to treat both the attacker and two officers shot while subduing the perpetrator.

On Sunday, the officers - both hailed as "true heroes" by the prime minister for preventing further deaths - emerged from comas.

Prosecutors launched a terror investigation after ministers previously said the 24-year-old Polish attacker - who remains in a critical condition - was apparently inspired by "far-right ideologies".

A British national and Austrian woman were among those killed alongside four Poles.

Professor Michal PÄdziwiatr was having lunch with a colleague, named by local media as Dr Mateusz Wierdak, and their families in central Krakow when they heard gunshots.

PÄdziwiatr told the BBC: "We saw the shooting attack. And what a surgeon can do in a situation like this?... We decided to help the victims as soon as possible.

"We rushed into the area where the shooting was and started our rescue, because there were no ambulances available, there were no professionals around."

World.title: Seven dead and more than 100 injured after trains collide in Egypt
World.content:
At least seven people have died in a train crash near the Egyptian city of Giza, with more than 100 injured.

The country's railway authority said two trains travelling south from Giza and Cairo collided, causing several carriages to derail and fall down an embankment.

Images from the scene showed people looking inside overturned carriages for injured passengers as a massive emergency response was launched.

Egyptian President Abdul Fattah al-Sisi said he had ordered state authorities to "investigate the circumstances of the accident, and hold accountable anyone found to have been negligent".

The public prosecutor's office warned the death toll could rise.

World.title: Homes and temples glow across India to mark Diwali
World.content:
Millions across India are celebrating Diwali, the Hindu festival of lights, illuminating homes, temples, offices and streets with oil lamps and colourful lights to symbolise the triumph of light over darkness.

The festival falls on the darkest night of the Hindu lunar month of Kartik, when the moon is not visible in the sky.

Although Diwali traditions vary across India's regions and communities, the festival is widely marked by prayers, family gatherings, the exchange of sweets and the lighting of firecrackers.

But the celebrations come amid growing concerns over air pollution, particularly in northern India.

Seasonal weather conditions and the burning of crop residue contribute to deteriorating air quality, while firecrackers set off during Diwali can make the situation worse.

Air pollution in the Indian capital Delhi has reached such hazardous levels that it is the most polluted Diwali festival in a decade. New measures to improve air quality do not seem to have been successful.

India's financial capital, Mumbai, has also experienced high pollution levels in recent weeks.

In an effort to limit pollution, India's Supreme Court on Monday permitted the manufacture, sale and use of certified "green" firecrackers in Delhi and surrounding areas for a limited period.

These firecrackers are designed to produce 20-30% fewer emissions than conventional fireworks. But critics have questioned how effective they are at reducing pollution and raised concerns that conventional firecrackers could still make their way into the capital from neighbouring states.

World.title: Iran executes three men for 'armed unrest' after January protests
World.content:
Iran has executed three men accused of carrying out armed unrest during January's anti-government protests, according to state media.

Hassan Dioband, Hamid Kazemi and Reza Zanganeh were accused of throwing Molotov cocktails and grenades, using bladed weapons and firearms, and setting fire to public facilities in the city of Karaj, west of Tehran, Iran's state news agency Tasnim, external reported.

The executions are the latest in a series linked to the protests, including those of people accused of having ties to Israel and the United States.

The number of executions in Iran has increased since US-Israeli strikes on the Islamic Republic began in late February.

The protest movement initially sparked in December last year by the high cost of living rapidly evolved into widespread anti-government demonstrations that peaked on 8 and 9 of January.

Iranian authorities reported more than 3,000 deaths, and blamed the violence on "terrorist acts" orchestrated by the US and Israel.

However foreign-based NGOs gave higher figures and the BBC received multiple accounts from Iranians of security forces opening fire on unarmed protesters.

Tasnim reported that the three men were executed after the Supreme Court upheld their convictions and found them guilty of "participating in operational activities on behalf of the Israeli Zionist regime, the United States and hostile groups".

The damage allegedly included an electricity substation in Karaj which caused power outages in some areas.

Dioband was arrested on 11 January after investigations identified him as a suspect in attacks on public property and incitement to violence.

Ten others accused of taking part in the unrest under his supervision were later arrested.

Reuters news agency reports that they received prison terms of 5 to 10 years.

The latest executions in Iran come after the UN human rights chief Volker TÃ¼rk said he was alarmed by the rise in death penalties.

In August, TÃ¼rk said at least 56 people had been executed on national security-related charges since 19 March, including 27 in cases linked to January's nationwide anti-government protests.

Iran is thought to be the world's second-most prolific executioner after China. Last year, it put to death at least 2,159 people, according to Amnesty International.

The human rights group said that was the highest figure on record since 1981 and included 45 executions of suspected dissidents on national security-related charges.

World.title: Aramco Tower hit in heart of Saudi capital as Houthis launch fresh strikes
World.content:
The Aramco Tower, a skyscraper in the Saudi Arabian capital's central financial district, had been hit by an air attack.

A statement issued via the Houthi-controlled Saba news agency confirmed the group had targeted Riyadh's business zone on Saturday, without mentioning the Aramco Tower by name.

The Saudi energy ministry said the tower had suffered only "minor damage" and no one had been killed or injured.

Footage authenticated by BBC Verify shows more extensive damage to the building, with at least one floor appearing to have been badly hit by a missile or drone strike.

Windows on more than one level appear to have been shattered by the strike.

The Houthis also said Riyadh's airport and Aramco oil storage facilities were targeted in separate strikes. Saudi Arabia said its air defences had intercepted and destroyed several missiles.

The strikes were the latest claimed by the Yemen-based armed group against targets deep inside Saudi Arabia, which the Gulf power has struggled to contain in recent months.

It came a day after the Houthis accused a Saudi-led coalition of killing at least 33 people, including women and children, in an air strike on Yemen.

Footage broadcast by Houthi-run television channel Al Masirah showed rescuers pulling bodies from the rubble of several buildings in al-Shariyah, a town to the east of the capital, Sanaa.

Saba said 39 people had been injured in the strike. Saudi Arabia has not commented.

A Saudi-led coalition has been fighting the Houthis for more than a decade in support of Yemen's internationally recognised government, which has lost control of a large swathe of the country to the rebel group.

Although the conflict had largely been dormant in recent years, fighting has intensified following the outbreak of the Iran war.

An informal ceasefire unravelled in July after the Tehran-backed Houthis announced a "maritime embargo" against Saudi Arabia and began missile and drone attacks on Saudi airports, oil facilities and tankers in the Red Sea.

The Houthis said they were retaliating for what they have called a Saudi blockade of their territory, as well as an air strike on Sanaa airport Saudi Arabia said had been to prevent an Iranian aircraft from landing there.

Major fighting has since resumed between Houthi forces and troops aligned with Yemen's Saudi-backed government.

The United Nations says more than 1,600 people have been killed and more than 300,000 displaced since fighting resumed.

World.title: 'Flat', 'tired', 'cynical': Unusually gloomy Kiwis deliver New Zealand's tightest election in years
World.content:
New Zealand voted in a new government as fog choked the capital, Wellington, on Saturday - and the mood was as palpable as the grey weather.

"It's pretty flat," 21-year-old Imogen Vlutger says. "There's this kind of apathy and a bit of dread."

"Tired. I think we're all tired," Symone, 28, admits.

"I didn't even vote," one man in his 40s sheepishly confesses. He couldn't bring himself to tick any of the boxes, he explains, declining to chat further.

"Wellington's a bit of a bubble," another voter says, expressing a caveat I heard often, before describing feeling disillusioned.

But polling shows this is a pervasive sentiment across the country: the national mood is low and faith in politics is even lower.

More than half the country no longer sees it as a land of opportunity, a recent study found, while a similar portion fears that the future looks even worse.

Many Kiwis feel the economy is in ruins, there are no jobs, the cost of living has become sky high, the sense of community that used to be a source of national pride is breaking down and there's no sense of genuine progress on policy solutions.

A record number of them are abandoning ship in search of brighter futures elsewhere.

Saturday's election also saw a record number of voters desert the two major parties, giving neither a clear mandate.

But it brought new highs for parties across the spectrum: the left-leaning Greens, the right-wing libertarian Act Party and the centrist Opportunity Party â the latter of which had never won a seat in parliament before but could now hold the balance of power with seven.

World.title: Paraguay's former president charged after bank collapse
World.content:
Prosecutors in Paraguay have charged former president Santiago PeÃ±a over his alleged role in a banking scandal that led to his impeachment.

He has been accused of breach of trust and administration for personal gain.

PeÃ±a, who denies any wrongdoing, was forced from office after a bank collapse triggered a crisis that left more than half of the country's population without access to their accounts.

He was arrested on Friday minutes after lawmakers, including from his own party, unanimously voted to remove him from office following the collapse of Ueno Bank, which has links to his private business interests.

He had offered to step down but rather than accept his resignation, senators impeached PeÃ±a and charged him with misconduct, meaning he has been stripped of the immunity usually granted to ex-presidents.

PeÃ±a, who until last year held shares in the company that owned the bank, has denied any wrongdoing.

The impeachment charges that led to PeÃ±a's removal alleged he had conflicts of interest, manipulated regulatory oversight, diverted pension funds, and participated in an institutional cover-up involving the central bank.

PeÃ±a's deputy, Pedro Alliana, has been sworn in as the new interim president and promised not to "abandon" the millions of people affected by the scandal.

"Compatriots who are now going through a difficult time as a result of the financial collapse will be fully compensated," said Alliana, who will serve as president until 2028.

The demise of the digital bank left more than half of Paraguay's population without access to their savings after it was seized by Paraguay's central bank.

Long lines of people trying to withdraw money from Ueno branches snaked down the streets of the capital Asuncion on Tuesday and Wednesday.

An estimated three million depositors remain unable to access their savings and pensions, prompting public outrage particularly in the capital, AsunciÃ³n.

Protests erupted across the country in response, with thousands taking to the streets on Thursday to demand their money.

Earlier demonstrations featured clashes with the police, who used tear gas and water cannons on the crowd.

PeÃ±a's impeachment passed with 44 out of 45 senators voting in favour of it. One lawmaker was absent.

"It was never my intention to betray the trust you placed in me," PeÃ±a said in a video posted on X announcing his resignation, adding his priority was "the peace of mind of Paraguayans who entrusted their savings to our financial system".

Afterwards, senate president Basilio NÃºÃ±ez said PeÃ±a was found guilty of "dereliction of duty".

World.title: Pope in 'pretty good health' as he starts Latin America tour
World.content:
Pope Leo XIV has told reporters travelling with him to Latin America he is "in pretty good health", in his first comments on his condition since having surgery for lung cancer.

The Pope has arrived in Uruguay, the first stop of a 12-day tour which he is undertaking only three weeks after his operation.

The pontiff, 71, also said he was "very happy" to be able to make the trip which was thrown into doubt last month when doctors discovered a tumour during a routine scan.

The tour will cover Argentina and a much anticipated return to Peru, which the Vatican described as a "homecoming" as the Pope was based there for many years as a missionary, then a bishop.

"I must confess that, from the very first day, I never had any doubts; I was convinced that this journey had to go forward," the Pope told journalists on his plane to Uruguay.

"Thanks to the marvellous medical staff... I believe I am in quite good health," Pope Leo confirmed.

Last month's operation to remove a tumour was successful and his doctors say the cancer has not spread.

On Friday, he arrived in Monetevideo to a seafront lined with crowds shouting his name as his Popemobile passed.

In his first speech of the trip, the Pope said universal healthcare should be "accessible to everyone".

He told the crowd in Plaza Independencia the care he received made him think of the "many men and women who lack the means to obtain a timely diagnosis" or receive treatment.

He capped his day with a prayer at the Montevideo Cathedral.

Pope Leo will cover more than 20,000 miles on his sixth international tour.

On Sunday he will travel to Argentina, the homeland of his predecessor Pope Francis who did not return during his own papacy.

The Pope said his visit was about being near the people who were looking to the Church for a message of "hope".

World.title: The Atiku factor, By Wole Olaoye
World.content:
Former Vice-President Atiku Abubakar is still on the ballot, contrary to the supposed nullification of all of his party’s (ADC’s) 470 candidates in the 2027 elections by Justice Peter Lifu.

For almost 24 hours, his candidature seemed to have died; then, like the sphinx, it resurrected from the ashes of the nationwide controversy that greeted Justice Lifu’s judgement through the definitive pronouncement of retired veteran journalist and INEC’s Commissioner in charge of information, voter education and stakeholder engagement, Mohammed Kudu Haruna.

Not unexpectedly, conspiracy theorists took over the airwaves. They said the development was orchestrated by the ruling APC to prevent Atiku from trouncing President Tinubu at the polls. APC denies the charge and suggests that Atiku and his party are delusional.

Independent observers are asking, is there an Atiku factor in the forthcoming presidential elections?

Heavyweight

Anyone who denies Atiku’s political weight in contemporary Nigerian politics does not deserve to be taken seriously. A man who scored 6,984,520 against President Tinubu’s 8,794,726 cannot be considered a paperweight at all. With less than two million more votes in 2023, he could have dragged the contest to a runoff despite his trailing Tinubu in scoring 25% across two-thirds of Nigeria’s 36 states.

You don’t have to like Atiku to concede that he is tough meat. You won’t find me contesting for President at the age of 80, though.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

But some people were already calculating what could have been. If Atiku were technically disqualified from contesting the 2027 presidential election by the courts—whether through party leadership nullifications affecting his nomination ticket or constitutional eligibility rulings—there would have been political, electoral, and regional repercussions.

Atiku is indubitably a central gravitational force for opposition politics. His disqualification would have accelerated conversations around a unified opposition ticket under alternative figures such as Peter Obi, Rabiu Kwankwaso, or emerging northern leaders.

Without his name on the ballot, Atiku’s massive northern base would either have been split among other northern opposition figures, defected to local state-level structures, or resorted to apathy.

Were Atiku to exit the race, the ruling All Progressives Congress (APC) and President Bola Tinubu would face a significantly fractured opposition field. Historically, a divided opposition in Nigeria works in favour of the incumbent party by diluting the anti-incumbency vote across multiple candidates.

The hope among APC faithful would be to capture orphaned northern voters whose heavyweight candidate is no longer on the ballot. Anyone who has monitored how the ruling party opened its arms to opposition governors to the extent that the fractious opposition parties were reduced to screaming about an impending one-party state would know that a presidential contest without Atiku would throw open the political bazaar in the north. And there are no prizes for who the highest bidder would be.

APC, Beware!

However, the ruling party is best advised to be careful of what it wishes for. Already, opposition parties and civil society groups were saying that Justice Lifu must have been acting on a script authored by the APC. While there is no direct evidence to substantiate that allegation, a technical disqualification of Atiku could inflame public cynicism regarding judicial independence in election-related matters.

Without doubt, the removal of Atiku Abubakar from the 2027 presidential contest along with other candidates of ADC on account of a leadership tussle within the party will spell doom for the political organisation and its members.

But, wait. The way karmic forces coalesced in the 2026 US midterm elections was parabolic for many discerning people all over the world. Many who cast their ballot for the Democratic Party said they were actually voting against Mr Trump and his policies, which have had a cumulative effect of picking their pockets.

There are over 54 million registered voters in the North. If Atiku Abubakar is removed from the ballot, the North will experience a seismic shift.

The Northwest, with over 25 million votes, is the largest single electoral bloc. Rabiu Kwankwaso & NNPP did well there the last time. APC is also a strong force in the area. If there is no major northern candidate of the stature of Atiku in opposition, Rabiu Kwankwaso becomes the most prominent northerner on the ballot. Let no one be surprised if disillusioned northwest voters committed to ethno-religious sentiments rally around Kwankwaso.

That is not to say that APC wouldn’t have any cards to play in the circumstances. The ruling party would actively leverage incumbent APC governors in Sokoto, Kebbi, Jigawa, Kaduna, and Katsina to capture orphaned votes.

However, economic dissatisfaction across the region means these votes would not automatically transfer to the ruling party without significant local patronage and concessions.

In the Northeast, Atiku’s absence leaves a void that no single national candidate can inherit. In 2023, Atiku scored approximately 51.7 per cent (about 1.7 million votes) of the total votes cast in the zone. He won five out of the zone’s six states (Adamawa, Bauchi, Gombe, Taraba, and Yobe). He trailed only in Borno, Vice-President Shettima’s home state.

Some pundits say that if Atiku was not on the ballot, opposition votes could scatter toward an alternative opposition coalition (such as an Obi/Kwankwaso team), or the situation might induce lethargy.

Consolidation

By the same logic, Borno and Yobe would likely consolidate further under the APC, as Shettima would be the sole remaining high-profile standard-bearer from the sub-region on a major ticket.

Unlike the core Far-North, voters in states like Benue, Plateau, Nasarawa, Kogi, and Niger often vote on security concerns, religious balance, and local politics rather than so-called northern solidarity.

Voters in the Middle Belt who backed Atiku in the past because he was the face of opposition might shift toward Peter Obi or smaller entities like SDP. In spite of the security challenges and unwholesome economic situation, however, governors of APC-controlled states may pull all stops to ensure that they deliver their areas to President Tinubu and the APC.

Voter apathy is one of the other strategic outcomes that may attend the disqualification of Atiku. If northern voters feel disenfranchised by legal disqualifications of leading figures, overall voter turnout in traditional high-volume voting corridors could drop significantly.

Some northern political elites and traditional stakeholders read their own tarot differently. They would rather have a southern president through 2031 to maintain informal rotation of power between the North and the South. The only proviso is that the southern caucus assures them of a smooth transfer of power back to the North in 2031.

Even with legal harnesses threatening to rein in Atiku and his presidential dream, it appears that the ship of his candidacy has set sail, and there is no stopping it until it berths on 16 January, 2027.

And the common man who has suddenly become the beautiful bride in the ongoing political bazaar does not care whether it is the eagle or the kite that perches at the victory post on January 16. All he wants is a better tomorrow. And that can’t be too much to ask.

Wole Olaoye is a Public Relations consultant and veteran journalist. He can be reached on [email protected], Twitter: @wole_olaoye; Instagram: woleola2021

World.title: Atiku, Tinubu, Justice Lifu and death of “Àà tií gbó̩?”, By Festus Adedayo
World.content:
A man listened to the erratic command of his libido and slept with the daughter of his friend. In a twinkling of an eye, the act became public knowledge. The offender faced such immense social shame that one would think he had been isolated in the forest as lepers were in previous centuries. The circle of friends connecting him to the girl’s father ostracised him completely; he could not step out of his home. Wherever the scandal was discussed, the rhetorical phrase that sealed the conversation was a throwback to traditional Yoruba thought of “Àà tìí gbó̩?” It translates to mean, What will the world say?

That story is neither a fable of pre-modernity nor a Nollywood screenplay. It was an ad-lib from a live story shared recently by Africa’s foremost historian, Professor Toyin Falola. He did this during a public lecture organised by the Ibadan Social Group (ISG) on its 60th anniversary, a session I had the privilege of compering.

Most of the structural and moral crises we face as a nation and as individuals today, if broken down to their finest granules, stem from the complete collapse of “Àà tìí gbó̩?” The Igbo have their rendering of this concept; the Hausa have theirs.

Consider how Nigerian politicians lie without hesitation, how their promises lack ethical footing, or how they plunder the public till with brazen abandon. The EFCC Chairman recently revealed how an official deployed ₦29 billion earmarked for a power project to acquire personal real estate. He faces prosecution primarily because he falls on the wrong side of the political divide, while many who looted far more sums walk free. Why? They align with the prevailing establishment.

I have dwelt ad nauseam on the falsehoods routinely issued from Aso Rock as a metonymy for falsehoods from President Bola Tinubu. I have similarly refrained from focusing on Atiku Abubakar, persuaded that his presidency – God forbid – could never deliver the structural renewal Nigerians require. Meanwhile, public perception often paints Peter Obi’s narrative as equally questionable, indeed labeling him as living a life of lies.

Step away from politics onto the everyday social plane, and the retreat of moral hesitation is just as stark. Recently, a young man was captured on CCTV in Lagos bolting away from a bridal party’s suite at a hotel with a bag containing a laptop and valuables. Unbeknownst to him, his face – like that of the man who breached his friend’s fiduciary trust – has been broadcast throughout the world for public scorn, permanently tarnishing his family’s name. If the lives of these actors were governed by “Àà tìí gbó̩?”, none would have strayed so casually from the path of decency.

Falola invoked “Àà tìí gbó̩?” to address the flight of shame and honour from Nigeria’s social and political engagements. Deeply ingrained in the Yorùbá moral worldview, “Àà tìí gbó̩?” literally translates to an instinctual sense of shame. Among my people, “Àà tìí gbó̩?” is not interpreted merely as a negative emotion, nor is it a sign of personal weakness; it is a foundational ethical and social virtue which is also approximated as Ìtìjú. They both share same ethical foundation. What differentiates both Ìtìjú and “Àà tìí gbó̩?” is that they diverge sharply from the Western ethical tradition’s interpretation of shame. Unlike West’s reading where shame is frequently categorised as a destructive psychological state or a toxic vice, in Yorùbá ethics, Ìtìjú and “Àà tìí gbó̩?” function as active moral compass. They are sentries of conscience, self-restraint and modesty.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

When a social order is guided by these principles, actors remain conscious that no individual acts solely for themselves, but on behalf of the community. When you achieve genuine honour, you do so on behalf of the collective; when you commit an abomination, the community shares in the disgrace. This interconnectedness forces the individual to ask an existential question before taking action: “How does this choice affect my name, my lineage, and my community?” When a society abandons those two words, moral decay inevitably takes root.

This dynamic aligns with the insights of the late Ghanaian philosopher Kwasi Wiredu, who noted that traditional African ethics are humanistic and community-dependent: “Morality in traditional African societies is based on human interests, social harmony, and duty to community, where wrong actions are condemned because they tear the social fabric, not merely because they breach an abstract rule.”

Pardon my brief detour into philosophy; I was momentarily seized by the spirits of my teachers at the University of Lagos – Professors CS Momoh, Sophie Oluwole, TDP Bah, Kolawole Ogundowole, Jim Unah, and their peers. By the way, within the traditional Yoruba cognitive map of honour and shame, the man in Falola’s narrative who slept with his friend’s daughter ultimately took his own life. I will soon liken him to the Bariba ethnic group of Nigeria and Benin Republic.

Today, Nigerians across all strata proudly wear badges of dishonour without qualms. Leaders display it, the impoverished endure it, and the wealthy flaunt it. The executive manifests it, the judiciary mirrors it, and Senate President Godswill Akpabio epitomises legislative shamelessness at its peak. With the internment of Ìtìjú and “Àà tìí gbó̩?”, we are merely fiddling with the carcass of a country built on a compromised ethical foundation.

When Ìtìjú retreats, the social fabric breaks down irretrievably. Modern Nigerian political culture operates as an inversion of Wiredu’s ethos, relying on the death of public reproach. Reproach no longer deters our political actors; instead, shamelessness is treated as a strategic asset.

Look at recent developments in the judiciary, which recall the biblical narrative of Babel, where human hubris provoked divine intervention, resulting in linguistic and structural chaos. That account has it that God was so overtly provoked that His punishment was the confusion He threw into the speeches of builders of the Tower, leaving “Babel” to symbolise linguistic chaos.

Justice Peter Lifu of the Federal High Court in Abuja nullified the Senator David Mark-led National Working Committee (NWC) and Caretaker Committee of the African Democratic Congress (ADC). He cited violations of the party’s constitution, the Electoral Act, and the 1999 Constitution. This ruling effectively voided all congresses and primaries conducted under that leadership, including the 2027 presidential candidacy of Atiku Abubakar.

Yet, earlier on July 2, 2026, Justice Musa Liman of the same Federal High Court in Abuja (Suit No. FHC/ABJ/CS/1637/2025) had affirmed that exact same NWC. When two courts of coordinate jurisdiction issue diametrically opposed rulings on identical matters, the resulting judicial chaos is self-evident and Babelian.

While observers expressed concern over these conflicting directives, a Minister of the Federal Republic casually asserted that nothing would happen even if the ADC were excluded from the ballot. That statement echoes the rhetoric of Chief Remi Fani-Kayode, notoriously known as “Fani-Power” during the First Republic.

As Deputy Premier and Deputy Leader of the NNDP ahead of the October 11, 1965 Western Region elections, Fani-Kayode famously declared that even if citizens refused to vote for his party, it would still retain power. As recorded in Billy Dudley’s An Introduction to Nigerian Government and Politics (1982) and Bola Ige’s People, Politics and Politicians of Nigeria (1940–1979), Fani-Kayode, whom Ige labeled “the most fascist of them all,” boasted that “invisible bodies” would supply the necessary votes. After the compromised election, he declared: “A ti f’òjé b’olóòsà l’ówó, ó ku baba ẹni tí ó bóo!” meaning, “The bronze ring has been securely fitted to the High Priest’s finger; let anyone who dares attempt to remove it!”. The tone of modern political rhetoric from Minister Festus Keyamo remains strikingly similar.

Consider Justice Lifu’s controversial ruling alongside the revelations of retired Supreme Court Justice Uwani Musa Abba-Aji during her 70th-birthday valedictory session in Abuja last week. She disclosed that she was under EFCC investigation prior to her elevation to the apex court and noted that the United States had imposed a travel ban on a seven-member Supreme Court panel – which included herself, Chief Justice Kudirat Kekere-Ekun and former Chief Justice Ibrahim Tanko Muhammad, following the highly contested January 2020 judgment in the Imo State gubernatorial dispute between Hope Uzodimma and Emeka Ihedioha. When you see Uzodinma manifest the traits, for seven years of being in the saddle in Imo, of a home that is at peace as long as the illegitimate child within it is yet to attain the age of majority, you will see the cancerous, spiritual implications of handing over democratic power to an impostor.

These developments reflect a widespread perception, both locally and internationally, that the principles of Ìtìjú and “Àà tìí gbó̩?” have been functionally abandoned within critical state institutions. By the US slamming bans on the Justices, it tells you that the United States, too, like the narratives that are traded on the streets of Nigeria, believes that in Nigeria’s judiciary, the twin of Ìtìjú and “Àà tìí gbó̩?” are dead.

Just as the US believed that Nigeria’s Supreme Court Justices were everything but above board like Caesar’s wife, Nigerians also believe that in that Friday judgment, the voice was indeed Justice Lifu’s, but the hands were Aso Rock’s. Since the commencement of the 2027 elections, Aso Rock has demonstrated inexplicable dread for a free and fair elections. It has deployed frightening subterfuges that demonstrated its frown at electoral competition.

So when that ADC judgment came, Nigerians merely threw into the equation the Yoruba proverbial philosophy of “Àjé ké lánàá, omo kú l’ónìí“ – the witch owl bird cried/chirped yesterday and the child died today. To them, it is not non sequitur, nor is it devoid of logic. It reflects the people’s philosophy of indisputable cause and effect, also called the omen-and-proof. To them, some events, though circumstantial, not random coincidences, are however explicit warning or premonition of an impending tragedy. When political maneuvers align seamlessly with judicial outcomes, citizens view them not as coincidences, but as deliberate actions.

Governments and leaders in Nigeria repeatedly engage in actions devoid of Ìtìjú and “Àà tìí gbó̩?” because, as Toyin Falola argues in The Power of African Cultures (2022), contemporary African crises stem from a fundamental disconnect between modern state mechanics and the indigenous moral codes of pre-colonial societies. Submitting his thoughts on African cultural epistemologies, Falola emphasizes that the crisis of contemporary African governance is not merely structural or financial; it is an ethical rupture, a historical abandonment of indigenous codes that once rendered human dignity non-negotiable. As Wole Soyinka famously said that “the man dies in all who keep silent in the face of tyranny,” it may not be wrong to conclude that equitable governance collapses when moral accountability vanishes.

This collapse of moral restraint becomes obvious when contrasting democratic practices across jurisdictions. Where mature political systems rely on institutional self-correction and public accountability to address breaches of convention, Nigerian electoral politics remains largely unburdened by such restraint. Cash and patronage are openly distributed at polling units, and compromised officials announce results despite documented irregularities. Contemporary political actors show little concern for this ongoing moral regression.

Here, there is the death of what Yoruba again call àbùkù – translated to mean any of the words, stigma, disgrace, insult, embarrassment – and the triumph of impunity.

The Ghanaian philosopher Kwame Gyekye summarised this ethical imperative in his works on African communitarianism and political ethics: “A person is not merely a physical entity, but a moral agent whose actions must reflect an awareness of shared humanity. When a leader loses the capacity for moral self-restraint, they forfeit the philosophical right to lead.”

The Baatonu (Bariba) people, who share centuries of political, military, and cultural history with the Yoruba, historically maintained an uncompromising ethical code regarding personal honour. In her 1984 study, “Between Death and Shame: Dimensions of Pain in Bariba Culture” (published in Social Science & Medicine), anthropologist Carolyn Sargent documented an environment where personal integrity took precedence over survival. This worldview, she wrote, is expressed in the Bariba maxim: “Sekuru ka go go buram bo,” meaning, between death and shame, death possesses the greater beauty.

Though modernity is fast eroding this gallantry among the Bariba, Sargent wrote: “For a Bariba to display pain would indicate a lack of courage. Cowardice, in Bariba tradition, is the essence of shame (sekura) and rather than live in shame, a true Bariba would kill himself… The Bariba realise that life consists of many ordeals. The tests of life for a man are war, the burdens of his friends and relatives. and protecting the honor of his family.” When his honour evaporates, the Bariba takes his own life. It tells you how precious honour is to the Bariba.

For Nigeria’s leadership and citizenry alike, honour currently remains in abeyance. Yet, we must recognise that a society incapable of asking “Àà tìí gbó̩?” is a society moving toward structural decay. Formal laws, statutory constitutions and electoral amendments are necessary tools, but they are insufficient on their own. Without an underlying moral architecture that compels individuals to self-regulate, out of a commitment to personal integrity and a healthy fear of public disgrace, institutional rules will be continuously bypassed.

The ultimate imperative is the restoration of collective honour. In chants, songs and family praise names called oríkì, Lagosians mouth collective honour but seldom put it into practice. In traditional songs, they say, if Lagosians’ ancestral home, located at the back of Igbeti, which is the core, homeland foundation of Lagos, is not put to shame, Lagos, (Èkó) the metropolis, can never be disgraced. It is rendered as, “Bí ojú kò bá ti èyìn Ìgbètì, ojú kò le ti Èkó.”

This principle demands that a shared sense of honour must anchor both the leaders and the led. It forms the essential core of our common humanity. Only when that foundation is kept firm and untarnished can Nigeria stand upright without shame.

Festus Adedayo is an Ibadan-based journalist.

World.title: Decoupling Sovereignty Index (6): Recovery sequencing and the logic of sovereign re-coupling, By Max Amuchie
World.content:
A government can spend billions rebuilding a territory and still fail to restore its authority.

It can construct local government offices, rehabilitate schools, establish health facilities and introduce formal systems of taxation. It can deploy officials, launch livelihood programmes and announce the return of normal administration.

Yet if residents cannot travel safely along the roads connecting these facilities, if public officials cannot perform their duties without intimidation, and if armed organisations retain the capacity to extract revenue or punish cooperation with the state, the visible structures of recovery may conceal a deeper institutional weakness.

The buildings may stand. The programmes may be funded. The administrative procedures may exist.

But can the state sustain them?

This is the question addressed by the Recovery Sequencing Score, one of the two higher-order analytical scores within the Decoupling Sovereignty Index (DSI).

The first higher-order diagnostic, the Convergence Indicator, examines whether the forces of decoupling across Money, Land and Mind are becoming mutually reinforcing. The Recovery Sequencing Score turns to the other side of the problem: whether interventions intended to restore state authority are being pursued in an order capable of sustaining their results.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

Its central proposition is that the sequence of recovery matters.

A programme may have worthwhile objectives and adequate funding yet remain structurally vulnerable because it assumes that conditions exist when they do not. Where the state cannot provide sufficient protection or establish credible authority, the institutions it seeks to restore may be unable to function as intended.

The Recovery Sequencing Score is designed to make this vulnerability visible.

The Problem of Inverted Recovery

Development programmes often measure progress through outputs: facilities constructed, personnel trained, funds disbursed, beneficiaries reached or administrative procedures introduced.

Such measurements are useful. They establish whether planned activities have taken place.

But outputs are not the same as sustainable recovery.

A health centre may be completed without the staff being able to reach it safely. A local government office may reopen without having the practical authority to implement its decisions. A tax administration programme may formalise payments while residents remain exposed to parallel demands from armed groups.

In each case, the intervention may deliver its immediate output without establishing the conditions necessary for that output to produce a lasting institutional gain.

The problem is not that infrastructure, services or administrative reform are unimportant. They are essential components of effective governance.

The problem arises when institutional construction is mistaken for institutional functionality, or when the formal reappearance of the state is treated as proof that its authority has been restored.

The DSI describes this as an Inverted Sequence: an attempt to establish or consolidate institutional functions without adequately accounting for the prior conditions needed to sustain them.

The term is intended to draw attention to the structural vulnerability of recovery programmes that overlook the relationship between protection, compliance, territorial credibility and institutional function.

Consider a territory in which armed actors control important roads, intimidate traders and restrict access to agricultural land.

The government establishes a local administrative office and launches a programme to formalise commercial activity. Yet the armed actors retain the ability to block movement, impose illegal payments and threaten people who cooperate with public officials.

The state has reintroduced formal structures, but its capacity to protect the people and activities on which those structures depend remains compromised.

Resources may be wasted. Officials may be unable to operate consistently. Residents may be exposed to additional risks. The programme’s benefits may remain concentrated in locations where the state already exercises effective authority.

The resulting failure cannot necessarily be attributed to the programme’s objectives. It may arise from a mismatch between the sequence of intervention and the conditions prevailing in the territory.

The Recovery Sequencing Score is designed to assess that mismatch.

The Restoration Sequence: Protection, Compliance, Territorial Credibility, Institutional Function

The conceptual foundation of the Recovery Sequencing Score lies in the Trinity of Sovereignty Decay (TSD), which identifies a sequence connecting the restoration of effective authority to the conditions required for institutional performance.

The sequence is:

Protection → Compliance → Territorial Credibility → Institutional Function.

Each stage addresses a distinct requirement.

Protection establishes the physical conditions under which people can live, move, work and interact with public institutions without unacceptable exposure to violence or coercion. It also concerns the state’s capacity to protect public officials, infrastructure and essential economic activity.

Protection does not require the complete elimination of every security threat before any other activity can begin. It requires an adequate and contextually defined level of security for the activity being undertaken.

Compliance concerns the extent to which people and organisations comply with lawful public authority. Compliance may be encouraged by effective enforcement, but durable cooperation also depends on predictability, fairness and the credibility of state commitments.

Where residents expect that cooperation with public institutions will expose them to retaliation without protection, formal commands may produce little sustainable compliance.

Territorial credibility develops when the state’s authority becomes sufficiently consistent and dependable that residents and institutions can reasonably expect it to persist. A temporary security presence does not automatically establish such credibility. It must be supported by the demonstrated capacity to protect people, enforce lawful decisions and maintain access over time.

Institutional function refers to the capacity of public institutions to perform their intended responsibilities under these conditions. Administrative offices must be able to operate, officials must be able to perform their duties, and public services must be accessible and sustainable.

The sequence expresses a structural relationship: institutional functions are more likely to endure when the conditions required to support them have been established.

It does not mean that these stages are completely separate or that they always unfold in a rigid, one-directional progression. In practice, public services can strengthen compliance, fair administration can improve legitimacy, and effective institutions can reinforce protection.

Nor should the sequence be interpreted as a reason to postpone urgent humanitarian assistance until territorial control has been fully restored.

Its purpose is to identify dependencies that recovery programmes must recognise, not to impose an inflexible timetable on every intervention.

Why Protection Must Come First

Protection occupies the foundational position because other forms of recovery depend on the ability of people and institutions to operate within the territory.

Where armed actors control access routes, threaten residents or impose coercive restrictions, ordinary economic and administrative activity becomes difficult to sustain.

Farmers may be unable to reach their fields. Traders may avoid markets. Teachers and health workers may be unable to travel to their workplaces. Residents may decline to participate in public programmes because doing so exposes them to retaliation.

Under these conditions, the formal reintroduction of institutions does not automatically restore their practical reach.

The state must establish sufficient protection for people to resume activities and for public institutions to function. The requirements will vary by context: the security needed to reopen a school is not identical to that required to sustain a major transport corridor or a resource-processing facility.

The relevant question is whether protection is adequate for the specific functions the recovery programme seeks to establish.

This is why the DSI’s approach must be sensitive to territorial conditions rather than assume that a uniform security threshold applies everywhere.

The Recovery Sequencing Score is intended to assess whether those conditions have been adequately considered in the design and implementation of recovery efforts.

Compliance Is Not the Same as Submission

The second stage, compliance, requires particular care.

In territories where the state has lost effective authority, people may obey whichever actor possesses the capacity to punish disobedience. An armed organisation may impose rules, collect payments and regulate movement. Residents may comply because they fear retaliation or have no practical alternative.

Such behaviour demonstrates the exercise of coercive power. It does not necessarily demonstrate legitimacy.

The state’s objective should therefore not be to reproduce coercive compliance under a different flag. It should be to establish lawful, predictable and sufficiently credible authority that people can engage with public institutions without being exposed to unacceptable risks.

Protection can make such engagement possible. Fair and consistent administration can help sustain it. The repeated performance of public responsibilities can gradually strengthen expectations that state authority will remain effective.

The relationship is not automatic. Compliance depends on context, institutional conduct and the experiences of residents. Nevertheless, a recovery programme that overlooks the conditions under which people can safely cooperate with the state risks mistaking formal participation for a durable restoration of authority.

The Recovery Sequencing Score is intended to help analysts examine this distinction within the broader sequence of restoration.

Territorial Credibility and the Problem of Temporary Control

A security operation may displace an armed organisation from a particular location. But the restoration of territorial credibility requires more than a temporary change in who occupies that location.

Can residents travel safely after the operation? Can farmers return to their land? Can public officials remain in place? Can the state protect people who cooperate with it? Can commercial activity resume without being subjected to renewed coercion?

These questions concern the durability of state authority.

Where a government repeatedly enters a territory and then withdraws, leaving residents exposed to retaliation, the practical credibility of its commitments may weaken. People may become reluctant to cooperate with officials because they expect the state’s presence to be temporary.

By contrast, when protection and lawful public authority are sustained over time, residents have stronger grounds for expecting that the state will continue to perform its responsibilities.

Territorial credibility is therefore not merely a question of physical presence. It concerns the demonstrated reliability of public authority.

For the DSI, the distinction is crucial. A snapshot of territorial control may not reveal whether the state can sustain that control or whether the conditions supporting recovery remain fragile.

The Recovery Sequencing Score is intended to encourage an assessment of these underlying dependencies rather than rely solely on the visible presence of government institutions.

Institutional Function as an Outcome of Sustainable Restoration

The final stage is institutional function.

Public institutions are essential to the exercise of effective sovereignty. They administer justice, provide services, regulate economic activity and organise the relationship between the state and its population.

But institutions do not function in isolation from the territories in which they operate.

An administrative office cannot exercise meaningful authority if its officials are unable to travel safely or enforce lawful decisions. A school cannot deliver sustained educational services if teachers cannot reach it or families cannot send their children safely. A public revenue system cannot operate fairly and effectively where residents are subjected to competing demands from armed organisations.

The question is not simply whether institutions exist, but whether they can perform their functions consistently.

The restoration sequence places institutional function at the point where protection, compliance and territorial credibility provide the conditions for public authority to operate more sustainably.

This does not diminish the importance of institution-building. It clarifies the conditions under which institution-building is more likely to produce durable results.

The state must ultimately restore functioning institutions. But the institutional architecture cannot substitute for the protection and credible authority on which its effective operation depends.

What the Recovery Sequencing Score Measures

The Recovery Sequencing Score is designed to assess whether a recovery programme is being built on a sustainable foundation or is structurally vulnerable to relapse.

This is different from measuring whether recovery has already occurred.

A programme may produce immediate gains while remaining exposed to the return of coercive control, renewed territorial insecurity or the collapse of local administrative functions.

The score’s purpose is to examine whether the pathway of intervention adequately addresses the dependencies between protection, compliance, territorial credibility and institutional function.

In practical terms, it is intended to help analysts identify situations in which governments or development agencies are investing in institutional functions without sufficient attention to the conditions needed to sustain them.

The score should not be interpreted as a guarantee that an intervention will succeed or fail. Outcomes are influenced by many factors, including political decisions, local conditions, external support and the behaviour of armed actors.

Its proposed contribution is narrower but significant: to make the structural logic of recovery an explicit subject of assessment.

A rigorous implementation will require transparent scoring rules, operational definitions for each stage, evidence requirements and guidance for dealing with situations in which stages overlap or develop unevenly.

Those specifications are essential if the score is to be applied consistently by different researchers and practitioners.

From the Diagnosis of Decoupling to the Sequencing of Recovery

Beyond its 19 universal indicators and two higher-order diagnostic scores, the DSI incorporates a Resource Capture Module to examine how resource extraction, processing and trafficking sustain shadow authority by connecting economic power to territorial control.

Documented in the forthcoming DSI Methodology and Indicator Manual, the module extends the framework’s application to resource-driven systems of decoupling.

Together, the Convergence Indicator, Recovery Sequencing Score and Resource Capture Module deepen the DSI’s diagnostic and analytical capacity, linking the assessment of decoupling to the sequencing of recovery. Ultimately, restoring sovereignty requires more than rebuilding institutions; it requires restoring their capacity to protect people, exercise lawful authority and perform their responsibilities. When recovery is wrongly sequenced, institutions may be rebuilt without restoring state authority.

From the Desk to the World

Max Nwabueze Amuchie is a scholar-journalist, media CEO and founder and curator of Sundiata Post Research Repositories (Harvard Dataverse & CERN-Zenodo). He is an Expert Member and Peer Reviewer, Behavioural Sciences at ScienceOpen. Email: [email protected]. X: @MaxAmuchie

World.title: Lagos police ask political parties to notify command ahead of 2027 rallies
World.content:
The Lagos State Police Command has asked political parties to send it notice ahead of rallies, campaigns, processions and other political gatherings as preparations for the 2027 general elections gather pace.

The Commissioner of Police, Tijani Fatai, said the notice would enable the command to make security arrangements and deploy personnel to cover the events.

Mr Fatai made the appeal in a statement shared on X on Sunday by the police spokesperson, Abimbola Adebisi.

He stated that the command would provide security for all political parties, candidates and their supporters without discrimination. He, however, warned that activities capable of disrupting public peace would not be tolerated.

The commissioner said parties that failed to notify the police or disregarded security arrangements, resulting in a breach of peace, would be held accountable under the law.

He also referred to a security meeting held on 15 October ahead of the elections, where political parties and other stakeholders were urged to cooperate with security agencies and comply with security guidelines.

The police’s appeal comes against the backdrop of their statutory responsibility to provide security for political activities. Section 91 of the Electoral Act 2022 requires the police to provide adequate security for the peaceful conduct of rallies and processions.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

READ ALSO: Lagos police foil plot to traffic Kaduna girls to Ivory Coast

It also protects the right of registered political parties, aspirants and candidates to hold lawful rallies.

Mr Fatai urged political parties to cooperate with the command to ensure that political activities across the state were conducted peacefully.

The notice, as framed by the police command, is not a request for permission to conduct political activities.

The position of the law based on subsisting court judgements is that police permits are not required to hold such political activities or organise protests.

World.title: Abiodun commends DSS, Police for rescuing kidnap victims, vows Ogun won’t be criminals’ safe haven
World.content:
Ogun State Governor, Prince Dapo Abiodun, has commended the Director-General of the Department of State Services (DSS), Mr Oluwatosin Adeola Ajayi and the Inspector-General of Police, Olatunji Rilwan Disu, for their roles in the safe rescue of 10 passengers abducted from a commercial vehicle around Orita Fufu, Awa-Ijebu, in Ijebu North-East Local Government Area of the state.

Abiodun particularly applauded the DSS Director-General for providing critical intelligence and sophisticated security equipment that aided the tracking of the kidnappers and facilitated the rescue operation.

He also commended the Inspector-General of Police for his prompt directives and intervention, which galvanised the Ogun State Police Command and other security operatives into action, culminating in the release of the victims unharmed.

The governor, in a statement, declared that his administration would not allow kidnappers and other criminal elements to turn any part of the state into a safe haven, assuring residents that the government was intensifying efforts to ensure that criminals had no place in Ogun.

He warned that those who threatened the security of residents and commuters would be relentlessly pursued until they were brought to justice. He also urged residents to support security agencies by providing timely and credible information about suspicious persons, movements and activities in their communities.

Abiodun reiterated his administration’s commitment to strengthening collaboration with security agencies and providing the necessary support to protect lives and property across the state.

He called on residents to remain vigilant and cooperate with security operatives, stressing that collective action and prompt information-sharing were essential to preventing crime and maintaining peace in Ogun State.
