World.title: Law marker calls for cancer screening
World.content:
Lima Constituency Member of Parliament Kelvin Kunda has called on Zambians to prioritise regular cancer screening, warning that late detection continues to contribute to cancer-related deaths.

Mr Kunda has said that early detection remains critical in improving treatment outcomes urging members of the public not to wait until they experience symptoms before seeking screening services.

Speaking during the Rotary Club of Maluba’s Free Annual Cancer Screening event at Twikatane Mall in Barlastone Park in Lusaka today, Mr Kunda said cancer is a major health concern requiring collective efforts from Government, the private sector and communities.

He cited estimates from the International Agency for Research on Cancer indicating that approximately 16,600 Zambians are diagnosed with cancer annually, while nearly 9,800 die from the disease.

Mr Kunda mentioned that many people continue to lose their lives because cancer is detected at advanced stages when treatment is more difficult and costly.

“Not knowing does not protect you. Knowing does,” he said, urging people to overcome fear, stigma and misconceptions surrounding cancer screening,” he said.

He said early detection improves chances of successful treatment, reduces the financial burden on families and helps to prevent some cancers, particularly through screening for cervical cancer.

Mr Kunda has commended the Rotary Club of Maluba for sustaining its free cancer screening and awareness initiative for 22 years, noting that about 4,400 people have been educated on cancer prevention and have been screened through the programme.

He has called for more partnerships to expand access to screening services, particularly in underserved communities calling on churches, community health volunteers and other local groups to promote awareness.

Meanwhile, Rotary Club of Maluba President Chanja Makai said the club is targeting to screen 700 people during this year’s initiative.

Ms Makai said the annual programme has been running for 22 years, with prostate and breast cancer screening introduced alongside cervical cancer screening as the initiative expanded.

She said the services are being provided free of charge in partnership with health professionals from Kanyama Level One Hospital and CDH, with screening available for breast, cervical and prostate cancer.

“We are hoping to capture about 300 men and 400 women. So men will be testing for both prostate and breast cancer,” she said.

Ms Makai has encouraged members of the public to attend with their families, adding that screening is quick and can help detect cancer even among people who are not experiencing symptoms.

She said the club has also heard testimonies from cancer survivors who have lived cancer-free for several years after diagnosis and treatment, demonstrating the importance of early detection.

And Synergy Seeds Zambia Chief Executive Officer Brian Mhango said the company is proud to partner with the Rotary Club of Maluba and other stakeholders in making cancer screening services accessible to communities.

Mr Mhango said the initiative reflects the importance of promoting good health as a foundation for strong families, productive workplaces and thriving communities.

“Early detection saves lives, and screening is one of the most important steps we can take towards protecting our health,” he said.

He has urged members of the public not to wait until they feel unwell before taking their health seriously.

World.title: 2027 budget to be judged by results-Nkoma
World.content:
Government said the 2027 National Budget will be measured by results and not pronouncements.

Minister of Industry Noel Nkoma said the Budget will be judged by the businesses that grow the investments and materialise jobs among others.

He was speaking at the Zambia Institute of Chartered Accountants (ZICA) 2027 Post-Budget Analysis Dinner in Lusaka.

Mr Nkoma said the National Budget is the Government’s most powerful tool for driving national development, as it reflects Government’s priorities, aspirations and policy direction.

He said the 2027 Budget comes at a pivotal moment in Zambia’s economic transformation journey and has been crafted around the Grow Zambia Agenda.

He said the agenda seeks to stimulate economic expansion, support enterprise development, create jobs, increase productivity, attract investment and improve the quality of life for all citizens.

The Minister added that it was fitting for stakeholders to gather after the presentation of the Budget to analyse its provisions and understand its implications for the Grow Zambia Agenda.

He said the budget process is strengthened by stakeholder participation both before and after the Budget is presented.

“Before formulation, Government undertakes extensive consultations with business associations, professional bodies, civil society, academia and other key stakeholders to ensure the Budget reflects the realities of the economy and responds to the needs of citizens and industry,” he said

Mr Nkoma said discussions at forums such as the ZICA dinner help businesses understand emerging opportunities, enable investors to assess likely economic trends and allow stakeholders to align their plans with national development priorities.

He said such engagements strengthen collaboration between Government and the private sector, which remains a critical pillar of Zambia’s economic transformation agenda.

The Minister said the Government recognises that sustainable economic growth cannot be achieved through public sector interventions alone, but requires a vibrant and competitive private sector capable of investing, innovating, producing and creating employment.

He said the Budget therefore seeks to empower businesses, improve the operating environment and unlock opportunities for entrepreneurship and industrial development.

ZICA President Joseph Matimba, stated that the Budget comes at an important time as Zambia seeks to consolidate macroeconomic stability while accelerating growth, stimulating investment and addressing the challenges facing people.

He named the cost of living, unemployment, poverty, energy security and low productivity as critical areas requiring sustained attention.

“The National Budget must therefore be assessed not only in terms of fiscal allocations and policy measures, but also in terms of its ability to stimulate productive economic activity, support enterprise development and improve the livelihoods of ordinary Zambians,” Mr Matimba said.

He said the industrial sector has a particularly important role to play, noting that a stronger manufacturing base, increased local production and greater value addition are essential to creating jobs, reducing dependence on imports and strengthening Zambia’s competitiveness in regional and international markets.

Mr Matimba said the Budget must also be viewed within the Government’s Grow Zambia Agenda, which seeks to accelerate economic transformation and create inclusive growth through expanding production and investment in agriculture, mining, energy, manufacturing and tourism.

Meanwhile, ZICA Chief Executive Officer, Anthony Bwembya, said that the National Budget is more than a statement of Government’s revenue and expenditure priorities, but reflects national aspirations and provides a framework for stimulating investment, supporting industrial development, creating employment and improving livelihoods.

“Through sound financial management, transparency, accountability and professional advice, our members contribute to strengthening public financial management, supporting business growth and building confidence in our economy,” Mr Bwembya said.

World.title: Mundubile, Makebi Zulu Wait On Tuesday Ruling After 70 Days In Mukobeko
World.content:
Mundubile Bail Fate Rests On Tuesday Ruling As Tonse Condemns 70-Day Detention

The High Court will rule on Tuesday, 10 November, on whether Brian Mundubile and 17 others can proceed with their bid for constitutional bail. The State has asked the court to throw out the application on a technicality, arguing that it was filed in the wrong form. Opposition leaders are describing the prolonged detention as cruel and illegal.

A panel led by Mr Justice Mulenga reserved its ruling after hearing arguments in chambers on a preliminary issue raised by the State. Mr Mundubile is the losing presidential candidate of the National Reconciliation Party for Unity and Prosperity (NRPUP). He is joined in the application by his former running mate Makebi Zulu, Lusaka business executive Harry Findlay and 15 others. The group sued the State alleging gross violations of their constitutional rights. They then applied for constitutional bail, asking to be released either unconditionally or on reasonable conditions set by the court.

Attorney General Mulilo Kabesha, State Counsel, raised the preliminary issue. He urged the court to dismiss the bail application on the grounds that it had been wrongly commenced as a civil application instead of a criminal one. The State’s position is that the form of the filing goes to the heart of the court’s authority to hear the matter at all.

Acting Chief State Advocate Chibesa Mulonda developed that argument on behalf of the State. He submitted that the court could not grant constitutional bail when the application had been brought in civil rather than criminal format. He contended that, in those circumstances, the court had no jurisdiction to hear the application.

The defence pushed back hard. Lawyers for Mr Mundubile and the 17 others include three State Counsel: Bonaventure Mutale, Chifumu Banda and Sakwiba Sikota. They urged the court to reject the objection, sustain the application and hear it on its merits. The State maintained its position that the application should be dismissed for being irregularly filed.

The ruling leaves two possible paths. Mr Justice Mulenga said that if the preliminary issue did not succeed, the court would proceed straight to the substantive bail hearing on the same day. A ruling in the State’s favour would end the application in its current form and send the detainees’ lawyers back to refile.

Outside the courtroom, the opposition has escalated its language. Tonse-Pamodzi Alliance secretary general Muhabi Lungu said the continued incarceration of Mr Mundubile, Mr Zulu and the others at Mukobeko Maximum Prison for more than 70 days, without a plea before a High Court judge, was cruel. In a television interview, he said the detention was illegal because the country was not under a state of emergency.

“It’s not right and fair to charge Brian Mundubile, Makebi Zulu and 17 others and keep them in prison for 70 days without a plea before a judge. It’s not right; it’s illegal. We are not under a state of emergency. 70 days is not 48 hours, especially when the state says it has been probing this case for the last three years ahead of the arrest,” Mr Lungu said.

Mr Lungu accused the State of dragging its feet in the treason matter while the accused remained behind bars. He framed the choice facing prosecutors in stark terms: prove the case or free the accused.

“You can clearly see the State is dragging its feet in the treason matter while our leaders suffer. If you don’t have evidence, let them go, release them. If you have evidence, let the trial start and do it expeditiously so that the whole world sees what you accused them for,” he said.

The Tonse official went further and described the detention as an abuse of state power. In his view, it was aimed at punishing dissent rather than delivering justice. He said the opposition’s reading was that the Government wanted to demonstrate its power to punish.

“Our speculation is that government just wants to show that it can punish you, that abuse, that dictatorship, its cruelty, it’s not governance,” Mr Lungu said.

He tied the case to the final report of the European Union (EU) election observer mission, which he said confirmed that Zambia’s democratic space was shrinking. Mr Lungu said the mission was correct that the boundaries between the Electoral Commission of Zambia (ECZ) and the police had been unclear during the election. He cited uneven policing, misuse of public resources and questions over the independence of the electoral body. He added that former Botswana president Ian Khama and other outside observers had issued similar warnings.

“It’s wrong to jail people arbitrarily and then question why international observers say there’s shrinking democracy,” Mr Lungu said. “The police act selectively in Zambia under this government, one rule for those that support the government of the UPND, another that restricts those that have divergent views.”

The alliance is also demanding that the treason trial be opened to live coverage. Mr Lungu said past treason trials involving army generals, such as the late Christon Tembo, were covered openly. He said the present case should be held to the same standard.

“Here we are with a treason trial of civilians, namely Brian Mundubile; our leaders, including the media, are barred from covering the proceedings. Give us live coverage,” he said.

Access to the court itself has become a point of friction. Green Party leader Peter Sinkamba said blocking the Lusaka High Court premises had become a culture under the United Party for National Development (UPND) government whenever there was a case involving Mr Mundubile. Mr Sinkamba said he had gone to the court to file documents but met obstruction from police officers manning the premises during the bail hearing.

Tuesday’s ruling now carries weight well beyond the 18 applicants. If the court upholds the State’s objection, the detainees face further delay while the application is refiled. If it rejects the objection, the court will move straight to whether Mr Mundubile, Mr Zulu and the others should be released while their case proceeds. Either way, the decision will shape the course of the most closely watched prosecution of the post-election period

World.title: Here Is Who Pays More Under Zambia’s 2027 Budget Tax Measures
World.content:
High earners, small companies, mobile money users and mining shareholders face a heavier tax load from January 2027. Finance and National Planning Minister Dr Situmbeko Musokotwane has proposed a package of revenue measures expected to raise an extra K10.8 billion. The package raises Value Added Tax (VAT) to 16.5 per cent from 16 per cent and adds a new top Pay As You Earn (PAYE) rate of 39.5 per cent. It also lifts corporate income tax on lower-rated income, increases the mobile money levy across all bands and sharply raises duties on plastics.

Dr Musokotwane set out the measures when he presented the K284.8 billion 2027 National Budget to Parliament. He said the successful implementation of the Grow Zambia Agenda required strong, sustainable and predictable domestic revenue. The proposals, he said, would balance support for productive economic activity with the need for individuals and businesses to contribute fairly to national development. The measures would take effect on January 1, 2027.

The new PAYE band is aimed at the top of the income ladder. Individuals earning more than K37,000 a month will pay a top marginal rate of 39.5 per cent on the portion of income above that line. Dr Musokotwane moved to reassure most salaried workers that their payslips would not change under the measure.

“In simple terms, those earning K37,000 per month and below will continue to be taxed under the current regime and will therefore not be affected by this measure. Only the additional income above K37,000 per month will be taxed at 39.5 per cent,” Dr Musokotwane said.

Companies will also pay more. The corporate income tax rate will rise by five percentage points on income currently taxed at 20 per cent and below. VAT moves to 16.5 per cent, which the minister described as part of the Government’s commitment to strengthen domestic revenue mobilisation. Because VAT applies to most goods and services, it will touch nearly every household budget.

Mobile money users will reach deeper into their wallets. The minister proposed to increase the mobile money levy across all bands, so every transaction tier will cost more. For the millions of Zambians who send, receive and save money on their phones, this is likely to be the measure they feel most often.

The mining sector faces a new set of charges. Dr Musokotwane proposed to raise withholding tax on dividends paid by mining companies to 15 per cent from zero, and to introduce a five per cent export duty on zinc concentrates. Mining, mineral processing and exploration licence fees, area charges and related fees will also rise. He said this would align Zambia’s licensing regime with international good practice.

Plastics are the target of the steepest increases in the package. Customs duty on single-use plastics will double to 200 per cent from 100 per cent. An additional duty of K8 per bottle will be introduced on plastic bottles, and the extra duty on selected plastic articles will rise to 30 per cent from 15 per cent. The measures are framed as part of the Government’s environmental sustainability agenda.

A cluster of import duties is designed to shield local industry. Customs duty on imported ceramic tiles will rise to 40 per cent from 25 per cent. Selected imported aluminium bars, rods and profiles will attract a 20 per cent selected goods sales tax and 25 per cent customs duty. The selected goods sales tax on imported meat, including beef, sheep and goat meat, will rise to 30 per cent from 20 per cent.

Shoppers will also see the effect on cooking oil and packaging. Crude soya bean and sunflower oils will attract 15 per cent customs duty and a 10 per cent selected goods sales tax to encourage local production. The selected goods sales tax on imported cement packaging and woven bags will be harmonised at 30 per cent. The minister also proposed ending the customs duty exemption and VAT zero-rating on energy-saving appliances. Second-hand clothing and handbags will be excluded from the duty relief given to approved public benefit organisations.

The package is not all tightening. Dr Musokotwane proposed a 100 per cent customs duty suspension and a VAT exemption on imported raw materials used to manufacture sanitary products locally. Customs duty will also be suspended on safari vehicles, hospitality equipment and communications infrastructure. That relief supports the target of five million international tourist arrivals under President Hakainde Hichilema’s Grow Zambia Agenda.

Small-scale gold miners received a direct incentive to trade through official channels. The minister proposed to cut mineral royalty for artisanal and small-scale miners who sell to Government-approved aggregators to three per cent from six per cent. The measure is meant to pull a largely informal trade into the tax net. It sits alongside plans for a state gold trading agency to aggregate production.

Businesses that report losses year after year will face a narrower minimum alternative tax. Dr Musokotwane said the regime would apply only where a business recorded losses for three consecutive years.

“This will ensure that only businesses with a persistent pattern of loss declaration are brought into the alternative tax net while allowing businesses facing recurring downturns to recover and return to profitability,” Dr Musokotwane said.

The tax drive supports a budget that leans more heavily than ever on money raised at home. Domestic revenues of K233.7 billion will fund 82.1 per cent of spending, up from 58.7 per cent in 2021 and 76 per cent in 2024. Borrowing will account for K41.9 billion and grants from cooperating partners for K9.2 billion. The minister was blunt about the reasoning.

“There are no donors to pay, we must pay ourselves,” Dr Musokotwane said.

Debt remains a heavy claim on that revenue. The Treasury has set aside K67.6 billion for debt service in 2027, made up of K50.8 billion for domestic debt and K16.8 billion for external debt. Debt service sits within K90.5 billion, or 31.8 per cent of the budget, allocated to general public services.

Early reaction from economic and business voices was broadly positive. International Monetary Fund (IMF) Resident Representative for Zambia Dr Reginald Darius described the budget as growth-oriented and said revenue mobilisation would be critical to preserving fiscal stability and debt sustainability. Zambia Association of Manufacturers president Ashu Sagar said the increase in certain taxes was a move to support the social sector. Zambia Chamber of Commerce and Industry (ZACCI) chief executive officer Emmanuel Mumba said the incentives for manufacturing were a plus for local value addition.

To give effect to the measures, Dr Musokotwane proposed amendments to the Income Tax Act, the Customs and Excise Act and the Value Added Tax Act, among other laws. Parliament will now debate the proposals before they take effect in the new year.

World.title: Africa: CANEX WKND 2026 Showcases Africa's Creative Brilliance in a Night of Fashion and Awards
World.content:
Glitz, glamour and a vibrant celebration of African creativity took centre stage at the CANEX WKND 2026 fashion show in Lagos, Nigeria.

Designers from across the continent brought their unique interpretations of African fashion to the runway.

Held under the theme “One People, United in Culture, Creating for the World,” the evening celebrated the richness and diversity of Africa’s creative industries. It showcased an impressive blend of contemporary designs, traditional craftsmanship, cultural heritage and innovative fashion.

The runway featured collections reflecting Africa’s evolving fashion identity, with designers demonstrating the continent’s growing influence in global style and the creative economy.

From music performances accompanying the models to bold silhouettes, intricate detailing and contemporary interpretations of traditional African textiles, the presentation highlighted the talent, originality and entrepreneurial spirit driving the continent’s fashion industry.

Canex Nigeria's Federal Minister of Industry, Trade and Investment (FMITI), Dr Jumoke Oduwole at the CANEX WKND fashion show.

The event was attended by Nigeria’s Minister of Industry, Trade and Investment, Dr Jumoke Oduwole. Her presence underscored the importance of the creative economy in advancing Africa’s industrial development, trade and economic diversification.

Canex A night of celebrations at the CANEX WKND fashion show and awards ceremony.

Beyond fashion, the evening brought together Africa’s wider creative community, with awards recognising outstanding contributions across the film, publishing and gastronomy industries. The celebrations highlighted the interconnectedness of Africa’s cultural sectors and their growing potential to create employment, stimulate investment and strengthen the continent’s presence in international markets.

The showcase also reflected the broader vision of the Creative Africa Nexus (CANEX), an initiative established by the African Export-Import Bank (Afreximbank) to support and scale the continent’s creative and cultural industries.

Canex African designers showcased some of their colourful pieces during CANEX WKND in Lagos, Nigeria.

Afreximbank has committed US$2 billion in financing between 2024 and 2027, quadrupling its original US$500 million commitment announced in 2020. The bank expanded its financing in response to growing demand for investment across Africa’s creative ecosystem, spanning music, film, fashion, sport, publishing and gastronomy. The 2024 edition of CANEX WKND, held in Algiers, attracted participants from 81 countries.

Through its investment in creative enterprises, market access and international partnerships, CANEX seeks to transform Africa’s cultural wealth into sustainable economic opportunities, while enabling local creators to compete on the global stage.

World.title: Africa: CANEX Opens Doors for Gambian Fashion Entrepreneurs Seeking Global Recognition
World.content:
For Gambian fashion entrepreneur Ndey Bassin Faye, building an internationally recognised brand begins with empowering women, celebrating local culture, and embracing African-made textiles. At CANEX WKND 2026 in Lagos, she and fellow entrepreneurs are looking beyond borders to build connections that could help transform their businesses and the continent's fashion industry.

When Ndey Bassin Faye discusses her fashion brand's global expansion, she also refers to promoting Gambian culture internationally.

The founder of Bassin's Couture, established in 2016, is one of three Gambian fashion and tailoring entrepreneurs, Mariama Jallow, Ndey Bassin, and Ida, attending the Creative Africa Nexus Weekend (CANEX WKND) 2026 in Lagos, Nigeria.Their attendance is sponsored by the Andandorr programme, with support from EU YEP – Tourism and Creative Industries.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

For entrepreneurs, the four-day gathering is more than an opportunity to showcase their work. It is a chance to meet potential partners, connect with suppliers, learn from industry experts, and explore new markets for their businesses.

At the heart of Faye's work is a commitment to women and girls. Through Bassin's Couture, she uses fashion not only as a business opportunity but also as a means of empowering women to pursue entrepreneurship while promoting Gambian culture through design.

Like many African fashion entrepreneurs, she faces challenges that extend beyond creativity and craftsmanship. One of the biggest obstacles is accessing materials.

"One of the challenges we face is the difficulty of sourcing diverse fabrics, particularly those outside of Gambian culture," says Faye.

She highlights the challenges of sourcing materials from other African countries, noting that, in some instances, it is easier to access supplies from Europe and China than from within the continent.

While the continent is home to rich textile traditions, cotton-producing countries, and a growing community of designers, connecting the different parts of the value chain remains difficult.

For Faye and her partners, CANEX offers an opportunity to help bridge some of those gaps. She hopes to use the gathering to establish relationships with suppliers, meet fellow designers, and explore collaborations that could strengthen her business and expand its reach.

"I want us to go international. I want our brand to be seen and to be known internationally," she says.

She also wishes to see more African materials incorporated into African fashion.

The Gambia has a tradition of handweaving, and Faye is proud to work with locally grown cotton. By incorporating hand-woven fabrics into her designs, she is taking practical steps towards building a fashion business that promotes local resources while celebrating the country's cultural identity.

Building a fashion industry that supports African designers

The challenges facing entrepreneurs such as Faye are part of the bigger conversations at CANEX, particularly during different masterclasses offered by experts in the textile industry. In a masterclass about how African fashion businesses could strengthen their marketing management and expand into global markets, luxury brand consultant Anita Ehui highlighted the structural difficulties that continue to affect African fashion businesses, particularly in manufacturing, textiles, sourcing, quality control, and pricing.

"I think we have a big manufacturing problem, whether in textiles or production itself, and that makes things difficult," Ehui said.

She explained that while many designers aspire to manufacture their products entirely on the continent, achieving this can be challenging due to limitations in material availability, production capacity, and quality.

Designers are often forced to make compromises, whether on quality, pricing, or design, because the necessary resources and infrastructure are not always readily available. Ehui encouraged entrepreneurs to prioritise African sourcing and production wherever possible, arguing that increasing demand for locally manufactured products could help strengthen the continent's manufacturing ecosystem.

However, she also cautioned against some common mistakes made by emerging fashion businesses.

One common mistake is overcomplicating business decisions, such as designing and selling products based solely on personal preferences rather than genuine customer demand.

For African fashion businesses aiming for growth, identifying the correct market is crucial. Instead of trying to appeal to everyone, entrepreneurs should understand their target customers, their desires, and the most effective ways to communicate the value of their products.

She highlighted how CANEX provides an important platform for designers to connect with potential customers and fosters conversations that can lead to partnerships and new ideas.

"CANEX is giving fashion designers a platform. It is also connecting some of the brands with customers," she stated.

She added that gatherings like CANEX create opportunities for collaboration, knowledge-sharing, and has potential to expose creators to new perspectives.

"When we gather at CANEX, there is always a conversation that can spark a collaboration or even open your mind to something new," she said.

Close 

From Local to Global Markets

For the three Gambian entrepreneurs, these conversations are particularly important as they plan the next phase of their businesses. Access to industry experts through masterclasses, exposure to other African brands and suppliers, and opportunities to engage with potential business partners offer valuable insights into building sustainable fashion enterprises.

Organised by the African Export-Import Bank (Afreximbank) and hosted by the Federal Government of Nigeria, CANEX WKND brings together leading African and diaspora creatives, investors, and policymakers from various sectors including music, film, fashion, sport, publishing, gastronomy, and visual arts.

The four-day event is designed to facilitate partnerships, encourage investment, and expand access to international markets for Africa's creative industries.

For Faye, the journey towards that future is already underway. The vision is to reach international markets without losing the local identity that makes the brand distinctive. Faye and Ehui agree that African fashion can compete globally, but the continent must first make it easier for African creatives to work, source, produce, and grow together.

World.title: Africa: CANEX Aims to Empower African Creatives to Compete in Global Markets and Drive Economic Growth
World.content:
CANEX WKND 2026 opens in Lagos, Nigeria, an initiative of the Afreximbank aimed at boosting creatives from across the African continent.

Creatives from across the continent are gathering in Lagos, Nigeria, for the Creative Africa Nexus (CANEX). This initiative brings together Africa's creative talent, investors, policymakers, and industry leaders to unlock the economic potential of the continent's cultural industries.

Dubbed CANEX WKND, the four-day event attracted more than 15,000 registrations from across the global creative community, under the theme "One People, United in Culture, Creating for the World."

Hosted by the Federal Government of Nigeria and organised by the African Export-Import Bank (Afreximbank) through its Creative Africa Nexus programme, the event runs from 5 to 8 November. It aims to transform Africa's growing cultural influence into sustainable businesses, increased trade, investment, and employment opportunities.



"CANEX was established to offer a comprehensive suite of solutions aimed at developing the capacity of Africa's creators and enhancing the value retained within the continent, through CANEX finance," said Dr George Elombi, President and Chairman of the Board of Directors of Afreximbank.

From film and television to music, fashion, publishing, sport, gastronomy, and visual arts, CANEX WKND is positioning the creative economy as an increasingly important contributor to Africa's economic transformation.

For a continent with the world's youngest population, the creative industries offer significant opportunities to harness the talents, innovation, and entrepreneurial ambitions of young people. However, translating this potential into sustainable livelihoods requires more than talent and international recognition. It requires access to finance, skills development, markets, technology, and the commercial infrastructure necessary to build viable businesses.

This is the gap Afreximbank's CANEX initiative seeks to address.

The bank recognises that financing is not the industry's only challenge; a holistic approach is needed for the industry to thrive.

"We can put financing skills into music and movie productions, yet the value we derive could still be low. We must, therefore, focus on building the creative ecosystem, focusing not just on idea generation, creation, and production, but particularly on value capture from those activities that we now know attract the greatest value. These include vending and production, and CANEX was created for that purpose," said Elombi.

He noted that the budget has increased significantly since CANEX started to meet the needs and demands.

"When CANEX began, we had a budget of U. S$500 million for the creative economy. We soon found out that it was too small, so we raised it to U.S. $ 1 billion, and that was also too small. In 2024, we raised it to U.S.$2 billion," he noted.

One of the key discussions of this event is to encourage creatives and provide a platform for practical discussions on financing creative enterprises, commercialising intellectual property, and strengthening the continent's position in global creative markets.

"Africa already has its cultural influence; our challenge is to build economic power. Look at Afrobeats, Nollywood, our fashion, literature, and visual arts: our creativity is thriving more than ever before. However, recognition is not the same thing as ownership, and global popularity does not automatically translate into prosperity," noted legendary Nigerian actor Richard Mofe-Damijo.

Mofe-Damijo emphasised the need for access to better finance, stronger protection for intellectual property, reliable institutions that work, and businesses that can grow beyond success stories.

Financing will also take centre stage at the Creative Economy Finance Summit, presented by Afreximbank in partnership with the Creative Economy Practice at Co-Creation Hub. The summit will bring together financial institutions and investors to examine how creative-economy transactions can be structured, financed and de-risked.

Among many topics, discussions will also explore one of the world's most compelling topics, artificial intelligence, examining how African creatives can leverage digital technologies to develop products capable of competing internationally.

Close 

On the list of prominent figures from across the continent and diaspora are Nobel Laureate and writer Professor Wole Soyinka, Emmy Award-winning actor Uzo Aduba, filmmaker and actor Funke Akindele, actors Richard Mofe-Damijo and Thuso Mbedu, and former professional footballers Didier Drogba and Jay-Jay Okocha, musicians Davido, Fally Ipupa, Flavour, Libianca and Charlotte Dipanda.

Cultural ministers from across the continent are also in attendance, including from Côte d'Ivoire, South Africa, and Rwanda, alongside representatives from the International Finance Corporation and Afreximbank.

Speakers highlighted that strengthening access to financing, protecting intellectual property, and improving distribution channels are essential for African creatives to compete internationally and retain a greater share of the value they generate. For Afreximbank, supporting the creative industries is also part of a wider strategy to diversify African economies, promote intra-African trade, and strengthen the continent's participation in global markets.

World.title: Africa: A Just Energy Transition Cannot Leave Water Behind
World.content:
guest column

As Africa weighs how to power its industries and expand electricity access, water must be part of the equation. Ahead of COP31, Dr Jonty Cogger and Paul Wani Lado draw on South Africa’s experience to argue that a just energy transition must test proposed fossil fuel investments against their water demands—and protect the communities whose supplies could come under pressure.

South Africa's energy debate often focuses on electricity supply, energy security and economic growth. Oil and gas infrastructure is increasingly presented as part of the answer to these challenges. This framing hides a key test for any proposed development: whether its promised benefits justify the strain it will put on scarce water, and whether affected communities will carry an unfair share of the costs.

South Africa is a water-scarce country. Local communities increasingly struggle with unreliable water services, crumbling infrastructure and growing demand for water. Given this, plans to expand fossil fuel infrastructure need far closer scrutiny than they usually get.

Climate change makes matters worse by bringing more heat, more drought and less predictable rainfall. Writing for the Endangered Wildlife Trust, Dr Ian Little warns that a strong El Niño during the 2026/2027 summer season could bring below-average rainfall, higher temperatures, lower river flows and less water reaching dams. It could also cut crop yields, strain livestock farming and increase the demand for irrigation. In a country where water and food systems are already under pressure, this combination of risks shows why water security, food security and climate policy must shape any decision to expand fossil fuels further.



Oil and gas are not just a matter of energy policy. Expanding them affects the environment, the climate, water security and the rights of local communities. Yet debates about new gas infrastructure tend to focus on the promise of energy and industrial growth, rather than taking a hard look at the environmental costs and the local communities that may pay them.

Calling gas part of a just energy transition does not make it just. More electricity or investment does not, on its own, tell us who benefits, who pays the environmental, social and economic costs, and whether those costs can be avoided. Nor does calling gas a transitional fuel solve the problems of building fossil fuel infrastructure that will last for decades.

The risk is that South Africa repeats an old development model under the banner of a new transition where powerful economic interests reap the benefits of resource-hungry industry and local communities are left to deal with the environmental costs.

Water makes this contradiction especially clear because it links national energy choices to direct local effects. A project sold as improving energy security may make others less secure if it competes with households, farmers and nature for a limited and increasingly unreliable supply of water.

Putting water at the centre of the just transition means treating it as a firm limit on development, not just one factor to consider after energy and investment decisions have been made. Government should assess from the outset how proposed fossil fuel and industrial projects would affect how much water is available, its quality, and the ability of communities and ecosystems to cope as the climate worsens.

As government considers expanding gas infrastructure and attracting energy-intensive industries, it must account for how much water these developments will need. The critical question is whether the combined demand from multiple developments, together with existing uses and worsening climate pressures, can be met without harming communities' access to water, the health of ecosystems or the needs of other lawful water users.

This scrutiny must be based on evidence that is public and can be independently checked. Decision-makers should disclose how much water proposed projects need, where that water would come from, the condition and capacity of the water systems involved, what would happen in a drought, and the combined demands of existing and likely future developments.

The same scrutiny must apply to the infrastructure needed to support these developments, including pipelines, power stations and related industrial facilities. Decisions about these projects cannot ignore the water systems and communities they depend on.

Close 

Local communities should not have to face less reliable water supply so that fossil fuel expansion and industrial growth can go ahead. If government is serious about a just energy transition, it must require open water assessments that account for climate change and the combined impact of all projects before approving new developments, and it must show that communities will continue to have enough reliable water. Economic benefits should not be assumed to outweigh environmental and social costs; they must be weighed against them.

Dr Jonty Cogger is a public interest attorney at the Centre for Environmental Rights whose work focuses on using legal strategies to challenge pollution and climate change.

Paul Wani Lado is an attorney at the Centre for Environmental Rights where his work focuses on the extractives industry, particularly mining and upstream oil and gas projects.

World.title: Africa: Deadly Viruses Know No Borders, Nor Should Our Resolve to Stop Them
World.content:
Sjoerd Sjoerdsma, Dutch Minister for Foreign Trade and Development Cooperation, and Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, Director-General of the World Health Organization at WHO headquarters in Geneva, Switzerland.

guest column

In this guest column for AllAfrica, the Dutch Trade and Development Minister and the head of the World Health Organization stress that addressing viral health crises anywhere protects everyone everywhere. The government of the Netherlands is committing funding both for the current Ebola crisis and flexible funding to quickly respond to new or emerging global threats.

COVID-19 may feel like a distant memory to many. But the virus claimed millions of lives around the world, including approximately 50,000 in the Netherlands. The lesson is clear: preparedness is not optional.

Preventing health crises abroad is in the interest of all countries, including the Netherlands.

Governments everywhere face competing priorities and constrained budgets. But infectious diseases do not respect national borders. In an interconnected world, health threats that emerge in one place can quickly become risks for all of us. No country can safeguard its health security alone.

That lesson is evident today in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC), where a major Ebola outbreak is unfolding in a region already affected by insecurity, displacement and limited access to health services.

Already the outbreak has crossed national boundaries, underlining how quickly a health threat in one country can become a shared international concern.

Responding effectively requires rapid action, strong local leadership and international solidarity. Under the DRC Government's leadership, the World Health Organization (WHO) is working closely with the Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention, local authorities, communities and partners to contain the outbreak in the DRC and save lives.

Mystic Stock Photography / Shutterstock.com The MV Hondius, a cruise ship owned by the Dutch company Oceanwide Expeditions experienced a Hantavirus outbreak last year. The Netherlands and the World Health Organized collaborated to safely evacuate passengers and crew.

To support these efforts, the Netherlands is providing €7 million to WHO for the Ebola response. But responding to outbreaks requires more than emergency funding alone. It requires flexible, predictable financing that can be directed rapidly to where needs are greatest. That is why the Netherlands is also providing a new €10 million flexible contribution to WHO for future emergencies, enabling the WHO to rapidly respond to health threats while helping countries strengthen preparedness and prevent future outbreaks whenever possible. This is additional to the existing €9.6 million yearly core funding to the WHO.

No country can safeguard its health security alone.

Some may ask why the Netherlands, or any country, should invest in health emergencies far from its own borders when domestic health systems also face challenges. The answer is simple: diseases do not stop at borders. Supporting countries to detect and contain outbreaks early is not only the right thing to do. It protects local populations while reducing the risk of wider international spread. Investing in health security abroad is also an investment in health security at home.

Outbreaks are most effectively controlled at their source. Local leadership is essential. National authorities understand their communities, their health systems and the challenges they face. WHO's role is to support those efforts, coordinate international expertise and ensure that countries have access to the tools, funding and technical assistance they need.

International cooperation remains the foundation of effective health security. This year, for example, a hantavirus outbreak on a Dutch-flagged cruise ship was swiftly contained through rapid collaboration among countries and partners coordinated through WHO. During an earlier outbreak caused by the "Sudan virus" species of Ebola in Uganda, investments that helped advance an Ebola vaccine developed by the International AIDS Vaccine Initiative (IAVI) and Batavia Biosciences contributed to global preparedness efforts. These examples demonstrate that cooperation works.

Dany Bitita/WHO Two new candidate vaccines to join Ebola trial as treatment research advances.

Yet this progress cannot be taken for granted. The international health system is under growing strain, even as health threats continue to increase. Climate change is altering the distribution of infectious diseases. Europe has already seen growing concern from vector-borne diseases, including West Nile virus, while other diseases such as dengue and malaria are expanding into new regions. At the same time, funding for global health, including for WHO, is declining.

Diseases spreading to new areas amid decreased global health funding is dangerous.

This is a dangerous combination. The need for cooperation, preparedness and rapid response is growing, just as the resources required to sustain them are coming under pressure.

We therefore call on European governments to strengthen their support for global health security by increasing flexible and unearmarked contributions to WHO. Such investments enable outbreaks to be detected earlier, contained more rapidly and addressed where they begin, before they become larger regional or global crises.

No one can rule out the possibility of another pandemic. . But we can ensure that we are better prepared for the next one. Strong health systems in the DRC, and in countries everywhere, are not only vital for the local communities. They are an investment in a safer, healthier and more secure future for us all.

Sjoerd Sjoerdsma is the Dutch Minister for Foreign Trade and Development Cooperation. Dr. Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus is Director-General of the World Health Organization.

World.title: Kenya: Kenya Cult Leader Paul Mackenzie Sentenced to 200 Years
World.content:
Paul Mackenzie was found guilty in October of the murder of 190 children.

A court in Kenya has sentenced Paul Mackenzie to 200 years in prison for the murders of 190 children and an adult. He told them to starve themselves to death as part of his apocalyptic religious cult.

Kenyan religious sect leader Paul Mackenzie was sentenced to 200 years in prison on Friday, at the culmination of a trial following the discovery of hundreds of corpses in the woods.

A self-proclaimed pastor and longstanding leader of a new age Christian apocalyptic cult called the Good News International Church, Mackenzie was convicted in October of 191 counts of murder in the deaths of one adult and 190 children.

Justice Diana Kavedza said the sentence was comprised of 100 years for 183 counts of murder by starvation and another 100 years for eight counts of murder by direct homicide.

He could have faced the death penalty, which is still technically on the books in Kenya.

However, like several countries that have kept capital punishment in their legal code but stopped actually using it, Kenya has not executed anybody since 1987.

While the charges against Mackenzie pertained to 191 deaths, some 400 people were found dead in what became known as the "Shakahola Forest Massacre." Mackenzie's so-called church had been operating since 2003, based in the coastal town of Malindi.

Mackenzie had denied the charges, saying that he did not force the cult followers to starve.

A total of 28 accomplices were given various prison sentences for their roles in the deaths.

World.title: Tanzania: Tanzania Opposition Leader Lissu Cleared of Treason but Jailed for Incitement
World.content:
A Tanzanian court on Friday sentenced opposition leader Tundu Lissu to four years in jail for inciting unrest, after earlier in the day clearing him of treason - meaning he avoided a possible death sentence. The verdict follows a disputed presidential election and a deadly crackdown on protesters, in a case that has drawn international condemnation and raised concerns about political freedom in the country.

A panel of three judges at the High Court in Dar es Salaam, Tanzania's commercial capital, convicted the 58-year-old leader of the country's main opposition party, Chadema, over remarks he made calling for electoral reforms.

"We are satisfied that through his statements, the accused intended to disrupt elections and instigate violence," a judge told a courtroom packed with supporters, French news agency AFP reported.



Lissu has been detained since April 2025. He has denied any wrongdoing, arguing that his campaign was lawful and the charges against him politically motivated.

Facing heavy security, Tanzania protesters fear repeat of election violence

Campaign in the dock

His arrest came six months before the October 2025 vote, shortly after he launched a drive for changes to Tanzania's electoral system under the slogan "No Reforms, No Election".

Prosecutors argued that his statements were intended to disrupt the vote and threaten the government, amounting to treason.

Lissu, a lawyer who represented himself during the trial, maintained that his comments had been taken out of context and that he had committed no crime.

"My hope is that you will carry that heavy historical burden without bias, with courage and with the dignity carried by your judicial oaths," he told the panel in his closing arguments.

Tanzania's Hassan makes historic Russia visit amid frayed ties with West

Criticism abroad

The trial drew criticism from British and European Union lawmakers, who described it as politically driven and called for Lissu's immediate release.

"The use of capital punishment against a political opponent risks turning the justice system into an instrument of political repression," they wrote in a letter to President Samia Suluhu Hassan.

Security was tightened across Dar es Salaam and around the courthouse ahead of Friday's verdict, as Lissu's supporters gathered for the hearing.

Groups were mobilising to travel to the city, police said on Wednesday, warning against "those who want to stage a coup".

Elections, coups and crackdowns: Africa's mixed democratic record in 2025

Close 

Death toll in dispute

Lissu's arrest, Chadema's disqualification and alleged abductions of government critics helped fuel protests during last year's presidential election.

Hassan won with 98 percent of the vote after her two main challengers, including Lissu, were excluded. The opposition dismissed the result as a "mockery" of democracy.

A government-appointed commission put the death toll at at least 518, blaming protesters for the violence. Opposition groups and human rights organisations say the authorities killed thousands.

Accusations that security forces used excessive force have been rejected by the government. The election was fair and transparent, Hassan has insisted, blaming foreigners for the unrest.

(with newswires)

World.title: Namibia: Distance No Longer a Death Sentence
World.content:
Namibia's air ambulance is expected to reduce some journeys that take hours by road to minutes or a few short hours by air, depending on the distance and emergency.

A 12-year-old boy who needed urgent medical attention died while waiting to be transferred from Katima Mulilo to Windhoek, a tragedy that has now become one of the reasons behind Namibia's first State-owned air ambulance service.

The boy's death, followed by the loss of patients who could not be transported quickly enough after a road accident along the Otjiwarongo road, exposed the cost of delays in Namibia's emergency healthcare system.

Health minister Esperance Luvindao recounted the painful experiences on Wednesday as the country officially launched its first State-owned air ambulance service,

a move expected to reduce the time critically ill and injured patients spend travelling to specialised hospitals.



"Unfortunately, in the early hours of the next morning, I got a call that this 12-year-old boy had passed away," Luvindao said, recalling the incident involving the patient from Katima Mulilo.

"This was heartbreaking. Because I knew that a young life had just been lost," she narrated. The minister said another emergency occurred in April 2026 when a road accident along the Otjiwarongo road left patients needing urgent transportation to Windhoek. "Unfortunately, this was not possible and lives were lost," she said.

The experiences, she said, forced the health ministry to look for solutions that could save lives while the government continues with plans to build more hospitals.

The launch, officiated by Vice President Lucia Witbooi in Windhoek, marks a major change in how the country intends to respond to medical emergencies, particularly in remote areas where patients face long journeys to reach referral hospitals.

For patients who need urgent specialist care, the difference between reaching a hospital in time and waiting hours could determine whether they survive.

Witbooi said the service was intended to ensure that a person's chances of survival were not determined by where they live.

"No Namibian should lose their life simply because they live far from a hospital," she said.

She added that the country's vast geographical size and the distance between remote communities and referral hospitals had long created challenges for emergency medical care.

The air ambulance is expected to reduce some journeys that take hours by road to minutes or a few short hours by air, depending on the distance and emergency.

The service includes a Learjet air ambulance equipped with medical equipment to provide critical care during flights.

Government Air Transport Services will provide aircraft and pilots in collaboration with the ministries of health and works and transport. It will also use helicopter evacuation services through cooperation with the Namibian Police and the Namibian Defence forces to respond to emergencies in areas where helicopters are needed.

Specialised medical personnel will accompany patients requiring urgent care, while emergency service centres at national referral hospitals will help ensure patients receive treatment immediately after landing.

Luvindao said the service was developed as a practical response to the country's healthcare challenges, rather than waiting for the construction of more referral hospitals.

"While we build those hospitals, Namibians want service. While we build those hospitals, there is another 12-year-old boy that might have severe head injuries and need urgent transportation. And so it is our role to make a plan, not just for the future, but for now," she said. She said the government was working towards constructing four hospitals in the coming years, but acknowledged that such projects require substantial financial resources and time.

Close 

The air ambulance, she said, would complement existing ground ambulance services and provide an additional option for patients whose conditions require urgent specialist intervention.

The ministry has also activated an emergency callcentre to coordinate requests, verify referrals and dispatch the service.

Luvindao said the centre would serve as a single point of coordination to ensure that patients with justified medical needs are transferred promptly.

The service will prioritise patients who require urgent specialist treatment, including those with serious trauma, neurological, cardiac and obstetric emergencies, as well as patients whose conditions make road transport unsafe or too slow.

The initiative requires cooperation between the health sector, aviation authorities, emergency responders and security institutions. - [email protected]

World.title: Dallas public defender’s chief investigator charged with wife’s murder after bloody apartment discovery
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

A Texas investigator who spent years working on capital murder cases is now accused of killing his wife of roughly 35 years, less than two weeks after filing for divorce.

Jimmy Spurger Jr., 54, the chief investigator for the Dallas County Public Defender’s Office, faces a first-degree felony murder charge after his wife, Maria Spurger, was found stabbed to death inside their downtown Dallas apartment Friday night.

Emergency crews found Maria on a couch with a knife in her neck and her husband sitting on a bed in another room, covered in blood, according to an arrest affidavit obtained by Fox 4 Dallas.

Spurger filed for divorce Oct. 26, less than two weeks before the killing, according to Dallas County court records. The case was still open, with a Nov. 3 entry indicating Maria had not been served with the divorce papers.



TEACHER FOUND DEAD WITH THROAT SLIT; DETECTIVES SCRUTINIZE HUSBAND’S SHIFTING STORY

Dallas County Judge Clay Lewis Jenkins said Sunday that he had ordered Spurger suspended and his access revoked.

"Upon notice of this tragic murder yesterday, I instructed Administration to place the employee on suspension and remove his access," Jenkins wrote on X.

Firefighters received a welfare check call around 10:40 p.m. Friday and went to the couple’s apartment on North Akard Street, according to the affidavit.

No one answered their repeated knocks. When firefighters forced the door open, they found furniture blocking the entrance.

They moved it aside and found Maria unresponsive on the couch. Spurger was sitting on a bed in the bedroom, but he did not answer when firefighters asked whether he was OK.

The crews backed out and called police.

Officers arrived around 11:13 p.m. and found Spurger covered in blood, with a small knife beside him. Several empty pill bottles covered in blood were in the kitchen, according to the affidavit. No one else was found inside.

IVY LEAGUE-EDUCATED PEDIATRICIAN ALLEGEDLY MURDERED BY HUSBAND WHO THEN SET HOME ON FIRE: POLICE

Maria was pronounced dead at the apartment. Spurger was taken to Methodist Central Hospital, and investigators said they could not interview him because he may have taken multiple pills.

He was booked into the Dallas County Jail Saturday on a murder charge and is being held without bond, according to jail records.

RETIRED POLICE SERGEANT SHOOTS DEPUTY CHIEF WIFE AND THEIR DAUGHTER IN WEALTHY, COASTAL ENCLAVE HOME

Before his arrest, Spurger oversaw investigators who helped public defenders prepare criminal cases, according to the Dallas County Public Defender’s Office website. His biography says he served as chief investigator for 11 months.

He spent more than 13 years with the office, primarily in its Capital Murder Division, where his work included examining evidence and interviewing witnesses.

FORMER CORRECTIONS OFFICER ACCUSED OF KILLING WIFE, FORCING KIDS TO HELP

Before joining the public defender’s office, Spurger spent more than 20 years in law enforcement, specializing in homicide investigations and crimes against people, according to the website. During his final decade in law enforcement, he supervised child abuse and family violence investigations for the Dallas County District Attorney’s Office.

Police have not released a motive and said the killing remains under investigation.

Anyone with information is asked to contact Detective C. Johnson at 214-671-3584 or chanesia.johnson@dallaspolice.gov.

World.title: Tensions flare as demonstrators target Jewish restaurants, drawing massive counterprotest
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

Tensions flared in a Philadelphia neighborhood Sunday after a bike ride organized to boycott several Jewish-owned restaurants sparked overwhelming backlash from the city's Jewish and pro-Israel communities.

The "boycott ride" targeted at least six restaurants in Philadelphia's Rittenhouse Square, labeling them "Zionist establishments" and calling for them to leave, according to pro-Palestinian group Philly Bike On Your Left, which organized the event.

As riders cycled through the streets waving Palestinian flags, hundreds of Jewish and pro-Israel community members turned out to oppose the demonstration, with heated exchanges unfolding across several city blocks. Dozens of diners also lined up outside the targeted restaurants in a show of solidarity with the Jewish-owned businesses.

The boycott also drew sharp criticism for taking place on the eve of the anniversary of Kristallnacht, the 1938 Nazi pogrom against Jews in Germany and Austria marked by widespread anti-Jewish violence, including attacks on homes, synagogues and businesses.

PHILADELPHIA 'BOYCOTT RIDE' TARGETING JEWISH BUSINESSES DRAWS CONDEMNATION FROM CITY, STATE LEADERSHIP

The Philadelphia police told Fox News that at least three people were arrested in connection with the protest, including a woman accused of assault, a man accused of disorderly conduct and a 17-year-old male accused of assaulting police.

Meanwhile, a female counterprotester reported being assaulted by an unknown individual.

Two officers also sustained minor injuries during the arrest of one individual, according to the outlet. Neither required medical treatment.

No property damage was reported, and conditions returned to normal by late afternoon, police said.

Police said about 500 people participated in total, including roughly 300 pro-Palestinian demonstrators, 200 of whom were on bicycles, and 200 pro-Israeli counterprotesters.

ANTI-ISRAEL AGITATORS CLASH WITH NYPD OFFICERS NEAR SYNAGOGUE

Videos circulating on social media showed demonstrators and counterprotesters shouting at one another.

In one video, a restaurant displayed a Palestinian flag alongside a sign reading "No public restroom" on its entrance door.

A man confronted the restaurant on camera, accusing it of sending a message that the Jewish community was not welcome.

The protest, organized in late October, targeted six businesses whose owners organizers accused of being "Zionist business owners."

"We see them for the disgusting humans they are," the group said.

"There are business owners in our community who have raised funds for the Israeli military, hosted Israeli soldiers, were praised by Benjamin Netanyahu, or expressed support for Israel," the group added.

The demonstration prompted the Jewish Federation of Greater Philadelphia to call for a counter-demonstration in early November.

GERMAN OFFICIALS WARN ISLAMIST, FAR-LEFT RHETORIC DRIVING SPIKE IN ANTISEMITIC ATTACKS

"This is antisemitism. It is Jew-Hatred, plain and simple," the organization said.

"The ride falls on the eve of the anniversary of Kristallnacht, November 9-10, 1938, when Nazi-organized mobs destroyed thousands of Jewish businesses, homes and synagogues in Germany and Austria, while thousands of Jews were beaten, assaulted and sent to concentration camps. The public targeting of Jewish businesses should alarm every person of conscience. We cannot allow such hatred to become normalized in Philadelphia."

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

The organizers, however, pushed back against the criticism, claiming their ride had been "grossly misrepresented" and describing themselves as a nonviolent social cycling group.

World.title: Donna Mills on why she never married despite decades-long romance: 'I was always so independent'
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

"Knots Landing" star Donna Mills is revealing the reason that she has never walked down the aisle despite her 25-year romance with actor Larry Gilman.

During a recent appearance on the "Still Here Hollywood Podcast with Steve Kmetko," the 85-year-old actress, who has been in a relationship with Gilman, 76, since 2001, opened up about why she has chosen to avoid marriage.

"I was always so independent," she told Kmetko. "I’m still very independent."

RITA WILSON IGNORED HER MOTHER'S OLD-SCHOOL MARRIAGE ADVICE, AND IT LED HER TO TOM HANKS

"I just didn’t ever want to be subject to whatever you have to do when you get married," Mills continued. "I also didn’t want to say I was going to love somebody forever."

"I don’t know if I would do that or not," she admitted with a laugh.

‘CHARLIE’S ANGELS’ STAR JACLYN SMITH LIVED APART FROM HER HUSBAND FOR 17 YEARS DURING THEIR 35-YEAR LOVE STORY

Mills shared the topic of marriage had also come up between herself and her daughter Chloe, who recently tied the knot herself.

"It’s funny because my daughter asked me that. My daughter just got married," Mills said. "And she just had a baby."

After Kmetko told her that she didn't "look like a grandmother," Mills pointed to a necklace she was wearing that was inscribed with the word "Grandma," which she said was a gift from Chloe.

"She gave me this, and I wear it all the time," Mills said.

Mills explained that she and Chloe have had many conversations about what name her grandson would call her.

"And I said, "'Oh, I know. Glamma,'" Mills told Kmetko with a laugh. "But she didn't like that."

The Daytime Emmy Award winner Chloe adopted as a newborn in 1994 when she was 54. Seven years later, Mills began dating Gilman, whom she has described as an "incredibly kind, funny, wonderful man."

"I love him," she told The Daily Beast in 2022. "I’m lucky to have found him. I found him late, but I found him. Everybody loves him. He’s great."

NICOLE KIDMAN, RACHAEL RAY, TED DANSON KEEP MARRIAGES HOT WITH UNCONVENTIONAL RULES

Prior to meeting Gilman, Mills and advertising executive Richard Holland, who was previously married to singer Chaka Khan, had an on-and-off relationship for around 20 years starting in 1979.

When asked why she has never married, Mills said, "I don’t remember anyone ever getting down on one knee."

TIM MCGRAW WARNS OF ‘MOST DANGEROUS’ TIMES IN MARRIAGE AFTER 30 YEARS WITH FAITH HILL

The "Nope" star also cited her independent streak and explained why she and Gilman never felt the need to marry after meeting later in life.

"I am so freaking independent. I just am. I’m very independent and by the time Larry and I met we were both pretty established," she said. "To combine everything at that point is really difficult. So we just combined our lives but not our finances and stuff like that. It’s much cleaner, much better."

GREAT RELATIONSHIPS HAVE 3 ESSENTIAL INGREDIENTS — AND ONE FACTOR THAT CAN RUIN EVERYTHING

Mills shared that maintaining her independence had always given her a sense of security, even while sharing her life with a partner.

"I’ve always felt a woman being independent was important," she said. "It made me feel safer, I guess, to know that I can take care of myself. I want someone to be in my life to love and be with, to be a companion and to go places and all that, but if I have to I can take care of myself."

"And really, I had enough marriages as Abby!" she added, referring to the character she played on "Knots Landing."

Mills became a television sensation playing the glamorous and ruthless Abby Cunningham on "Knots Landing" from 1980 to 1989.

Abby tied the knot four times over the course of the hit primetime soap, though one union was annulled almost immediately after the wedding.

Mills and Gilman share a home in the Los Angeles neighborhood of Brentwood, where they have a vineyard. In 2015, Mills told Closer Weekly that the vineyard was a gift from her longtime partner.

"Larry planted a vineyard for me last year," Donna shared. "He’s really such a good guy."

The couple went on to launch Mandeville Vineyards, a small-scale wine brand produced from grapes grown on their vineyard in Brentwood's Mandeville Canyon.

World.title: Will College Football Playoff committee drop LSU Tigers out of playoff picture after blowout loss?
World.content:
The release of the first College Football Playoff poll recently was treated with shock, disdain, and outright anger from many fans across the sport. Unless they root for the SEC.

SEC teams were shockingly, and consistently overrepresented and overranked, to the point that prominent rival coaches openly speculated about a connection between ESPN, the SEC, and the committee's willingness to abandon any pretense of objectivity.

This page may contain affiliate links to legal sports betting partners. If you sign up or place a wager, FOX News may be compensated. This content was created by a team that works independently from the FOX newsroom.

Defending national champion Curt Cignetti, as one example, was blunt about his perception of the committee's bias.

TIM BRANDO JOINS DAN DAKICH ON 'DON'T @ ME' TO DISCUSS INDIANA COACH CURT CIGNETTI'S CFP 'BIAS' COMMENTS

"SEC gets a lot of love from ESPN and all their writers that they don't technically pay but march to their drum," he said. "That's why you see all these SEC teams up there, and some good two-loss teams from the Big Ten not quite as high. But like I said, it's all going to be played out on the field."

"Come on. These people, and there’s a whole bunch of them, they march out of the tent, and they’re given instructions on what to say," he added. "And they follow the company line. Right, and I don’t need to go any further."

There's little doubt that the SEC's marketing efforts have been extremely effective at ensuring voters ignore results and focus on perception instead. And the biggest winner might have been the conference's most effective marketer: LSU Tigers head coach Lane Kiffin.

Kiffin has been loudly decrying the conference's move to nine games, correctly realizing that the extra losses , which put the SEC on equal footing with the Big Ten and Big 12, will be tough to overcome when evaluating resumes. To combat this, he's spent most of the past year campaigning for the benefit of the committee. Saying, incorrectly, that the SEC is Just Different and deserves to be treated like special snowflakes relative to other conferences.

"The conferences are so different," he said recently. "They are. They’re different stadiums, they’re different environments, they’re different middle to bottom of them. So you’re not playing equal schedules, they’re not even close. If you took an SEC team and gave them another one of those conference’s schedules, they’d average two more wins. Well, that’s a big deal. So, I say all that to say you had to go to more teams, because the system’s broke in how they pick them."

Pretty much all of that is wrong. But his propaganda efforts, based on the first week's poll, clearly worked. Losses in the SEC simply don't matter as much as they should, a trend that was obvious in 2025 when the Alabama Crimson Tide were blown out by Georgia in the conference championship game and didn't drop a single spot. The committee decided ahead of time that they should be in, so they determined that the SEC Championship Game could only help the winner, and not hurt the loser.

Will that same preferential treatment be given to the loser of a, say, Utah-BYU Big 12 Championship Game? Of course not. Because of the stadiums or something. Returning to Kiffin's diatribe though, one stat that he curiously never brings up is the SEC's recent performance when the games actually matter. And unfortunately for him and them, it's not very good.

In 2025-2026, the SEC went 1-8 in bowl games. They were 0-3 in the College Football Playoff against non-SEC P4 opponents. Texas A&M went 7-1 in the SEC and was a tiebreaker away from reaching the conference championship game, then scored all of three points against a lowly Miami Hurricanes team at home. In their awe-inspiring temple of an SEC stadium.

World.title: Hakeem Jeffries says he’s a ‘hard yes’ on impeaching Pete Hegseth
World.content:
House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., said he is a “hard yes” on supporting efforts to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, which are expected to be brought to a vote this week.

Asked in an interview on ABC’s “This Week” whether he would support Rep. Thomas Massie, R-Ky., in his efforts to impeach Hegseth, Jeffries confirmed he supported the push.

“I’m a hard yes on the Hegseth resolution,” Jeffries said. “The so-called secretary of defense has abused his power, undermined our national security and engineered this reckless and costly war of choice in Iran, which has skyrocketed prices on the American people and made the country less safe.”

“Pete Hegseth has got to go,” he added.

Jeffries’ support is a major endorsement of impeachment efforts against Hegseth and signals how other House Democrats could ultimately vote on the measure. The impeachment push also tests how far lawmakers are willing to go to oust Hegseth after voters have given low marks to the administration’s handling of the war in Iran, which factored into the midterm election results.

Asked on ABC News whether Jeffries believed all other House Democrats would support the impeachment resolution, he said they would “have that conversation Tuesday morning.” The House is back in session this week, and the impeachment resolution is expected to be filed early this week, with a vote to follow.

Massie has been a vocal critic of Hegseth and the war in Iran. He previously filed a resolution to impeach Hegseth in September, but Republican leaders canceled planned votes, and the House left early, pushing the vote to after the election.

NBC News reported last week that President Donald Trump has told allies that he was considering replacing Hegseth. Trump, though, has publicly denied that he plans to replace Hegseth, telling reporters last week that he was “doing a very good job.”

At the same time, Hegseth has forcefully pushed back on Massie’s impeachment plans, referring to Massie in a social media video last week as a “disgruntled, defeated congressman.”

“It’s all about the politics of personal destruction,” Hegseth said in the video. “Didn’t work against President Trump, and it won’t work with me. You can rest assured of that.”

Massie, though, said on social media last week that his “Hegseth impeachment resolution is a much gentler version of what’s coming when Dem’s control Congress.” Democrats, Massie said, would “have hearings & trials.”

Rep. Yassamin Ansari, D-Ariz., also introduced a resolution to impeach Hegseth in April. In a post sharing Jeffries’ comments Sunday, Ansari said that Hegseth “must be held accountable.”

“Let’s get this to the floor and voted on this week,” she said in the post.

World.title: Trump says he was ‘only kidding’ about making UFC head Dana White press secretary
World.content:
President Donald Trump said he was joking when he offered the job of White House press secretary to Dana White, the CEO and president of the Ultimate Fighting Championship, putting an end to more than 24 hours of speculation about whether the announcement was serious.

“I will tell you, I was only kidding, but Dana loves the idea, and there’s only one Dana, he’s great,” Trump told reporters Sunday evening on the tarmac in Palm Beach, Florida.

Trump’s comments come a day after he sent out a surprise post on Truth Social saying he had offered White the job. The position has been vacant since Katie Zacharia left the role after just five days last month.

“I am pleased to announce that the Great Dana White, a violent Fighter and Warrior, has been offered the job of Press Secretary of the United States,” Trump wrote on Truth Social.

Trump suggested in his post that White should bring several UFC fighters, including Khabib Nurmagomedov, Justin Gaethje and Amanda Nunes, as assistants to defend against the “Lunatic Left.”

“Dana will be a Press Secretary like none other. Dana, please take the job!” he added.

White said at a boxing event in London on Saturday evening that he was heading to Washington that night and had a meeting scheduled with Trump on Monday.

Trump told reporters that the Monday meeting was still on, but it was unrelated to the press secretary position.

“So he’s actually coming tomorrow,” Trump said Sunday night. “Of course, I was kidding ... But Dana is actually coming tomorrow, actually, for other reasons. I think he was going to be in Washington, so he’s going to come over and see me.”

When Trump posted on Truth Social earlier Saturday, it was unclear whether his offer was a serious one.

Shortly after Trump posted, White posted on Instagram what appears to be an AI-generated image of himself behind the lectern in the White House briefing room, captioned, “On to the next chapter.”

White also added a screenshot of Trump’s post to his Instagram Story.

Trump and White have long been friends and Trump has attended many UFC fights while he has been in the White House.

White this year also organized a UFC fight on the South Lawn of the White House, an event that was part of a slate commemorating the U.S.’s 250th birthday.

Many Trump administration officials and Republican lawmakers attended the fight in July.

A spokesperson for the White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Zacharia had replaced Karoline Leavitt, who had been White House press secretary since Trump returned to office in January of last year. Leavitt announced in August that she would leave her post to spend more time with her family.

The White House had another staff shake-up Friday, when chief of staff Susie Wiles said she would step down. Trump named longtime aide Stephen Miller as her replacement.

Wiles’ departure made her the seventh woman to leave the Trump administration this year. So far, all of them have been replaced by men, except Zacharia and Leavitt, as a press secretary has not yet been named.
