This also signs you up to our weekday newsletter, Africa Intelligence. Nothing arrives until you click the confirmation link, and you can stop either with one click. Privacy policy

Why Nigeria Wants More Fish

The ministry puts annual demand at about 3.6 million tonnes against domestic output of about 1.4 million tonnes, a shortfall of more than 2.2 million tonnes. It says output has risen from 1.1 million tonnes, without giving the period.

Nigeria covers the gap with imports that cost close to US$1 billion a year in foreign exchange, the ministry says. The ministry did not say how much of that bill the new loans would replace.

The ministry also listed a Technical Committee on Accelerating Fish Production, a government working group inaugurated in August 2026, and the digitising of fish import licences. It is promoting a “Fish City” and “Fish Terminal” investment portfolio, which it says is meant to attract private capital but did not describe in detail.

What It Means for You

For US readers, Nigeria is a large emerging market where food imports weigh on the currency and on inflation, as our report on World Bank efforts to mobilise private cash in Nigeria also shows. A credible fish programme could trim import demand over several years, but nothing in the announcement shows that yet.

Investors in Nigerian sovereign or state debt should note that the loans would go to individual states. That adds state-level borrowing to the picture, and the terms are not public.

What Is Not Known

The ministry has not published the repayment period, the interest rate, the loan size per state or the date money will flow. We found no World Bank project page for this US$200 million, so it is unclear which World Bank programme would carry it.

It is also unclear whether the US$200 million is new money or part of financing already agreed with Nigeria. The ministry did not say when its post-training roundtable with the states will meet.

More: Nigeria news in English, every day from The Rio Times.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is the US$200 Million World Bank Loan Confirmed?

The Nigerian ministry announced it on 8 November 2026. We found no World Bank project document for it, so treat the amount as the ministry’s statement.

Who Would Get the Money?

State governments, as concessional loans for fisheries and aquaculture, the ministry says. Rivers, Bayelsa, Delta and Cross River states sent commissioners to the training.

Why Does Nigeria Import So Much Fish?

The ministry says demand is about 3.6 million tonnes a year and domestic output about 1.4 million tonnes. Imports fill the shortfall at close to US$1 billion a year.

Sources: Federal Ministry of Marine and Blue Economy of Nigeria, statement on the executive training on the aquaculture investment guide, 8 November 2026; World Bank, Nigeria country page, read 9 November 2026 (no matching project found).

World.title: Trump Says Deportation Policy Was Too Tough
World.content:
A mural in the Pilsen neighbourhood of Chicago, a long-time Mexican-American district. File photo, 2014. Photo: Acediscovery, CC BY 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

President Donald Trump said on Sunday 8 November 2026 that his mass-deportation policy may have been too tough, five days after his Republican Party lost control of the US House of Representatives. For readers in the United States and across Latin America, the remark raises a simple question about whether the removal flights to Guatemala, Honduras and Mexico will slow down.

So far, nothing on the ground has changed. On Friday 6 November, the day the interview was recorded, Trump named Stephen Miller, the main architect of the deportation drive, as his White House chief of staff.

What: Trump said of mass deportations, “Too tough,” and “I think it might be too tough, yeah.”

When: broadcast Sunday 8 November 2026, five days after the Tuesday 3 November midterm elections.

Who: Stephen Miller, architect of the policy, became chief of staff on Friday 6 November.

Why it matters: Guatemala alone received US$15.45 billion in remittances in January to July 2026.

As of 9 November 2026, 01:00 GMT

In plain English: Mass deportation means removing millions of people who live in the United States without legal papers. The midterms are the national elections held halfway through a president’s four-year term, and the chief of staff is the president’s top aide, who runs the White House.

Free daily brief — no card needed Get every Chile story in one morning email We build you a personalized brief around the topics you follow — free for 7 days. Love it? Your first month after that is US$1. Start my free brief Yes, email me my free daily brief — I can unsubscribe any time.

In plain English: ICE is Immigration and Customs Enforcement, the federal agency that arrests migrants and flies them out. Remittances are money that migrants send home to their families.

What Trump Said and What Changed

Asked about his deportation policy in the televised interview, Trump answered in English that it was too tough. He added: “I think it might be too tough, yeah.”

No order, memo or new rule softening the policy has been announced as of this report. Our earlier report on the government’s statement that deportations will continue still describes the official line.

The timing matters politically. Republicans lost control of the House of Representatives in the election held on Tuesday 3 November 2026.

The count was still being finished in several races, so the final seat total is not settled. Certified results come from each state’s election office, and we have not yet seen full certified totals.

Trump named Miller on Friday 6 November, before the interview aired. His promotion to chief of staff puts the policy’s author in charge of the whole White House.

That sends two signals at once. The president’s words suggest a softer tone, while his choice of aide suggests the enforcement drive will continue.

This also signs you up to our weekday newsletter, The LatAm Brief. Nothing arrives until you click the confirmation link, and you can stop either with one click. Privacy policy

Flights to Latin America and the Money Going Home

Human Rights First, a US rights group that tracks ICE flights, found that Guatemala and Honduras together received 41% of all removal flights in March 2026, and counted a record 245 flights to 38 countries in April 2026. Those are the group’s own counts, not official figures.

The Estadio Nacional in Tegucigalpa, the capital of Honduras, below hillside neighbourhoods. File photo, undated. Photo: Luis Alfredo Romero, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

Money flows are the other half of the story. Guatemala’s central bank (Banguat) said migrants sent home US$15.45 billion in January to July 2026, up 6.6% on a year earlier, and a record US$2.47 billion in July alone (data published Thursday 6 August 2026).

Honduras depends on the same flows, as shown in our report that Honduran remittances topped US$10 billion. Honduras is also where deportees land in large numbers, as our count of Honduran deportees near 38,000 shows.

What It Means for You

If you invest in or send money to Central America, the main risk is a shrinking pool of workers in the United States. Fewer migrants with jobs in the US means fewer dollars sent home, although the numbers have stayed high so far.

If you are a migrant or have relatives who are, do not read one interview as a change in the rules. Enforcement still runs under current law and the same agencies, so check official notices and speak to an immigration lawyer.

What Is Not Known

It is not known whether Trump will change any rule, flight schedule or detention practice. He gave no details, and the White House has not announced a new policy in the sources we checked.

We could not confirm a transcript beyond the broadcast excerpt, nor any changes for flights to Ecuador, Venezuela or Mexico. The final House seat count and certified results are also still to come.

Frequently Asked Questions

Did Trump change his deportation policy?

Not yet. He called the policy too tough in an interview, but no formal change has been announced, and he did not say what he would alter.

Will deportation flights to Latin America stop?

There is no sign of that. Flights to countries such as Guatemala and Honduras continue, and the new chief of staff is the policy’s main architect.

Why does this matter for remittances?

Migrants send money home to relatives, and deportations can cut those flows over time. Guatemala still received a record US$2.47 billion in July 2026.

Sources: The White House (whitehouse.gov) announcement of the chief of staff appointment of 6 November 2026; the broadcast excerpt of the interview of 8 November 2026; state election offices and the Clerk of the US House (clerk.house.gov) for election results; Banco de Guatemala remittance data of 6 August 2026 (banguat.gob.gt); Human Rights First ICE Flight Monitor reports for March and April 2026 (humanrightsfirst.org).

World.title: Argentina Inflation Stalls Before Vote Year
World.content:
Argentina’s inflation has stopped falling just as the country enters the year before a presidential election. Official figures show prices rose 1.9% in September 2026, up from 1.7% in August, while the yearly rate barely moved at 33.4%.

For US readers, the number matters because it shapes how much Argentine bonds and US-listed Argentine stocks are worth, and how long President Javier Milei’s cost-cutting plan can keep public support. The vote itself is due in October 2027.

September prices rose 1.9% in a month, against 1.7% in August; the yearly rate was 33.4%.

Economists in the central bank’s expectations survey (REM) expect 1.8% for October, with the official figure due on Thursday 12 November.

Prediction markets: Polymarket, a US prediction platform, gives Milei a 44.5% chance and Axel Kicillof, the Buenos Aires province governor, 33.5% to win the 2027 presidency (8 November 2026, 7:39 p.m. ET).

Power Index: Argentina ranks 4th of 14 in The Rio Times Latin America Power Index, with 60.2 points (November 2026 edition).

As of 9 November 2026, 00:33 GMT

In plain English: INDEC is Argentina’s national statistics office, and it publishes the official consumer price index each month. The REM is a monthly survey in which the central bank (BCRA) asks economists what they expect for prices, growth and the peso.

Why the Slowdown Has Stalled

INDEC said on Tuesday 13 October 2026 that prices rose 1.9% in September, and that they are up 23.6% since January. Over the past twelve months the rise was 33.4%, a hair below August’s 33.5%.

Services rose faster than goods for the fifth month in a row. Regulated prices, such as gas, electricity and prepaid health plans, rose 2.3%.

Core inflation, which strips out the most volatile items such as fresh produce and regulated prices, was 1.7%. That suggests the underlying trend is calmer than the headline, though not by a wide margin.

A simple calculation shows why the yearly figure is so stubborn. At 1.9% a month prices would climb about 25% in a year, and at 1.8% about 24%, so our earlier August report shows how far the pace has already fallen.

The Argentine flag above the central bank headquarters in Buenos Aires. Photo from the Rio Times library. photo, 2012. The headquarters of the Banco Central de la República Argentina in the San Nicolás district of Buenos Aires. Photo: Leandro Kibisz, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

What Economists Expect Next

The central bank published its latest REM survey on Thursday 5 November 2026, with 45 participants who answered between 28 and 30 October. They expect prices to rise 1.8% in October, a touch lower than September.

The same survey sees the peso at about 1,590 per US$1 in December, which is 9.8% above the December 2025 level. The peso is the central piece, because a weaker currency makes imported goods dearer and feeds into prices.

The survey now expects 0.7% growth for 2026, cut from 1.5%. We could not verify any forecast for 2027 inflation at the source, so we do not print one.

What Prediction Markets Say

On Polymarket, a US-based platform where users trade on real-world events, traders give Milei 44.5% to win the 2027 presidency, ahead of Axel Kicillof, the Buenos Aires province governor, at 33.5% and former economy minister Sergio Massa at 15.6%. Our explainer on Kicillof versus Milei sets out the contest.

About US$1.42 million has been traded in that market (read 8 November 2026, 7:39 p.m. ET). These prices are bets, not polls, and they can move with each inflation release.

Why we show this: prediction markets turn real-money bets into a live probability that moves within minutes of the news, which is why investors, campaigns and newsrooms in the United States now follow them closely. We show them next to polls and official results, never instead of them.

The National Congress building in Buenos Aires, seat of Argentina’s lawmakers. Photo from the Rio Times library.

What to Watch This Month

INDEC is due to publish October prices on Thursday 12 November 2026 at 16:00 Buenos Aires time (19:00 GMT), according to our economic calendar. A reading well above the survey’s 1.8% would reinforce the idea that disinflation has stalled.

What It Means for You

Investors in Argentine bonds and US-listed Argentine companies should watch the monthly figure and the peso together. A sticky 1.9% pace with a steady currency would be read as manageable, while a faster peso fall would raise the risk.

Travellers to Buenos Aires still face prices that move quickly, so compare costs in pesos with the current exchange rate. For the currency backdrop, read our report on the steady peso.

What Is Not Known

It is not known whether October inflation will come in at the survey’s 1.8% or above it. We also have no confirmed independent forecast for 2027 prices.

It is also unclear how a faster peso slide would change the path before the vote. We have not confirmed the exact election day in October 2027.

Frequently Asked Questions

What was Argentina’s inflation in September 2026?

Prices rose 1.9% in the month, up from 1.7% in August. The yearly rate was 33.4%, against 33.5% in August.

When is the next inflation figure?

INDEC is due to publish October prices on Thursday 12 November 2026 at 16:00 Buenos Aires time. Economists in the central bank’s expectations survey (REM) expect 1.8%.

Why does inflation matter for the 2027 election?

Prices shape household budgets and trust in the government’s economic plan. A stalled slowdown could weaken support before the October 2027 vote.

Sources: INDEC consumer price index for September 2026, released 13 October 2026 (indec.gob.ar); BCRA Market Expectations Survey (REM) of October 2026, published 5 November 2026 (bcra.gob.ar); Polymarket market “Argentina Presidential Election Winner” (polymarket.com). Related Rio Times reports: August inflation, Kicillof versus Milei and the steady peso.

World.title: Spain Drops Queen Letizia’s Bolivia Trip
World.content:
Spain’s Royal Household has called off Queen Letizia’s cooperation trip to Bolivia, palace sources say, citing insecurity in the Andean country and Spain’s early general election. It is the second delay after a first postponement in June 2026.

For US readers the decision is a signal about risk: Bolivia is still under a state of exception, and Washington already tells Americans to take extra care there. Travellers and investors should read it as a sign that the unrest has not settled.

Who: Queen Letizia of Spain and Bolivia’s president, Rodrigo Paz.

What: her aid trip to Bolivia is off again, with no new date.

Why: palace sources cite insecurity, and Spain’s election on Sunday 29 November 2026.

For US readers: the State Department lists Bolivia at Level 2, “exercise increased caution”.

As of 9 November 2026, 00:45 GMT

Power Index: Bolivia ranks 13th of 14 in The Rio Times Latin America Power Index, with 27.9 points (November 2026 edition).

In plain English: The Casa de Su Majestad el Rey is the Spanish royal household, which plans the king’s and queen’s agenda. AECID is Spain’s international development agency, and a state of exception is an emergency regime that lets a government deploy troops and limit some rights.

Why the Trip Was Called Off

The queen visits projects that Spain funds abroad through AECID, the Spanish aid agency. This year’s destination was Bolivia, and the visit had first been planned for late June 2026.

That first plan was put off because protests were blocking roads across Bolivia. Palace sources now say the security conditions for a large delegation still do not exist.

The second reason is political. Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez announced on Monday 5 October 2026 that Spain would vote early, and Royal Decree 806/2026 set the election for Sunday 29 November 2026.

The decree was published in the Official State Gazette (BOE) on Tuesday 6 October and dissolved parliament.

The city of La Paz, Bolivia’s seat of government, with Mount Illimani behind it.

What Bolivia’s State of Exception Means

President Paz declared a state of exception across the whole country on Saturday 20 June 2026, by Supreme Decree 5636, for 90 days, later extended by another 90 days. It followed about seven weeks of road blockades and protests, and it lets the army help clear highways.

Palace sources say the country is still under it. Our earlier reports track the measure, including how an earlier state of exception was extended, and the hard first year of Paz’s presidency.

Unrest has continued in other forms. Teachers have been warned over pay cuts during a strike, as we reported in our story on the teachers’ dispute.

Spain’s Election Context

Spaniards vote on Sunday 29 November 2026, after a campaign running from 13 to 27 November. The new parliament is due to meet on Wednesday 23 December.

The vote reshapes Spain’s foreign policy, including its aid budget for Latin America. Palace sources say the trip could return in the first half of 2027 if the next government agrees, and our guide to election day in Spain explains the vote.

What It Means for Travelers and US Readers

The State Department rates Bolivia at Level 2 overall. Check travel.state.gov before booking, because blockades can close roads and cut supplies to cities such as La Paz.

For investors, a royal trip is symbolic, but it shows how Madrid weighs the risk. The visit itself is only postponed.

The courtyard of the Casa de la Libertad in Sucre, Bolivia. photo. Courtyard of the Casa de la Libertad, Sucre, Bolivia, 2013. Photo: Henry Ponce Barco, CC BY-SA 4.0, Wikimedia Commons.

What Is Not Known

No new date has been set, and the Royal Household has not published a full statement that we could confirm. The queen raised the trip with Paz at the summit, according to palace sources; what was said is not known.

Frequently Asked Questions

Why was the queen’s Bolivia trip cancelled?

Palace sources cite insecurity in Bolivia and Spain’s early election on 29 November 2026. It is the second postponement after June.

Is it safe for Americans to visit Bolivia?

The State Department rates Bolivia Level 2, “exercise increased caution”. Check the current advisory before you travel.

When will the trip be rescheduled?

No date is fixed. Palace sources hope for the first half of 2027, subject to Spain’s next government and conditions in Bolivia.

Sources: Spain’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs (exteriores.gob.es), Royal Decree 806/2026 in the Official State Gazette (boe.es), Spanish government cabinet record of 5 October 2026 (lamoncloa.gob.es), Bolivia’s Supreme Decree 5636 of 20 June 2026, and the US State Department Bolivia travel advisory (travel.state.gov).

World.title: US Detention Reviews Fault Care in 23 Deaths
World.content:
The US agency that detains migrants has found fault with its own medical care in most of the deaths it reviewed. Documents from a records request by a US newspaper show that in 23 of 29 deaths between January 2025 and January 2026, investigators from Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) found that medical staff missed safe standards or withheld needed care.

The finding matters for US readers because ICE detention is funded by US taxpayers and overseen by Congress. It matters for Latin America because many of the dead are citizens of countries in the region, and their families live abroad.

Who: ICE, the US agency that holds migrants awaiting removal, wrote 29 internal death reviews for January 2025 to January 2026.

What: In 23 of the 29 cases, ICE’s own investigators found medical care fell short.

CPR: At least eight reviews describe CPR, the chest compressions that restart a heart, done wrongly or not at all.

Mexico: Mexico’s foreign ministry counts 18 Mexican citizens dead in US immigration custody or operations since January 2025.

As of 9 November 2026, 00:40 GMT

In plain English: ICE is part of the Department of Homeland Security, the US federal department that runs border and immigration enforcement. A death review is the internal report ICE writes after a detainee dies, judging whether staff followed the agency’s own rules.

Free daily brief — no card needed Get every Guatemala story in one morning email We build you a personalized brief around the topics you follow — free for 7 days. Love it? Your first month after that is US$1. Start my free brief Yes, email me my free daily brief — I can unsubscribe any time.

What the Internal Reviews Show

The 29 reports were obtained by a US newspaper through a public-records request. In 23 of them, ICE investigators concluded that medical staff left safe standards of care or failed to give services a detainee needed.

In only three of those 23 cases did investigators conclude that the lapses did not contribute directly to the death. The documents also describe at least eight deaths in which staff did not perform CPR correctly or did not perform it at all.

We have not seen the full set of 29 reports, so these figures rest on the newspaper’s reading of them. We therefore attribute them to the documents, not to our own review.

Separate reviews point the same way. On Friday 25 September 2026, ICE briefly posted a batch of mortality reviews on its public records library, and by 30 September they were no longer on the site.

This also signs you up to our weekday newsletter, The LatAm Brief. Nothing arrives until you click the confirmation link, and you can stop either with one click. Privacy policy

How Many Have Died, and Who Were They?

ICE’s own list shows 33 deaths in custody in calendar 2025. Press tallies of earlier years show no higher count since at least 2004.

Tallies published by late September 2026 count at least 56 deaths since Donald Trump returned to office in January 2025. ICE lists each death by fiscal year on its detainee death reporting page, with entries running through August 2026.

That page gives names and dates but no nationalities in the entries we checked. Mexico’s foreign ministry said in October 2026 that a man who died in Laredo, Texas, was the 18th Mexican citizen to die in immigration custody or enforcement operations since the start of Trump’s second term.

Other Latin Americans are among the dead. ICE announced that a 27-year-old Guatemalan man died on Monday 16 February 2026 at a Miami hospital after collapsing, with the cause under investigation.

The headquarters of ICE in Washington, the agency that writes the death reviews and runs the detention system. Photo: Ser Amantio di Nicolao, CC BY 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

What Congress and Government Say

ICE says it aims to post a news release on its website within two business days of a death. Spending laws passed by Congress also require ICE to make its reports on deaths in custody public within 90 days.

ICE’s Office of Professional Responsibility, the agency’s internal investigators, reviews each death. In October 2025, Senator Jon Ossoff, a Georgia Democrat, published an investigation that found 85 credible reports of medical neglect and 82 of detainees denied enough food or water.

What It Means for You

If you have a relative in ICE detention, ask the detaining office in writing for a medical check and keep a record of the request. Your country’s consulate can visit, press for care and help with the return of remains, as Mexico’s consulates say they do.

US readers who follow immigration policy should watch whether Congress forces faster, fuller release of these reviews. Our report on Costa Rica’s 77 citizens in ICE detention shows how Latin American governments track their people inside the system.

For wider context, read our report on continuing US deportations. Venezuelans’ legal status is covered in our report on the deportation shield.

The National Palace on the Zócalo in Mexico City, seat of the Mexican government, whose foreign ministry has announced Mexican deaths in ICE custody. photo. The Palacio Nacional, the government palace on the Zócalo square in Mexico City, 2015. Photo: Daniel Case, CC BY-SA 3.0, Wikimedia Commons.

What Is Not Known

The full text of the 29 reviews is not public in a form we can check, and the nationalities of most of the dead are unconfirmed. We do not know how many of the dead were from Latin America as a whole.

Counts of deaths differ by a few cases because sources define custody differently. It is not known whether ICE will change medical practice.

Frequently Asked Questions

What did the ICE death reviews find?

In 23 of 29 deaths between January 2025 and January 2026, ICE investigators found medical care fell short of safe standards, according to documents from a records request. At least eight reviews describe CPR done wrongly or not at all.

Where can families find out if a relative died in ICE custody?

ICE posts each death on its detainee death reporting page and aims to do so within two business days. Families abroad can also ask their country’s consulate in the United States for help.

Are deaths in ICE custody rising?

ICE’s own list shows 33 deaths in calendar 2025, higher than any year since at least 2004. Independent tallies count at least 56 since January 2025.

Sources: ICE detainee death reporting page (ice.gov/detain/detainee-death-reporting), ICE public records library, Office of Senator Jon Ossoff investigation report of October 2025 (ossoff.senate.gov), Mexican Ministry of Foreign Affairs statements of 2026 (sre.gob.mx), and the documents of a US public-records request.
