World.title: New Spirit ferries not using autopilot near Geelong after steering faults
World.content:
The operator of the new Spirit of Tasmania ferries has suspended autopilot use during transits of Port Phillip Bay as it probes the ships' steering faults.

Spirit IV was on its fifth-ever passenger voyage last Thursday when its primary steering system failed as it neared the bay en route to Geelong.

The issue occurred when the steering control was switched from autopilot to manual mode.

A back-up steering system ended up being used, and a tugboat was called to escort the ferry to Geelong, delaying its scheduled arrival by about four hours.

A track map shows Spirit IV made several turns outside Point Lonsdale before entering Port Phillip Bay. (ABC News: Hamed Akrami)

The incident came after a separate steering fault caused its sister ship, Spirit V, to briefly move outside the bay's charted shipping lane during a trial voyage in October.

Loading...

Both matters are now under investigation by the Australian Transport Safety Bureau.

On Monday, TT-Line chairman Ken Kanofski said last week's incident on Spirit IV involved a "frustratingly minor issue".

"There's an ongoing investigation, and I don't want to prejudice that by kind of declaring exactly that everything's been dealt with," Mr Kanofski told 936 ABC Hobart.

"When Spirit IV docked in Geelong, an inspection found a frustratingly minor issue with mechanical electrical processes in the steering console itself.

" And that was rectified and so the ship left that evening without incident. "

Ken Kanofski, pictured in May, says the steering issue on Spirit IV was caused by a "frustratingly minor issue". (ABC News: Kate Nickels)

Mr Kanofski said the autopilot, which allows a ship to automatically follow a pre-determined route, is no longer being used when approaching and departing Geelong.

"So at the moment, we're not using autopilot in the bay, in Geelong, in Port Phillip Bay," Mr Kanofski said.

However, the autopilot will still be used once the ship reaches the open waters of Bass Strait, he said.

Mr Kanofski said the autopilot was never used for the ferries' arrival and departure at Devonport, in Tasmania's north-west.

"It's a very different entry to port than Geelong," he said.

"Obviously in Geelong you come in through the heads, and you've got quite a long way to navigate to get to port.

"In Devonport it's a very short distance, and so that's always been a completely manual process.

"But we've taken a range of interim measures to ensure that the ships and the passengers are safe, and that's our number one priority here."

The new Spirit of Tasmania ferries began carrying passengers across Bass Strait in late October. (Supplied: David Wallace)

The ABC asked TT-Line when it plans to resume its use of autopilot during transits of Port Phillip Bay.

A spokesperson said it had "no plans to resume the use of autopilot for all channel and close quarter navigation."

They said the situation would be reviewed once the ATSB releases its report, which is due by the middle of next year.

On Sunday, Spirit IV conducted an exercise off Devonport that was described by TT-Line as a "planned, routine check of its equipment".

World.title: Arena 'electric' as 36ers debutant hits buzzer beater
World.content:
Adelaide 36ers have had an epic three-year run with 46 consecutive sellout games, but few crowds have been louder than on Saturday night when 16-year old Raheim "RJ" Brown Jr hit a buzzer-beating three-pointer on debut.

"It was a crazy moment to hit the shot," Brown Jr told ABC Sport.

" It was electric in the arena. My ears were ringing after. The fans were crazy. "

The 36ers stormed to a 28-point win over Illawarra in the NBL match at the Adelaide Entertainment Centre on Saturday.

The point guard, who turned 16 a week ago, had been on the court for just 73 seconds when he made the shot.

The Year 10 student made headlines across the basketball world in September when the then-15-year-old became the youngest player signed by an NBL club in 44 years; and now sits behind John Horder and Craig Viney (who both played at 15 years and 8 months old) as the youngest debutants in history.

"It was totally a surprise. I was just waiting for my opportunity and when the coach put me in I tried to make the most of it," Brown Jr said.

Sitting in the crowd of over 10,000 were RJ's parents Coco and Raheim Brown Senior, who were elated when their son was injected into the game.

"We've been to every game as a fan to support the team … we never knew when that time was going to happen but RJ was prepared for it," Brown Snr said.

"Once he got out there and hit the shot I was electrified like the whole of Adelaide was. It was a really proud moment."

Deonte Williams (left) celebrates after Raheim Brown Jr (right) shoots a three-point at the end of the game. (Getty Images)

Brown Jr is a product of the Adelaide 36ers High Performance Schools Program that works across numerous metropolitan schools including Woodville High.

His talent transitioned into the NBL1 where he averaged 20 points per game in the West Adelaide senior reserves side and was able to feature nine times for the Bearcats.

Now in the NBL, he is training and learning alongside six-time MVP Bryce Cotton and five-time championship coach Trevor Gleeson.

"Pre-game warm ups, going through plays, they're all super locked in. They all take care of their body," Brown Jr said.

"The biggest thing is the pace of the game. It's a lot faster than NBL1, or under-18s."

The 36ers will be hoping Saturday's win is the catalyst to boost their chances this season.

Sitting fifth with a record of 6-6 they'll likely regain injured winger Flynn Cameron for Thursday night's clash with Melbourne United; and unveil new recruit Bul Kuol in December.

You can hear ABC Sport's call of the Adelaide 36ers v Melbourne United from 6.30pm Thursday on ABC Listen through the Sport Extra button.

World.title: Two survivors of fatal helicopter crash in Indonesia named
World.content:
The two survivors of a fatal helicopter crash in Indonesia have been named, as authorities continue to investigate what caused the incident.

Local authorities said Australian Michael Betteridge and New Zealander Hugh Page survived after the helicopter they were flying nosedived into a river on the island of Borneo yesterday.

The aircraft was collecting water for firefighting operations from the Barito River in South Kalimantan province when it went down.

Video posted online shows people rescuing Mr Betteridge and Mr Page from the water shortly after the crash occurred, before they were treated at a military hospital.

A third Indonesian crew member, navigator Yayan Supyansuri, died and was found by rescue teams yesterday.

The helicopter was collecting water to fight fires when it crashed into a river in Borneo. (Supplied)

The helicopter was contracted to Indonesian authorities to help fight its worst forest and land fire season in more than a decade.

"The National Disaster Management Agency (BNPB) is committed to facilitating an official investigation by the relevant authorities to determine the exact cause of the crash," BNPB spokesperson Berton SP Panjaitan said.

"As a follow-up action, BNPB will conduct a comprehensive safety evaluation of aerial operations.

"The review will encompass the technical readiness of the fleet, water-bombing procedures, aircrew fitness and qualifications, weather conditions, and site-specific characteristics."

A spokesperson for Australia's Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade said in a statement it was "providing consular assistance to an Australian who was rescued safely following a helicopter crash in Indonesia".

"Australian officials are in close contact with local authorities following the incident," they said.

A spokesperson for New Zealand's Ministry of Foreign Affairs and Trade said in a statement it was aware of the crash and its embassy in Jakarta was making further enquiries.

Do you know more about this story? Contact Patrick Martin via email on martin.patrick@abc.net.au, or on Signal @patrickmartinabcnews.56. If you're sharing sensitive information, read our tips on how to contact us confidentially.

Second crash in a week

The crash comes after three Indonesian crew were killed when a separate water-bombing helicopter crashed on November 4 in Central Kalimantan.

The helicopter was carrying eight crew and also crashed while loading water.

Haze crisis reignites regional frustration Widespread fires in Indonesia are prompting calls for legal action or boycotts in neighbouring countries blanketed by the smoke, ahead of an ASEAN foreign ministers' meeting.

Forest and land fires have been burning across large swathes of Indonesia, particularly in the Indonesian portion of Borneo, known as Kalimantan, in Sumatra and in Papua.

The fires often burn in peatland, making them notoriously difficult to extinguish as embers continue to burn deep underground.

Indonesia's environment minister said more than 100,000 personnel had been involved in fighting fires across the country this year.

Toxic smoke and haze from the blazes has caused more than 400,000 acute respiratory infections, according to the country's health ministry.

The fires are commonly linked to land-clearing operations, with more than 240 people and 20 companies accused by Indonesian authorities of deliberately or negligently lighting fires.

World.title: Top NSW One Nation candidate repeats ‘frankly outrageous’ conspiracy theory in protest speech
World.content:
NationalNSWOne Nation Top NSW One Nation candidate repeats ‘frankly outrageous’ conspiracy theory in protest speech Anthony Segaert November 9, 2026 — 1:50pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. One Nation’s top NSW upper house candidate alluded to the far-right “great replacement” conspiracy theory in a protest speech at the weekend that Premier Chris Minns labelled “frankly outrageous and racist”. Stuart Bonds, the top upper house candidate for the party in NSW, told protesters at a rally against “mass migration” on Sunday that “we are being demographically replaced inside our own nation”. Stuart Bonds, One Nation’s upper house candidate, speaks at an anti-migration rally in Sydney on Sunday. Facebook/Stuart Bonds “We are in the fight of our lives. Make no mistake,” he told protesters in Sydney, adding the “socialist plan” was to “destroy and bring down and tear down the fabric of your civilisation”. Minns on Monday described the remarks as “horrific” and reliant on “a conspiracy theory that’s been imported from the US here to Australia”.



“It makes me think: well, this bloke’s heading the ticket for One Nation,” he said. “If they win the election, what ministry is he going to have? Trade, education, treasury?” Related Article Exclusive

NSW Votes ‘Clean energy journey is ours for the taking’: The pro-renewables past of NSW One Nation leader revealed One Nation is a growing threat to NSW Labor in the March 2027 state election and Minns repeated his view that Mike Newman, One Nation’s leader in the state, will “either be the premier or the opposition leader”. Resolve polling shows 25 per cent of NSW voters intend to vote for One Nation in March. After joking about a man named “Sanjay” who had crashed into the protest organisers’ truck before the event on Sunday, Bond said he would fight against Australia’s “demographic suicide” and becoming a “special economic zone of Asia”. The great replacement theory, which began in the late 1800s, posits that European and Western populations are being deliberately and systematically replaced by non-Western populations. Bonds made references to Asia in his speech.



Federal Assistant Multicultural Affairs Minister Julian Hill said it was “sadly not surprising a lead One Nation candidate is openly pushing racist, white supremacist conspiracy theories”, according to AAP. “The ‘great replacement theory’ is a widely discredited far-right, nationalist conspiracy with antisemitic roots. It’s also mathematically nonsensical … Australians can draw their own conclusions as to why One Nation constantly gets embroiled in issues of race and culture and want to import that kind of chaos and division into our beautiful country.” During the speech – in which Bond also covered abortion rates, white South Africans on “stolen land” and the Bondi Beach shooters – the One Nation candidate said he didn’t accept that “an immigrant arriving yesterday is as Australian as you or me”, to cheers from the crowd. “If we don’t support Australian mothers having Australian children, we are going to pay for other cultures’ children to be brought up in our lands,” he said. World.content:
US tech giant Meta has declined to commit to giving Australian teenagers the protections promised to young Americans under a settlement worth up to $US18 billion ($26 billion).

The deal with US states will set default two-hour daily limits and overnight blocks on teen Facebook and Instagram accounts. Meta did not admit wrongdoing.

Greens senator Sarah Hanson-Young pressed Meta regional director Mia Garlick at a Senate hearing on the Digital Duty of Care Bill this afternoon.

“Is it correct that right now there are protections that will be available to young people in the United States that are not available here in Australia,” Hanson-Young said.

World.content:

Former Swan Nick Blakey has officially started his North Melbourne career with an appearance on the opening day of pre-season training. Blakey, who crossed to his father John’s old club in a high-profile trade this off-season, joined the Roos’ first-to-fourth-year players at Arden Street on Monday, along with fellow senior players, including Harry Sheezel, George Wardlaw, Luke Parker, Griffin Logue and Tristan Xerri. Nick Blakey steps onto the training track as a North melbourne player. Owen Leonard / X The 26-year-old defender signed an eight-year deal with North Melbourne worth more than $11 million, with the Kangaroos handing over two first-round picks in the trade. North are beginning a new era under coach Jaymie Graham after sacking four-time premiership coach Alastair Clarkson.



Blakey remains one of the subjects in an ongoing Victoria Police investigation into sexual assault allegations at the Pullman hotel on August 17. Isaac Heeney, Chad Warner, James Jordon and Riley Bice were also present in the hotel room. Police now consider Bice and two other men who were there, including recently retired ex-teammate Taylor Adams, as witnesses to the pre-dawn events. Nick Blakey will follow in the footsteps of his father John (right) in playing for the Kangaroos. Nathan John, North Melbourne FC The players maintain their innocence and have denied any criminal wrongdoing. Essendon and Richmond were also among the clubs to resume pre-season training on Monday.



Like the Kangaroos, the Bombers also have a new coach, Mark McVeigh who attended training alongside the club’s new general manager of performance, John Longmire. Many of Essendon’s leading lights turned out for training with the first-to-fourth-year crew, headlined by captain Andy McGrath, Mason Redman, Jye Caldwell and Kyle Langford. New Essendon coach Mark McVeigh keeps a close eye on training on Monday. Getty Images Star Bomber Nic Martin has a big summer ahead after missing the entire 2026 season after suffering a setback in November last year while recovering from an ACL rupture. World.title: Beau Lamarre-Condon trial live updates: Former NSW Police officer’s cross-examination continues over alleged murders of Jesse Baird, Luke Davies
World.content:
Hello and welcome to our live coverage of Beau Lamarre-Condon’s criminal trial in the NSW Supreme Court in Sydney.

Lamarre-Condon, 31, has pleaded not guilty to two counts of murder over the deaths of Jesse Baird, 26, a former TV presenter, and Luke Davies, 29, a Qantas flight attendant, in Paddington on February 19, 2024. His case is that he acted in self-defence, the 15-person jury has been told.

The former NSW police officer started giving evidence on Thursday and returns to the witness box at 10am today for cross-examination by Crown prosecutor Brett Hatfield, SC.

Here are the key parts of his evidence about the men’s deaths:

Lamarre-Condon said he entered Baird’s Paddington share house through an open door on February 19, 2024, to collect some of his belongings – including a $25,000 Cartier ring and Casablanca shirts worth thousands – after their relationship ended in November 2023. He said he also had a key with him that Baird had cut for him in November.

He said his relationship with Baird was romantic but was not exclusive. He believed nobody was home despite the door being ajar when he entered the home, he said.

The accused had his police weapon with him because he had contemplated taking his own life on February 18 over work-related trauma and had intended to return it to Miranda police station later that day, he said.

He said he struck upon an idea that morning to dress as an Uber Eats delivery rider and used a motorcycle helmet, high-visibility clothing and bags he saw on a bike in Paddington. “I was worried if I knocked on the door it may be perceived as harassment ... because Jesse told me, ‘please refrain from contacting me’,” Lamarre-Condon said.

He entered the home after knocking three times and saying hello loudly and receiving no reply.

He ran upstairs and hid when he heard noises in the home and came back downstairs later, encountering Baird in the kitchen. He said he took off the high-visibility jacket upstairs and his firearm was “secreted under my shirt. You could not see it. It was actually to the rear of me on a plain-clothes holster so no one could be under the impression that I had a firearm on me”.

Baird did not recognise Lamarre-Condon with the helmet on and lunged at him with a knife, he said. He said at one stage the knife “tore my whole blue shirt open” and he was pinned to a wall in the kitchen.

He shot Baird once in the shoulder to disarm him and accidentally in the head when they fell to the floor.

“I 110 per cent stand by that first shot because if I didn’t do it Jesse Baird would be sitting here in the box today, and he would have to explain why he drove a knife into my throat,” he said.

“Jesse did not have his finger on the trigger,” he said. “It was my fault. I’ve said from the start I am guilty of manslaughter and I’m responsible for his death, but it wasn’t intentional.”

Lamarre-Condon said he found a phone and called Triple Zero and went into “police mode” to try to “save” Baird.

The accused said Davies grabbed the gun and pointed it at him, and later pulled the trigger and shot himself in front of Baird’s bedroom door. The Crown case is that Lamarre-Condon shot Davies through the door.

He admitted to cleaning Baird’s house and disposing of the men’s bodies before turning himself in to police on February 23, 2024.

Support is available from the National Sexual Assault, Domestic Family Violence Counselling Service at 1800RESPECT (1800 737 732), the Men’s Referral Service on 1300 766 491, and Lifeline on 13 11 14.

World.title: What to stream this week: Keira Knightley is back in Black Doves, plus five more picks
World.content:
What to stream this week (clockwise from top left): Yaga; Paolo; Abbott Elementary; The Mob; Black Doves; and The Oldest Person in the World.

Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

This week’s picks include the return of Keira Knightley and Ben Whishaw’s London assassins in Black Doves, Hudson’s Williams’ first post-Heated Rivalry gig, a bonkers reality show hosted by Parker Posey and season six of sweet-hearted sitcom Abbott Elementary. Black Doves ★★★★ (Netflix) Delightfully pulpy and propulsive, Netflix’s spy thriller Black Doves isn’t the show you’d expect to win over Keira Knightley, one of the few esteemed actors who had avoided television, missing the prestigious wave entirely. It’s maybe why, when the show’s first season dropped in 2024, I assumed it was a dour, restrained spy drama. In short, I was completely wrong. If anything, Black Doves’ first season was a little too chaotic, with copious blood, twists and tinsel, as spy duo Helen Webb (Knightley) and Sam Young (Ben Whishaw) fought for their lives, often destroying Christmas decorations across London in the process. Ben Whishaw as Sam and Keira Knightley as Helen Webb in Black Doves. With creator Joe Barton (Giri/Haji, Amadeus) back at the helm, season two doesn’t slow down but it’s less crowded, dropping both the festive season schtick and the excessive backstory. (The exception is a sluggish fourth episode cramming together flashbacks and side-plots.) Still undercover, Helen remains married to Wallace (Andrew Buchan), a British MP about to become PM through a Tory leadership spill – all to the plan of the Black Doves, the agency Helen works for, vacuuming up government secrets so they can be sold to the highest bidder.



Related Article ★★★★

Review I thought we didn’t need any more stories about Muhammad Ali. I was wrong Before you worry that moving into 10 Downing Street would impede Helen’s ability to undertake covert missions, Helen’s season two body count reaches double digits within 10 minutes as she sneaks off from a charity gala to crack into a hotel room safe. To be fair, she has help: With Sam leaving the Doves, Helen’s handler Reed (Sarah Lancashire) teams her up with Laila (Ambika Mod), a Gen Z agent who dismisses Helen as a “spy wife”. Wouldn’t the First Lady be tailed 24/7 by security? Not in the Black Doves world, where Helen can kill henchmen in broad daylight, unidentifiable due to a baseball cap that her allies call outright preposterous. As with the first season, don’t think too hard about it; that’s easy enough, as the plot speeds so fast any holes register as funny bumps. Ambika Mod as Laila and Keira Knightley as Helen Webb in Black Doves. What exactly is the second season’s plot? Reed goes missing and Helen doesn’t trust her replacement handler; Sam, wanting out, is blackmailed into a series of kills that could be linked to Reed. Both worry they’re losing their edge, regret when they violently lash out to prove otherwise – and, deep within, remain haunted by the killers they have become, with Knightley and Whishaw letting that fear flood through in overwhelming flashes. Much like Black Doves itself, Helen and Sam constantly chase the thrill of action, knowing they could fall apart completely if they pause for too long. That works for now, but maybe not another season. Hudson Williams in Yaga.



Yaga ★★★ (Binge) A witch from Slavic folklore descends upon a small Canadian town in Yaga – a sexy supernatural thriller and feminist exhumation of Baba Yaga, though it’s primarily been marketed as Hudson Williams’ first gig since Heated Rivalry. Two gigs, technically: Williams plays Henry, a brattish heir (blinding blue contacts), and his roommate (glasses, emerald eyes), neither making much impact. Related Article Australian TV Why it will be crime time (all the time) on Australian screens next year Yaga opens with Henry’s disappearance. His parents send in his longtime friend Rapp (Noah Reid, Schitt’s Creek) as an investigator, though he’s initially more focused on every woman her meets. Despite dripping with chauvinism, Rapp proves irresistible to many and intriguing to others, such as local detective Carson (Clark Backo) and the commanding university professor Dr Hargrove (Carrie-Anne Moss, The Matrix), a bone expert and author of a book titled Sexy Bones. At least one person isn’t a fan of Rapp: whoever nailed a burning chicken carcass to his hotel door, the first of many occult occurrences. While over-reliant on dream sequences and hallucinations, Yaga’s mystical moodiness is intoxicating – as is its strange sense of humour, such as the Russian-language covers of Blondie and Nancy Sinatra during the credits. Across the seven of eight episodes available for review, Yaga is intriguing yet a little heavy-handed, with lines such as “a witch is just somebody society has decided they’re afraid of” perhaps working better in creator Kat Sandler’s 2019 play of the same name. The Mob. DISNEY



The Mob ★★★ (Disney+) Parker Posey (The White Lotus) camps it up as host of The Mob, the latest reality riff on The Traitors, which leans into its mafia-theme with more cheese than a carbonara. Twelve celebrities form a crime family, compete with Mafia-themed challenges, and try to avoid being “whacked” by the Don, the group’s elected lead, who also can be rolled each episode. Too nonsensical to match The Traitors’ mind games, The Mob is best when competitors play into the mystery theatre feel. Debi Mazar (Goodfellas), Aida Turturro (The Sopranos) and Joe Gorga (Real Housewives of New Jersey) clearly have a great time. Abbott Elementary creator and star Quinta Brunson. Ser Baffo/ABC via AP Abbott Elementary ★★★★ (Disney+) Six seasons in, Abbott Elementary remains my go-to for a sweet-hearted sitcom. It’s a warm, funny mockumentary about teachers trying to make do at an underfunded, predominantly Black public school in Philadelphia, inspired by creator-star Quinta Brunson’s mum. For the most part, the series hasn’t messed with its magic. More episodes than not see terminally optimistic Janine (Brunson) overextend herself, such as the season six opener where she loses her sanity decorating her classroom. Jerome Niel in Paolo.



Paolo ★★★ (HBO Max) Admiration becomes deadly obsession in Paolo, a seven-part psychological thriller from France in the vein of Ripley. Where Paolo – a Portuguese piano mover played by a menacing Jerome Niel – learns that a high-society ex-schoolmate (Yoann Gasiorowski) is running in a local election, it stirs up powerful discomforts and desires, drawing Paolo to volunteer. It’s not long before blood spills, but Paolo’s a slow burn. A dense focus on the campaign’s machinations may link Paolo’s rage to a wider political context, but it will turn off those wanting France’s answer to Saltburn. French supercentenarian Jeanne Louise Calment, who lived to be 122 years old. The Oldest Person in the World ★★★★ (DocPlay) For the past decade, experimental documentarian Sam Green has travelled the globe meeting the oldest person in the world, a Guinness World Record title that continually shifts as the record holders die. Do they hold the secret to life? That’s what Green hopes to capture, though his interviews with supercentenarians – all but one are women – are often filled with platitudes, the weight of their experiences never quite translated. Via contemplative voiceover, Green questions our fascination with the world’s oldest people and is remarkably raw about his motivations, including a health scare, his brother’s suicide and son’s birth. Want more TV? We’ve got you.

World.title: Man accused of delivery driver murder exposes himself to court
World.content:
NationalVictoriaCrime Man accused of delivery driver murder exposes himself to court Roy Ward and James Costa Updated November 9, 2026 — 1:21pm ,first published November 9, 2026 — 6:32am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. The man charged with murdering a food delivery driver in central Melbourne was removed from a court video link after exposing himself. Robert Urbano, 51, appeared briefly in Melbourne Magistrates’ Court on Monday over the stabbing death of Feng Jianming, 47, and seriously injuring a fellow delivery rider. A court sketch of Robert Urbano’s video link appearance on Monday. Anita Lester The court was hearing details of Urbano’s schizophrenia diagnosis when he stood on a chair in his holding room, pulled his pants down and exposed himself to the camera. Magistrate John Livitsanos immediately removed Urbano, who is charged with murder and intentionally causing serious injury, from the hearing link.



Urbano, of Footscray, had been visibly agitated during the short appearance, pacing around, fidgeting and attempting to leave. At one point, Urbano interjected when Feng’s injuries were being discussed, saying that he was the one who had been hurt. Feng Jianming with his wife Xu Hongfeng and children Yawei and Changhui from several years ago. “I have injury on my hand,” Urbano said before being remanded in custody until March. Feng was working for food delivery platform HungryPanda on Friday night near Queen Victoria Market when he and another delivery rider confronted a man who was allegedly tampering with their bikes.



Police were called to Chongqing Chicken Pot City restaurant in Frederick Way soon after 8pm where they found a critically injured Feng. Another rider, 34, was allegedly found nearby with stab wounds. Paramedics performed CPR on Feng, but he died at the scene. The 34-year-old man was taken to hospital with serious injuries. Feng Jianming with his son Changhui. Few family photos exist due to Feng’s many years spent away from China supporting them. Urbano allegedly left the scene and was arrested in Footscray on Saturday morning. Feng’s death has sparked anger in Melbourne’s Asian community over public safety in the CBD while the safety and work conditions of delivery drivers has also come under scrutiny.



Hundreds of people joined an emotional rally at the State Library on Saturday night to honour Feng. His wife, Xu Hongfeng, and their adult children, daughter Yawei and son Changhui, expressed their heartbreak from their home in China. Police at the scene on Saturday. Joe Armao Xu told this masthead that Feng worked tirelessly to send money back to China to support his family, including his elderly parents. She said he had not returned home for nine years to save on airfares.



“He wanted to save the money and continue working,” she told this masthead through a translator. “But he promised that when our son got married, he would definitely return. That was the plan. He would come home for our son’s wedding, and then we could finally be together as a family. We thought we only had to wait another year or two.” A second vigil held outside the State Library for delivery rider Feng Jianming on Saturday evening. Alexander Darling Melbourne Lord Mayor Nick Reece, who attended the vigil, told this masthead he had spoken with HungryPanda management and offered to hold a roundtable to discuss safety conditions for delivery riders in the city. “Delivery riders have to be some of the most underappreciated people in our city,” Reece said.



“They deliver our meals, our packages, rain, hail or shine seven days a week and are often not well paid… and, as we have seen, their jobs are very risky as well, not just from other vehicles on the road but from horrible attacks like the one we saw last night.” An online fundraiser for Feng’s family has exceeded $420,000 in donations. With Alexander Darling Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: Victorian election hot seats: Melbourne’s west promised $400m in new transport services
World.content:
For people living in Melbourne’s fast-growing western suburbs, one of the most common and longest-running complaints has been a lack of buses, with some schoolchildren facing half-hour walks to the nearest stop – and an additional wait for a service to show up.

For Sydenham locals, Labor’s $400 million pledge to rewrite west Melbourne’s bus routes with services running on key routes every 10 minutes if re-elected on November 28, will no doubt be appealing.

Under the proposal, about two thirds of pre-existing routes will be upgraded to ‘turn-up-and-go’ services, with a bus promised every 10 minutes, seven days a week. Labor will also create a series of new routes across the west that will connect to train stations.

World.title: Forrestania high-grade gold hits fuel 35% WA resource surge
World.content:
Sponsored BusinessCompaniesBulls N' Bears Forrestania high-grade gold hits fuel 35% WA resource surge Brought to you by BULLS N’ BEARS Murray Ward November 9, 2026 — 1:19pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Emerging gold producer Forrestania Resources has delivered a trifecta of news from its WA gold operations, tabling a suite of high-grade drill hits that have underpinned a significant resource upgrade at its British Hill project, in addition to locking in a new separate ore purchase agreement to feed its soon-to-be-commissioned processing hub. The company’s latest 19-hole, 4246-metre reverse-circulation drill program at British Hill, 75 kilometres south-southeast of Southern Cross in the revered Yilgarn Mineral Field, returned a thick, high-grade and remarkably shallow intersection of 16m assaying 5.77 grams per tonne (g/t) gold from just 12m downhole. Forrestania Resources’ British Hill project sits 75km south-southeast of Southern Cross in Western Australia’s rich Yilgarn Mineral Field. Other significant hits included an even richer intercept of 2m at 13.36g/t gold from 231m depth, alongside 9m grading 5.48g/t gold from 202m and 11m running at 4.19g/t gold from 210m. The successful drill campaign has prompted Forrestania to upgrade the mineral resource estimate at British Hill by a whopping 35 per cent, taking it from 212,400 ounces to a new total of 5.7 million tonnes at 1.57g/t gold for a hefty 286,000 ounces.



‘Drilling is improving our understanding of the system and identifying opportunities for further resource growth.’ Forrestania Resources chairman David Geraghty Gold mineralisation at British Hill is hosted within sheared and quartz-veined rocks in the prolific Southern Cross-Forrestania Greenstone Belt. The company has lodged additional Program of Work applications to chase mineralisation interpreted to exist west of the current drilling, with a diamond drilling campaign also planned to begin shortly. Forrestania Resources executive chairman David Geraghty said: “Another demonstrably strong batch of results has reinforced our confidence in British Hill. High-grade mineralisation continues to be encountered across the deposit, while drilling is improving our understanding of the system and identifying opportunities for further resource growth. British Hill is increasingly demonstrating the attributes of a potentially valuable near-term gold development asset for Forrestania.” Capping off a busy day on the market, Forrestania also announced it has shored up its feedstock by executing an ore purchase agreement with Dundas Minerals to treat up to 750,000 tonnes of ore over an initial 24-month period from Dundas’ Rockland gold project. The ore is likely to feed the Lake Johnson processing facility, which is slated for commissioning in early 2027. The deal marks another key plank in the company’s now familiar “hub-and-spoke” strategy and follows a similar agreement for 400,000 tonnes of ore inked late last month with High-Tech Metals for its Mt Fisher gold project. These third-party deals also complement an earlier arrangement with Star Minerals for 400,000 tonnes of ore from its Tumblegum deposit, all designed to feed Forrestania’s two central processing hubs at Edna May and Lake Johnston.



The company is already hauling ore from its Taipan deposit to Edna May, where dry commissioning is now underway ahead of a targeted first ore processing in December. The second hub at Lake Johnston is slated for commissioning in early 2027, with ore from the burgeoning British Hill deposit already stockpiled at site ahead of the plant’s restart. Forrestania’s aggressive growth strategy has also been underscored by its takeover of Zenith Minerals. With 65.4 per cent of Zenith already tucked under its belt, the company appears to be firmly in the box seat as it hunts down the magic 90 per cent ownership mark needed to trigger compulsory acquisition. The offer for Zenith will close at 5pm (AWST) on November 12. The company has ruled out any further extensions unless legally compelled under section 624(2) of the Corporations Act 2001, which provides for an automatic extension in certain circumstances, effectively putting the clock on Zenith shareholders still weighing up their options. Taking control of Zenith will add another 675,000 ounces of gold to Forrestania’s inventory, bringing its global resource base to more than two million ounces. The moves come as Australia’s Office of the Chief Economist forecasts national gold production to rise from 340 tonnes in 2025–26 to 359 tonnes in 2027–28, with high prices encouraging miners to maximise output. While the spot gold price has been volatile after hitting record highs earlier in the year, projects that can demonstrate persistent grade and a clear path to a processing plant are becoming increasingly relevant.



With Forrestania on the cusp of firing up its Edna May processing hub, a resource upgrade at a key satellite deposit and another ore deal to bolster feedstock, the company looks to be systematically assembling the pieces of a significant WA gold production business. If the drill bit continues to deliver, it may not be long before British Hill adds even more ounces to a burgeoning production pipeline. Is your ASX-listed company doing something interesting? Contact: mattbirney@bullsnbears.com.au

World.title: Top NSW One Nation candidate repeats ‘frankly outrageous’ conspiracy theory in protest speech
World.content:
NationalNSWOne Nation Top NSW One Nation candidate repeats ‘frankly outrageous’ conspiracy theory in protest speech Anthony Segaert November 9, 2026 — 1:50pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. One Nation’s top NSW upper house candidate alluded to the far-right “great replacement” conspiracy theory in a protest speech at the weekend that Premier Chris Minns labelled “frankly outrageous and racist”. Stuart Bonds, the top upper house candidate for the party in NSW, told protesters at a rally against “mass migration” on Sunday that “we are being demographically replaced inside our own nation”. Stuart Bonds, One Nation’s upper house candidate, speaks at an anti-migration rally in Sydney on Sunday. Facebook/Stuart Bonds “We are in the fight of our lives. Make no mistake,” he told protesters in Sydney, adding the “socialist plan” was to “destroy and bring down and tear down the fabric of your civilisation”. Minns on Monday described the remarks as “horrific” and reliant on “a conspiracy theory that’s been imported from the US here to Australia”.



“It makes me think: well, this bloke’s heading the ticket for One Nation,” he said. “If they win the election, what ministry is he going to have? Trade, education, treasury?” Related Article Exclusive

NSW Votes ‘Clean energy journey is ours for the taking’: The pro-renewables past of NSW One Nation leader revealed One Nation is a growing threat to NSW Labor in the March 2027 state election and Minns repeated his view that Mike Newman, One Nation’s leader in the state, will “either be the premier or the opposition leader”. Resolve polling shows 25 per cent of NSW voters intend to vote for One Nation in March. After joking about a man named “Sanjay” who had crashed into the protest organisers’ truck before the event on Sunday, Bond said he would fight against Australia’s “demographic suicide” and becoming a “special economic zone of Asia”. The great replacement theory, which began in the late 1800s, posits that European and Western populations are being deliberately and systematically replaced by non-Western populations. Bonds made references to Asia in his speech.



Federal Assistant Multicultural Affairs Minister Julian Hill said it was “sadly not surprising a lead One Nation candidate is openly pushing racist, white supremacist conspiracy theories”, according to AAP. “The ‘great replacement theory’ is a widely discredited far-right, nationalist conspiracy with antisemitic roots. It’s also mathematically nonsensical … Australians can draw their own conclusions as to why One Nation constantly gets embroiled in issues of race and culture and want to import that kind of chaos and division into our beautiful country.” During the speech – in which Bond also covered abortion rates, white South Africans on “stolen land” and the Bondi Beach shooters – the One Nation candidate said he didn’t accept that “an immigrant arriving yesterday is as Australian as you or me”, to cheers from the crowd. “If we don’t support Australian mothers having Australian children, we are going to pay for other cultures’ children to be brought up in our lands,” he said. US tech giant Meta has declined to commit to giving Australian teenagers the protections promised to young Americans under a settlement worth up to $US18 billion ($26 billion).

The deal with US states will set default two-hour daily limits and overnight blocks on teen Facebook and Instagram accounts. Meta did not admit wrongdoing.

Greens senator Sarah Hanson-Young pressed Meta regional director Mia Garlick at a Senate hearing on the Digital Duty of Care Bill this afternoon.

“Is it correct that right now there are protections that will be available to young people in the United States that are not available here in Australia,” Hanson-Young said.

Former Swan Nick Blakey has officially started his North Melbourne career with an appearance on the opening day of pre-season training. Blakey, who crossed to his father John’s old club in a high-profile trade this off-season, joined the Roos’ first-to-fourth-year players at Arden Street on Monday, along with fellow senior players, including Harry Sheezel, George Wardlaw, Luke Parker, Griffin Logue and Tristan Xerri. Nick Blakey steps onto the training track as a North melbourne player. Owen Leonard / X The 26-year-old defender signed an eight-year deal with North Melbourne worth more than $11 million, with the Kangaroos handing over two first-round picks in the trade. North are beginning a new era under coach Jaymie Graham after sacking four-time premiership coach Alastair Clarkson.



Blakey remains one of the subjects in an ongoing Victoria Police investigation into sexual assault allegations at the Pullman hotel on August 17. Isaac Heeney, Chad Warner, James Jordon and Riley Bice were also present in the hotel room. Police now consider Bice and two other men who were there, including recently retired ex-teammate Taylor Adams, as witnesses to the pre-dawn events. Nick Blakey will follow in the footsteps of his father John (right) in playing for the Kangaroos. Nathan John, North Melbourne FC The players maintain their innocence and have denied any criminal wrongdoing. Essendon and Richmond were also among the clubs to resume pre-season training on Monday.



Like the Kangaroos, the Bombers also have a new coach, Mark McVeigh who attended training alongside the club’s new general manager of performance, John Longmire. Many of Essendon’s leading lights turned out for training with the first-to-fourth-year crew, headlined by captain Andy McGrath, Mason Redman, Jye Caldwell and Kyle Langford. New Essendon coach Mark McVeigh keeps a close eye on training on Monday. Getty Images Star Bomber Nic Martin has a big summer ahead after missing the entire 2026 season after suffering a setback in November last year while recovering from an ACL rupture. He last played in July last year. The Tigers are looking to take a leap in Adem Yze’s fourth season at the helm.



Recruits Kieren Briggs and Nathan O’Driscoll were among the Richmond players at training at Waverley Park as the Tigers’ future was on show, from No.1 draft pick Sam Lalor to fellow top-10 selections Sam Cumming and Josh Smillie, who appears to be healthy after an injury-ravaged start to his AFL career. Related Article Brisbane Lions Brisbane Lions close in on a successor to AFL coaching legend Fagan Athletic tall Ethan Read won Gold Coast’s two-kilometre time trial ahead of Ben Jepson and Zeke Uwland, while West Coast and Port Adelaide also resumed ahead of the 2027 season. As one of this year’s finalists, Melbourne were not on the training track on Monday, but did make a recruiting announcement of their own, confirming the appointment of freshly retired Collingwood great Steele Sidebottom. The 35-year-old, who played in two premierships among 375 games for the Pies will work for the Demons as a development coach. Keep up to date with the best AFL coverage in the country.

World.title: Beau Lamarre-Condon trial live updates: Former NSW Police officer’s cross-examination continues over alleged murders of Jesse Baird, Luke Davies
World.content:
Hello and welcome to our live coverage of Beau Lamarre-Condon’s criminal trial in the NSW Supreme Court in Sydney.

Lamarre-Condon, 31, has pleaded not guilty to two counts of murder over the deaths of Jesse Baird, 26, a former TV presenter, and Luke Davies, 29, a Qantas flight attendant, in Paddington on February 19, 2024. His case is that he acted in self-defence, the 15-person jury has been told.

The former NSW police officer started giving evidence on Thursday and returns to the witness box at 10am today for cross-examination by Crown prosecutor Brett Hatfield, SC.

Here are the key parts of his evidence about the men’s deaths:

Lamarre-Condon said he entered Baird’s Paddington share house through an open door on February 19, 2024, to collect some of his belongings – including a $25,000 Cartier ring and Casablanca shirts worth thousands – after their relationship ended in November 2023. He said he also had a key with him that Baird had cut for him in November.

He said his relationship with Baird was romantic but was not exclusive. He believed nobody was home despite the door being ajar when he entered the home, he said.

The accused had his police weapon with him because he had contemplated taking his own life on February 18 over work-related trauma and had intended to return it to Miranda police station later that day, he said.

He said he struck upon an idea that morning to dress as an Uber Eats delivery rider and used a motorcycle helmet, high-visibility clothing and bags he saw on a bike in Paddington. “I was worried if I knocked on the door it may be perceived as harassment ... because Jesse told me, ‘please refrain from contacting me’,” Lamarre-Condon said.

He entered the home after knocking three times and saying hello loudly and receiving no reply.

He ran upstairs and hid when he heard noises in the home and came back downstairs later, encountering Baird in the kitchen. He said he took off the high-visibility jacket upstairs and his firearm was “secreted under my shirt. You could not see it. It was actually to the rear of me on a plain-clothes holster so no one could be under the impression that I had a firearm on me”.

Baird did not recognise Lamarre-Condon with the helmet on and lunged at him with a knife, he said. He said at one stage the knife “tore my whole blue shirt open” and he was pinned to a wall in the kitchen.

He shot Baird once in the shoulder to disarm him and accidentally in the head when they fell to the floor.

“I 110 per cent stand by that first shot because if I didn’t do it Jesse Baird would be sitting here in the box today, and he would have to explain why he drove a knife into my throat,” he said.

“Jesse did not have his finger on the trigger,” he said. “It was my fault. I’ve said from the start I am guilty of manslaughter and I’m responsible for his death, but it wasn’t intentional.”

Lamarre-Condon said he found a phone and called Triple Zero and went into “police mode” to try to “save” Baird.

The accused said Davies grabbed the gun and pointed it at him, and later pulled the trigger and shot himself in front of Baird’s bedroom door. The Crown case is that Lamarre-Condon shot Davies through the door.

He admitted to cleaning Baird’s house and disposing of the men’s bodies before turning himself in to police on February 23, 2024.

Support is available from the National Sexual Assault, Domestic Family Violence Counselling Service at 1800RESPECT (1800 737 732), the Men’s Referral Service on 1300 766 491, and Lifeline on 13 11 14.

This week’s picks include the return of Keira Knightley and Ben Whishaw’s London assassins in Black Doves, Hudson’s Williams’ first post-Heated Rivalry gig, a bonkers reality show hosted by Parker Posey and season six of sweet-hearted sitcom Abbott Elementary. Black Doves ★★★★ (Netflix) Delightfully pulpy and propulsive, Netflix’s spy thriller Black Doves isn’t the show you’d expect to win over Keira Knightley, one of the few esteemed actors who had avoided television, missing the prestigious wave entirely. It’s maybe why, when the show’s first season dropped in 2024, I assumed it was a dour, restrained spy drama. In short, I was completely wrong. If anything, Black Doves’ first season was a little too chaotic, with copious blood, twists and tinsel, as spy duo Helen Webb (Knightley) and Sam Young (Ben Whishaw) fought for their lives, often destroying Christmas decorations across London in the process. Ben Whishaw as Sam and Keira Knightley as Helen Webb in Black Doves. With creator Joe Barton (Giri/Haji, Amadeus) back at the helm, season two doesn’t slow down but it’s less crowded, dropping both the festive season schtick and the excessive backstory. (The exception is a sluggish fourth episode cramming together flashbacks and side-plots.) Still undercover, Helen remains married to Wallace (Andrew Buchan), a British MP about to become PM through a Tory leadership spill – all to the plan of the Black Doves, the agency Helen works for, vacuuming up government secrets so they can be sold to the highest bidder.



Related Article ★★★★

Review I thought we didn’t need any more stories about Muhammad Ali. I was wrong Before you worry that moving into 10 Downing Street would impede Helen’s ability to undertake covert missions, Helen’s season two body count reaches double digits within 10 minutes as she sneaks off from a charity gala to crack into a hotel room safe. To be fair, she has help: With Sam leaving the Doves, Helen’s handler Reed (Sarah Lancashire) teams her up with Laila (Ambika Mod), a Gen Z agent who dismisses Helen as a “spy wife”. Wouldn’t the First Lady be tailed 24/7 by security? Not in the Black Doves world, where Helen can kill henchmen in broad daylight, unidentifiable due to a baseball cap that her allies call outright preposterous. As with the first season, don’t think too hard about it; that’s easy enough, as the plot speeds so fast any holes register as funny bumps. Ambika Mod as Laila and Keira Knightley as Helen Webb in Black Doves. What exactly is the second season’s plot? Reed goes missing and Helen doesn’t trust her replacement handler; Sam, wanting out, is blackmailed into a series of kills that could be linked to Reed. Both worry they’re losing their edge, regret when they violently lash out to prove otherwise – and, deep within, remain haunted by the killers they have become, with Knightley and Whishaw letting that fear flood through in overwhelming flashes. Much like Black Doves itself, Helen and Sam constantly chase the thrill of action, knowing they could fall apart completely if they pause for too long. That works for now, but maybe not another season. Hudson Williams in Yaga.



Yaga ★★★ (Binge) A witch from Slavic folklore descends upon a small Canadian town in Yaga – a sexy supernatural thriller and feminist exhumation of Baba Yaga, though it’s primarily been marketed as Hudson Williams’ first gig since Heated Rivalry. Two gigs, technically: Williams plays Henry, a brattish heir (blinding blue contacts), and his roommate (glasses, emerald eyes), neither making much impact. Related Article Australian TV Why it will be crime time (all the time) on Australian screens next year Yaga opens with Henry’s disappearance. His parents send in his longtime friend Rapp (Noah Reid, Schitt’s Creek) as an investigator, though he’s initially more focused on every woman her meets. Despite dripping with chauvinism, Rapp proves irresistible to many and intriguing to others, such as local detective Carson (Clark Backo) and the commanding university professor Dr Hargrove (Carrie-Anne Moss, The Matrix), a bone expert and author of a book titled Sexy Bones. At least one person isn’t a fan of Rapp: whoever nailed a burning chicken carcass to his hotel door, the first of many occult occurrences. While over-reliant on dream sequences and hallucinations, Yaga’s mystical moodiness is intoxicating – as is its strange sense of humour, such as the Russian-language covers of Blondie and Nancy Sinatra during the credits. Across the seven of eight episodes available for review, Yaga is intriguing yet a little heavy-handed, with lines such as “a witch is just somebody society has decided they’re afraid of” perhaps working better in creator Kat Sandler’s 2019 play of the same name. The Mob. DISNEY



The Mob ★★★ (Disney+) Parker Posey (The White Lotus) camps it up as host of The Mob, the latest reality riff on The Traitors, which leans into its mafia-theme with more cheese than a carbonara. Twelve celebrities form a crime family, compete with Mafia-themed challenges, and try to avoid being “whacked” by the Don, the group’s elected lead, who also can be rolled each episode. Too nonsensical to match The Traitors’ mind games, The Mob is best when competitors play into the mystery theatre feel. Debi Mazar (Goodfellas), Aida Turturro (The Sopranos) and Joe Gorga (Real Housewives of New Jersey) clearly have a great time. Abbott Elementary creator and star Quinta Brunson. Ser Baffo/ABC via AP Abbott Elementary ★★★★ (Disney+) Six seasons in, Abbott Elementary remains my go-to for a sweet-hearted sitcom. It’s a warm, funny mockumentary about teachers trying to make do at an underfunded, predominantly Black public school in Philadelphia, inspired by creator-star Quinta Brunson’s mum. For the most part, the series hasn’t messed with its magic. More episodes than not see terminally optimistic Janine (Brunson) overextend herself, such as the season six opener where she loses her sanity decorating her classroom. Jerome Niel in Paolo.



Paolo ★★★ (HBO Max) Admiration becomes deadly obsession in Paolo, a seven-part psychological thriller from France in the vein of Ripley. Where Paolo – a Portuguese piano mover played by a menacing Jerome Niel – learns that a high-society ex-schoolmate (Yoann Gasiorowski) is running in a local election, it stirs up powerful discomforts and desires, drawing Paolo to volunteer. It’s not long before blood spills, but Paolo’s a slow burn. A dense focus on the campaign’s machinations may link Paolo’s rage to a wider political context, but it will turn off those wanting France’s answer to Saltburn. French supercentenarian Jeanne Louise Calment, who lived to be 122 years old. The Oldest Person in the World ★★★★ (DocPlay) For the past decade, experimental documentarian Sam Green has travelled the globe meeting the oldest person in the world, a Guinness World Record title that continually shifts as the record holders die. Do they hold the secret to life? That’s what Green hopes to capture, though his interviews with supercentenarians – all but one are women – are often filled with platitudes, the weight of their experiences never quite translated. Via contemplative voiceover, Green questions our fascination with the world’s oldest people and is remarkably raw about his motivations, including a health scare, his brother’s suicide and son’s birth. Want more TV? We’ve got you.

World.title: Man accused of delivery driver murder exposes himself to court
World.content:
NationalVictoriaCrime Man accused of delivery driver murder exposes himself to court Roy Ward and James Costa Updated November 9, 2026 — 1:21pm ,first published November 9, 2026 — 6:32am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. The man charged with murdering a food delivery driver in central Melbourne was removed from a court video link after exposing himself. Robert Urbano, 51, appeared briefly in Melbourne Magistrates’ Court on Monday over the stabbing death of Feng Jianming, 47, and seriously injuring a fellow delivery rider. A court sketch of Robert Urbano’s video link appearance on Monday. Anita Lester The court was hearing details of Urbano’s schizophrenia diagnosis when he stood on a chair in his holding room, pulled his pants down and exposed himself to the camera. Magistrate John Livitsanos immediately removed Urbano, who is charged with murder and intentionally causing serious injury, from the hearing link.



Urbano, of Footscray, had been visibly agitated during the short appearance, pacing around, fidgeting and attempting to leave. At one point, Urbano interjected when Feng’s injuries were being discussed, saying that he was the one who had been hurt. Feng Jianming with his wife Xu Hongfeng and children Yawei and Changhui from several years ago. “I have injury on my hand,” Urbano said before being remanded in custody until March. Feng was working for food delivery platform HungryPanda on Friday night near Queen Victoria Market when he and another delivery rider confronted a man who was allegedly tampering with their bikes.



Police were called to Chongqing Chicken Pot City restaurant in Frederick Way soon after 8pm where they found a critically injured Feng. Another rider, 34, was allegedly found nearby with stab wounds. Paramedics performed CPR on Feng, but he died at the scene. The 34-year-old man was taken to hospital with serious injuries. Feng Jianming with his son Changhui. Few family photos exist due to Feng’s many years spent away from China supporting them. Urbano allegedly left the scene and was arrested in Footscray on Saturday morning. Feng’s death has sparked anger in Melbourne’s Asian community over public safety in the CBD while the safety and work conditions of delivery drivers has also come under scrutiny.



Hundreds of people joined an emotional rally at the State Library on Saturday night to honour Feng. His wife, Xu Hongfeng, and their adult children, daughter Yawei and son Changhui, expressed their heartbreak from their home in China. Police at the scene on Saturday. Joe Armao Xu told this masthead that Feng worked tirelessly to send money back to China to support his family, including his elderly parents. She said he had not returned home for nine years to save on airfares.



“He wanted to save the money and continue working,” she told this masthead through a translator. “But he promised that when our son got married, he would definitely return. That was the plan. He would come home for our son’s wedding, and then we could finally be together as a family. We thought we only had to wait another year or two.” A second vigil held outside the State Library for delivery rider Feng Jianming on Saturday evening. Alexander Darling Melbourne Lord Mayor Nick Reece, who attended the vigil, told this masthead he had spoken with HungryPanda management and offered to hold a roundtable to discuss safety conditions for delivery riders in the city. “Delivery riders have to be some of the most underappreciated people in our city,” Reece said.



“They deliver our meals, our packages, rain, hail or shine seven days a week and are often not well paid… and, as we have seen, their jobs are very risky as well, not just from other vehicles on the road but from horrible attacks like the one we saw last night.” An online fundraiser for Feng’s family has exceeded $420,000 in donations. With Alexander Darling Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: Victorian election hot seats: Melbourne’s west promised $400m in new transport services
World.content:
For people living in Melbourne’s fast-growing western suburbs, one of the most common and longest-running complaints has been a lack of buses, with some schoolchildren facing half-hour walks to the nearest stop – and an additional wait for a service to show up.

For Sydenham locals, Labor’s $400 million pledge to rewrite west Melbourne’s bus routes with services running on key routes every 10 minutes if re-elected on November 28, will no doubt be appealing.

Under the proposal, about two thirds of pre-existing routes will be upgraded to ‘turn-up-and-go’ services, with a bus promised every 10 minutes, seven days a week. Labor will also create a series of new routes across the west that will connect to train stations.

World.title: Forrestania high-grade gold hits fuel 35% WA resource surge
World.content:

Emerging gold producer Forrestania Resources has delivered a trifecta of news from its WA gold operations, tabling a suite of high-grade drill hits that have underpinned a significant resource upgrade at its British Hill project, in addition to locking in a new separate ore purchase agreement to feed its soon-to-be-commissioned processing hub. The company’s latest 19-hole, 4246-metre reverse-circulation drill program at British Hill, 75 kilometres south-southeast of Southern Cross in the revered Yilgarn Mineral Field, returned a thick, high-grade and remarkably shallow intersection of 16m assaying 5.77 grams per tonne (g/t) gold from just 12m downhole. Forrestania Resources’ British Hill project sits 75km south-southeast of Southern Cross in Western Australia’s rich Yilgarn Mineral Field. Other significant hits included an even richer intercept of 2m at 13.36g/t gold from 231m depth, alongside 9m grading 5.48g/t gold from 202m and 11m running at 4.19g/t gold from 210m. The successful drill campaign has prompted Forrestania to upgrade the mineral resource estimate at British Hill by a whopping 35 per cent, taking it from 212,400 ounces to a new total of 5.7 million tonnes at 1.57g/t gold for a hefty 286,000 ounces.



‘Drilling is improving our understanding of the system and identifying opportunities for further resource growth.’ Forrestania Resources chairman David Geraghty Gold mineralisation at British Hill is hosted within sheared and quartz-veined rocks in the prolific Southern Cross-Forrestania Greenstone Belt. The company has lodged additional Program of Work applications to chase mineralisation interpreted to exist west of the current drilling, with a diamond drilling campaign also planned to begin shortly. Forrestania Resources executive chairman David Geraghty said: “Another demonstrably strong batch of results has reinforced our confidence in British Hill. High-grade mineralisation continues to be encountered across the deposit, while drilling is improving our understanding of the system and identifying opportunities for further resource growth. British Hill is increasingly demonstrating the attributes of a potentially valuable near-term gold development asset for Forrestania.” Capping off a busy day on the market, Forrestania also announced it has shored up its feedstock by executing an ore purchase agreement with Dundas Minerals to treat up to 750,000 tonnes of ore over an initial 24-month period from Dundas’ Rockland gold project. The ore is likely to feed the Lake Johnson processing facility, which is slated for commissioning in early 2027. The deal marks another key plank in the company’s now familiar “hub-and-spoke” strategy and follows a similar agreement for 400,000 tonnes of ore inked late last month with High-Tech Metals for its Mt Fisher gold project. These third-party deals also complement an earlier arrangement with Star Minerals for 400,000 tonnes of ore from its Tumblegum deposit, all designed to feed Forrestania’s two central processing hubs at Edna May and Lake Johnston.



The company is already hauling ore from its Taipan deposit to Edna May, where dry commissioning is now underway ahead of a targeted first ore processing in December. The second hub at Lake Johnston is slated for commissioning in early 2027, with ore from the burgeoning British Hill deposit already stockpiled at site ahead of the plant’s restart. Forrestania’s aggressive growth strategy has also been underscored by its takeover of Zenith Minerals. With 65.4 per cent of Zenith already tucked under its belt, the company appears to be firmly in the box seat as it hunts down the magic 90 per cent ownership mark needed to trigger compulsory acquisition. The offer for Zenith will close at 5pm (AWST) on November 12. The company has ruled out any further extensions unless legally compelled under section 624(2) of the Corporations Act 2001, which provides for an automatic extension in certain circumstances, effectively putting the clock on Zenith shareholders still weighing up their options. Taking control of Zenith will add another 675,000 ounces of gold to Forrestania’s inventory, bringing its global resource base to more than two million ounces. The moves come as Australia’s Office of the Chief Economist forecasts national gold production to rise from 340 tonnes in 2025–26 to 359 tonnes in 2027–28, with high prices encouraging miners to maximise output. While the spot gold price has been volatile after hitting record highs earlier in the year, projects that can demonstrate persistent grade and a clear path to a processing plant are becoming increasingly relevant.



With Forrestania on the cusp of firing up its Edna May processing hub, a resource upgrade at a key satellite deposit and another ore deal to bolster feedstock, the company looks to be systematically assembling the pieces of a significant WA gold production business. If the drill bit continues to deliver, it may not be long before British Hill adds even more ounces to a burgeoning production pipeline. Is your ASX-listed company doing something interesting? Contact: mattbirney@bullsnbears.com.au
