World.title: Kaikohe's long-awaited community hub and library opens its doors
World.content:
A community hub and library 15 years in the making has opened its doors in Kaikohe.

It's hoped Te Kākahu, which cost $14.8 million to build, will instil pride, boost foot traffic and business on the Far North town's main street, and provide a safe place for young people to learn and be creative.

The complex includes a library, council service centre, a creative space, meeting rooms, a gaming room, a podcast studio and a café.

The creativity room is equipped with a 3D printer, laser cutter, T-shirt and screen printer, sewing machine and overlockers.

Locals and schoolchildren by the busload were keen to explore the new building, at the corner of Broadway and Raihara Street, after the 5am blessing on Monday.

Atutahi Ritchie, 9, from Ōhaeawai School, and her cousin Rosie Ritchie, 8, check out the new library’s book collection. RNZ / Peter de Graaf

They included nine-year-old Atutahi Ritchie from Ōhaeawai, on a class visit with her school librarian.

"It's fun and cool. The best part is probably the area where you get to make badges and do 3D printing."

The avid reader said she was coming back with her dad after school to borrow some books.

Far North Deputy Mayor Chicky Rudkin, centre, with Kaikohe East School pupils, from left, Tiare Tito, 10, Olivia Van Gaalen, 11, Jasen Stevens, 9, teacher Lainie Nathan, and Ford Tahere, 10. RNZ / Peter de Graaf

Far North Deputy Mayor Chicky Rudkin said the hub had been a long time coming.

"We're just so excited that it's here. It's going to be a great place to hang out, to connect, a place where children can come, rangatahi can come, kuia and kaumātua can come," she said.

"They can be creative, there are quiet spaces, there's places to tutu, there are places to sit and have hui, there will be a cafe opening soon. It's going to uplift our community and I'm really looking forward to the connections that will be built here."

She said the Far North's other main towns already had new libraries.

"Kaikohe deserves a beautiful space like Te Kākahu, just like lots of our other communities across Te Tai Tokerau have beautiful spaces."

Rudkin acknowledged those who had helped turn Kaikohe's dream into reality over the years, including former Deputy Mayor Sally Macauley - who helped come up with the concept 15 years ago - and steering committee chairman Babe Kapa.

Project manager Hori Tane says having a safe space for young people to meet, learn and share knowledge will be “incredibly positive” for Kaikohe. RNZ / Peter de Graaf

Project manager Hori Tane, of council-owned company Far North Holdings, said it was much more than a library.

"It's a central hub for the town of Kaikohe and should provide a lot more traffic through town, and just provide a really good, safe place for our tamariki and our whānau to gather and to share knowledge and grow together."

Tane said the site, on the main street in the middle of town, was chosen deliberately to instil pride.

"I think Kaikohe has been in need of something like this for a while. It's sharing the love around the North."

The 22-year-old, from Oromahoe and of Ngāti Rahiri/Ngāpuhi descent, said he felt "a bit anxious" when he was first asked to manage the project, but it had been a "fantastic" learning experience.

"I guess as a young person myself, not too far away from that age where I was wandering around libraries and the like, I think it's going to be incredibly positive for so many young people. Just to have that safe space to meet, to gather and to learn and share knowledge," Tane said.

Inside Te Kākahu, Kaikohe’s new community hub and library. RNZ / Peter de Graaf

Among those checking out the new facility was Timi Ngatai-Haenga, a former Waitakere librarian now living in Taheke, west of Kaikohe.

"I think it's going to be well used. There's a lot of resources, a lot of rooms. It's beautiful."

A long time in the making

The project has been a long time in the making with many changes along the way.

Designers including Kaikohe studio Ākau developed the plans based on input from hapū, schools and the community.

It was built by Far North firm Henwood Construction, three-quarters of whose employees live in Kaikohe, after a tender process led by council-owned company Far North Holdings.

The library interior under construction in June this year. Supplied / FNDC

The old Kaikohe service centre, at the council chambers on Memorial Drive, will remain open until 5pm on Monday.

From Tuesday all face-to-face council enquiries, such as paying for dog registration or rates, will take place at the new hub.

The project has evolved significantly over the years.

Originally the hub was planned to be built on the former Kaikohe Hotel site by a partnership comprising Te Rūnanga-ā-iwi o Ngāpuhi, the council and Far North Holdings.

At that point it was set to include new council offices and a museum, with a price tag of around $20m.

The council planned to contribute $11.8m, with the balance from grants and other sources.

The Kaikohe Hotel, which hosted Queen Elizabeth II in 1953 but later slid into decline, was demolished in 2014.

Aerial view of the hub site before construction began in mid-2025. Supplied / FNDC

Later, the plans were scaled back and the council opted to build the hub on the neighbouring site instead, buying the corner property occupied by Petersen Motors and a second-hand clothes store in 2020. By that time the budget was around $11m.

Construction started in August 2025.

Completion of the complex means all four of the Far North's main population centres now have a community hub bringing together library and council services.

Kaitāia's Te Ahu Centre, which incorporates a library, information centre, museum, cinema, cafe and community hall, opened in 2012.

Te Hononga in Kawakawa houses a library, Hundertwasser museum, gallery, council service centre and freedom camping facilities. It opened in 2020.

Carvings outside Kaikohe’s new community hub and library by renowned kaiwhakairo (carver) Allen Wihongi. RNZ / Peter de Graaf

Kerikeri's Procter Library was built in 2004 and largely funded by the Procter family. It gained a council service centre, previously located in rented premises in the John Butler Centre, in 2025.

The former Kaikohe Library, at nearby Marino Place, closed at the end of October. The council is still considering what to do with the building.

World.title: Two people who died in plane crash near Nelson named
World.content:
The two people who died in a plane crash near Nelson last Tuesday have been named.

They were Nicholas Charles Taylor, 67, of Alexandra, and Belgian national Alain Henri Copine, 76.

The Cessna 172P Skyhawk left the city's airport on the morning of 3 November and was later found to have crashed in a remote area south of Castor Peak in the Bryant Range, in the region's north-east.

The bodies of two people were recovered from the wreckage a couple of days later with help from the Defence Force and Fire and Emergency.

Central Otago Flying Club president Kurt Verduyn said the club was deeply saddened by the death of Taylor, who had served as its chief flight instructor for many years.

"He was a well-respected and much-liked member of our club and the wider local flying community, and his contribution to the area will be remembered," Verduyn said.

"Our thoughts are with Nick's family, friends, colleagues and everyone who knew him at this difficult time."

Screengrab / FlightRadar24

Transport Accident Investigation Commission has opened an enquiry into the crash, and said two investigators were trying to find out what happened and why.

Self-fly vacation company FlyInn has previously confirmed the Cessna was one of its planes.

"It is with an incredibly heavy heart we wish to advise one of our aircraft was involved in an accident in an area of New Zealand's South Island," the company said, in a statement.

World.title: Pacific Island teams fall short in RLWC semifinals despite historic campaigns
World.content:
The four Pacific Island teams in the 2026 Rugby League World Cup semifinals all bowed out of finals contention over the weekend.

While there was general disappointment they could not reach the final, the overall consensus has been that their different campaigns had been the best and that the future looks brighter than ever.

Fetu Samoa and the Fiji Bulikula were first timers in the women's competition semifinals.

The Samoa women's team were making their appearance at the event after 18 years, while their Fijian sisters made their first-ever world cup.

Both reaching the semifinals was history in the making.

In the men's competition, both the Toa Sama and Tonga XIII teams were making their second appearances in the semifinals, with Samoa chasing a possible second consecutive final appearance.

However, their campaigns ended at the weekend.

Fetu Samoa lost the New Zealand Kiwi Ferns on Friday night while the Bulikula went down to the Australian Jillaroos on Sunday night in Sydney.

Tonga fell short against the Kiwis on Saturday, while Toa Samoa also fell in the end against defending champions Australia.

Bulikula happy

Fiji Bulikula captain Sereana Naitokatoka said while the Jillaroos won their clash, the Fijians were satisfied with their campaign.

The side scored two tries against the champion Jillaroos, despite losing 30-14.

She said their focus in the match was to go out and enjoy themselves, knowing full well that the battle to win was going to be tough.

"I'm so happy, to be honest, what a game!" she told the post-match press conference after their 30-14 loss to the Jillaroos.

"It was so exciting, we just had fun, and I know that everybody enjoyed watching that.

"We only had one goal, and that was to come out here and have fun playing against the best in the world. And we're so blessed and grateful to be part of this World Cup as a team, representing our nations, our family back home, and everybody connected to us."

Naitokatoka said her message to the players was simple - have fun and enjoy the moments.

"I said to the girls in this circle, I think the team that's going to be coming out of this more happier is the one that's going to enjoy playing and having fun, not thinking too much, just run hard, play hard.

"That was our goal when we did it, and I did not see one dropped face out of any of the girls. Everyone came out there happy, knowing they've put their best throughout the whole 70 minutes."

Head coach Jone Wesele praised his players, adding they lived through the campaign with their focus of three pillars, which were stay connected, be skilful and be selfless.

He said the Bulikula have proven a point to the rugby league world.

"That's something that really came out again today," the former Fiji Bati player told the media.

"Their relentless effort, knowing that they are playing against a team who can strike anywhere in the field.

"Our girls really made them run for their money, and they did make a statement today, and they've showed the world of rugby league that they are not just here to make numbers."

He said he was proud of the team, especially in giving their all throughout their campaign.

Fiji Bulikula won matches against Papua New Guinea and France, while they were pipped by New Zealand in their opening pool match.

Their semifinal appearance means they have also qualified for the next world cup in 2030, having had to qualify for this world cup through a repecharge system, after they had lost the Oceania spot to Fetu Samoa.

Raecene McGregor celebrates after scoring www.photosport.nz

Fetu Samoa mistakes

Fetu Samoa head coach Frank Pritchard said their campaign was a success but admitted his disappointment at the mistakes the team made against New Zealand on Saturday morning in Newcastle.

The Kiwi Ferns won 32-0.

Pritchard said it was tough losing because they had prepared for success and possibly making the final.

"Was it eight nil the first half, and a couple of errors in the second half," he said.

"But that's footy, you know, we just got to compete to the end here.

"We can say that was successful campaign, but it was probably a tough day today because it wasn't how we trained all week and you know we didn't expect that.

"We're probably our own worst enemy today.

"We had 76 possession in that first half, first three errors were from our own mistakes, so you know just compounded stuff.

"So, to to compete and fight in the game, it was hard, but you know our girls, you know, we stayed in there. We competed, we just got to be better at the little things. "

He applauded the Kiwi Ferns for their win "they came out with game plan and stuck with it, and it'll be a tough grand final next week for both teams".

Pritchard said the future of the game is brighter for Samoa, with pathways and development plans set in place.

The bulk of their team is made up of players within the 20 to 23 year olds, as he pointed to their mission of putting Samoa on the rugby league map.

"We came into camp with the mission to come away and be successful and you know to put our little nation on the map and you know last week was a milestone for us, making a bit of history.

"We'll take a lot from this, big learning curve for us, and you know, we're a young team.

"The future is bright for us. I haven't had a chance to talk to the team yet but I'll tell them how proud I am. Proud coach, proud Samoan. Yeah, I'm proud of the girls. Proud of the efforts.

"We got good pathways with our chapters here in here in New South Wales and Queensland, so, we know what's coming through with talent.

"Only last week we were ranked fifth. We'll take all the positives that come with it, the journey through the World Cup has been great."

Captain Evania Isaʻako said they have made their own history during the world cup, even with a young squad.

"The little wins we've had on the field made history," she said.

"We are such a young group, and we definitely battled above our weight grade here.

"And you can't compete with the top two teams, but they've been together for a really long time and we've got girls here who made their first debut in this jersey and their debut World Cup.

"I just want to shout out a massive credit to those girls and were were successful, and today doesn't define our campaign."

Fetu Samoa lost to the Jillaroos in their opening pool match but defeated both Wales and England to book their semifinal spot.

Toa Samoa discipline

Toa Samoa co-captain Junior Paulo knows the code's future is in good hands and applauded his players despite the disappointment of falling short to the Kangaroos in the semifinals on Sunday night.

The Kangaroos won 44-12.

Paulo thanked divine intervention, fans, families and the government of Samoa for all the support they had received, despite the unfortunate semifinal loss to the Kangaroos.

"I want to thank our Lord, the man upstairs, for bringing us all here," he said.

"Most of all, I want to thank our fans. Despite the result today, it's still 685 to the world from the start.

"We spoke about that it was always for the culture, and we wouldn't change a thing. To the boys, there's not a bunch of other blokes that I want to take the field with, so we'll ride it.

"We'll ride it till the wheels fall off. So, love to all our people, especially to everyone that's turned out tonight during the conditions."

Paulo said they knew what they were capable of at the start of their campaign and applauded the Kangaroos for their win.

"We're unfortunate tonight," he said.

"That's a credit to the Aussie boys for turning up the way they did and putting out that performance.

"It was always going to be tough, but we wish them all the best next week. And you know, like I said Samoa's future is in good hands, so we look forward to it."

Head coach Ben Gardiner pointed to the lack of discipline and the bad start they had as factors that led to their semifinal loss.

"It was just not a great start to the game and the the back-to-back errors and penalties cost us in the first half," he said.

"It just led to tries, and when you put in that position where that goes against you so much at the start of the game, and then you're chasing points.

"It just gets a little bit too difficult to come back from."

Gardiner said there were also some controversial bunker calls during the game that went against his side.

Toa Samoa won two pool games against Papua New Guinea and France but lost to Tonga.

However, they qualified along with Tonga for the semifinals because of better points average ahead of England.

Mixed feelings for Tonga

Tonga head coach Kristina Woolf said "it was obviously a disappointing way to finish", after the 34-10 loss to New Zealand in Newcastle on Saturday.

But he added the team has had an outstanding World Cup.

"Have been really happy with everything that we've done and the way the way the players have carried themselves and represented their nation, it's been outstanding to be a part of," he said.

"You can feel the disappointment in there, and there's a quiet change room there for a long time. Everyone knows there's a bit of a missed opportunity with what the group's been able to do, and how talented the group is, and some of the footy we've played, it's a bit of a missed opportunity.

"But we just couldn't get it done tonight, and that's important we recognise that, and we're going to learn from that.

"But at the same time, like I said before, we've had four outstanding weeks together, and it's a group that's really come together well, really played well, represented their nation really well, and I think everyone should be really proud of.

"Once upon a time, we're happy just to be in the finals and be competitive, and now we see ourselves as real players that we believe we can win it. We just haven't been able to produce that."

He also pointed to the windy conditions that hit Newcastle in the second half of the game on Saturday, which forced a couple of errors for his side, especially defending against high kicks.

"We just didn't handle the conditions as well as they did in the second half," he said.

"And I think whoever's against the win in the second half is going to find it tough, and we just need to handle it a little bit better.

"It was hard, we just couldn't get past halfway, and as I said, they handled the conditions a little bit better than we did, and they deserve credit there. And we ended up under too much pressure in the end."

Co-captain Jason Taumalolo, who led the switch to Tonga from star players in 2017, said they made it a competition right up to halftime against the Kiwis, who handled the conditions a lot better.

However, despite the result, he was proud of the team.

"We looked a bit lost a couple of times there. But you know, to be in a World Cup semi-final is an achievement in itself," he stated.

"This camp we've had has been one of the best camps I've been involved with. The playing group, the staff have been second to none.

"I've enjoyed every part of it. We just couldn't get the result tonight, we couldn't get past halfway, and that's always going to put us under a lot of pressure, and you know when you're giving guys like Jerome Hughes and Ponga more time and possession, obviously they're going to put some points on you.

"But we did well to defend most of most of the plays, you know, but when you're under pressure that much, you kind of put pressure on yourselves."

Tonga won three out of three in pool play and won the 'Battle of the Pacific' against Samoa, topping the combined Pool B and C to secure their semifinal spot.

The finals this upcoming weekend will feature a double header between Australia and New Zealand in both the men and women's competitions.

Johnson frustrated

Meanwhile, a frustrated Shaun Johnson had told the media in Sydney he believes Samoa were "hard done by" in their defeat against the Kangaroos.

He has blasted out referee Adam Gee and questioned some major calls in the disappointing loss.

Samoa were controversially denied two tries by the Bunker, while the Aussies were awarded four more penalties on a wet night at Allianz Stadium.

Crichton's four-pointer in the first half was taken away after video official Chris Butler ruled Francis Manuleleua had knocked the ball into Reece Walsh.

That viewpoint differed from Roosters coach Trent Robinson on commentary.

"It's clearly a knock back," he said on Seven.

A second-half try, which wouldn't have impacted the result, was denied after on-field referee Gee ruled that Manuleleua had obstructed Liam Martin.

The Bunker official agreed, sticking with the no-try decision.

Johnson described the call as "diabolical".

"I don't want to take anything away from what the Aussies produced but I can't help but have this frustration around how the game was officiated," he said.

"I feel like Adam Gee got calls wrong and he was confusing in some of his calls and gave Australia the rub of the green tonight. They just got every little call.

"I can understand refs are humans and I can understand getting calls wrong at the moment. What I can't understand is going to someone who has all the technology at their disposal and overturning a call or giving an explanation on a call ... that's just incorrect. That's what I'm frustrated by.

World.title: Why additional MPs may cost millions
World.content:
Audio player for " What will cost me more, cooling my house down or heating it up? " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._v0.KrRTFtoPsaA8nSDloPZ4KejQJr59ANQpD9ULgGwzaM0/politics_election-2026/2459965%2Fwhy-additional-mps-may-cost-millions

What will cost me more, cooling my house down or heating it up? No Stupid Questions with Susan Edmunds Download MP3 11m

An overhang resulting in additional MPs could end up costing about $5 million more in the first year.

On the preliminary results, the typical 120-seat Parliament is expected to increase by 11 MPs, with both National and Te Pāti Māori winning more electorate seats than their party vote entitles them to.

National has an extra seven "overhang" MPs, while Te Pāti Māori has an extra four.

Victoria University associate professor in public management and policy Barbara Allen pointed to the new Speaker's Determination for 2026 which gives members of parliament who are not ministers a staff allocation of $215,818 in their first year in parliament, and a non-staff allocation of $62,145.

They also receive a salary of about $180,000 a year, a basic expense allowance of $19,300, IT hardware funding of $10,400 and $13,682 once per term in staff IT costs.

That adds up to a total of about $500,000 per member of parliament in the first year.

With 11 extra MPs, that adds at least another $5.5 million.

"That's based on an additional non-ministerial list MP. That doesn't include other allowances they might get," Allen said.

In addition, parties receive funding according to the number of members in their caucus.

"There's $26,500 per caucus member. That seems to be an extra amount that's not directly related to the MP themselves."

Offices would need to be found for the additional MPs.

She said overall the cost of the additional members of parliament would still be small in the scheme of the overall cost of government.

Simplicity chief economist Shamubeel Eaqub said data showed the average cost per member of parliament had dropped a little from more almost $750,000 in 2012, in 2025 dollars, to less than $700,000.

He said the bulk of that cost related to the wider business of running parliament rather than directly to the MPs themselves.

"The bigger issue is the erosion of trust, we have record low trust in government, in politics. This kind of stuff makes it worse."

Geoff Plimmer, associate dean of research in the school of business and government at Victoria University agreed the additional cost was a drop in the bucket.

"It's trivial when the government spends billions and billions every year. We need to pay our MPs reasonably well to get quality people. This is the democratic process at work. There are other discussions to be had about whether we need to look at the design of MMP but those are for down the line."

He said it could be moot whether another 10 seats could be added to Parliament's relatively small debating chamber.

"They're often not all always there. Maybe they can hot desk in parliament and experience what life is like for many public servants and others."

World.title: World Vision calls for child-centered climate financing ahead of COP 31
World.content:
Audio player for " Climate debt puts millions of children's futures at risk " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._v0.KrRTFtoPsaA8nSDloPZ4KejQJr59ANQpD9ULgGwzaM0/pacific/2464300%2Fworld-vision-calls-for-child-centered-climate-financing-ahead-of-cop-31

Climate debt puts millions of children's futures at risk Pacific Waves Download MP3 2m

With the United Nations annual climate talks set to begin this week, advocates are calling for urgent changes to how climate financing is administered so those most affected are not improverished further by a crisis they did not cause.

The 31st edition of the UN Framework Convention on Framework Convention on Climate Change (COP31) will be held in Antayla, Turkey, from the 9 to the 20 November. The global summit will bring together heads of state, ministers, scientists, business leaders, and civil society representatives from around the world.

World Vision is one of the global advocacy groups calling for change.

The organisation's United Kingdom-arm has just released a new report calling for climate financing to prioritise children most affected by this crisis.

The Inheritance Trap report looks at the cycle of how disaster recovery efforts divert funds away from essential services to cover climate debt and how it affects children in smaller nations, like those in the Pacific, where these disasters occur.

World Vision NZ's advocacy lead Rebekah Armstrong said the onus was not just on governments to build the infrastructure the Pacific needs.

"The Pacific should be leading all of this, and they are. It's great to see... [but] people should be listening, governments should be listening, businesses should be listening, and we need to increase climate finance and keep it as grants when there is a cost recovery," Armstrong said.

Brianna Piazza

According to the report, during disaster recovery efforts, governments steer funds away from essential services to cover climate debt.

But Armstrong said when countries do this, schooling and access to food are often affected.

"There's this kind of chunk of time where a child is losing out on some of the most important skills and abilities that they need," said Armstrong.

In the Pacific, the report looked at Papua New Guinea, Micronesia, Tonga, Tuvalu and Vanuatu.

World Vision

Similar concerns regarding climate finance had also been aired by Pacific leaders at the 2026 Commonwealth Heads of Government (CHOGM) in Antigua and Barbuda.

UN data from 2022 shows Pacific Small Island Developing States (PSIDS) contribute less than 0.03 per cent of the world's total greenhouse gas emissions, yet are amongst the most vulnerable to the impacts of climate change.

At CHOGM's opening ceremony, Samoa's Deputy Prime Minister Mulipola Anarosa Ale Molioo urged Commonwealth leaders to provide fairer, more accessible forms of climate finance, given the world was already moving beyond the critical 1.5 degrees Celsius warming threshold.

"Many nations and communities are facing permanent losses. But overshoot must not become an excuse for delayed ambition or inaction," she said, as reported by Pac News.

She also called on Commonwealth leaders to heed the calls from the recent Pacific Pre-COP31 discussions in Fiji and Tuvalu.

World.title: South Island house prices lifting faster: QV
World.content:
Audio player for " What will cost me more, cooling my house down or heating it up? " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._v0.KrRTFtoPsaA8nSDloPZ4KejQJr59ANQpD9ULgGwzaM0/business/2464083%2Fsouth-island-house-prices-lifting-faster-qv

What will cost me more, cooling my house down or heating it up? No Stupid Questions with Susan Edmunds Download MP3 11m

The direction property prices are heading depends a lot on which island you live in, data firm QV says.

The South Island has been stronger economically, and in property market terms, for some time but QV's latest update said the divergence had become more stark.

The national average home value dropped 0.9 percent to $890,508 in the three months to the end of October, compared to a 1.5 percent decline in the three months to September.

All of the North Island's main urban areas recorded a drop in values in the quarter.

Some of the biggest drops ranged from to 1.6 percent in Auckland to 2.9 percent in Rotorua.

In the South Island, most areas' values were flat or rising. Only Nelson and Timaru recorded small falls. Christchurch was up 0.6 percent in the quarter and Queenstown lifted 2.6 percent.

"At a national level, the housing market is still going backwards - just more slowly now. But it's not moving in unison. The national figure hides a pretty clear divide between the two islands," spokesperson Simon Petersen said.

"While much of the North Island remains stuck in the same old holding pattern, with buyers generally having plenty of choice and little reason to rush, parts of the South Island are recording some relatively steady growth."

"Housing markets are local. We do tend to talk about national averages and that sort of thing but it's natural for the market not to move in unison."

He said the average value on a national basis was now 2.2 percent lower than at the start of the year.

"There's still time for the market to make up some ground before Christmas - but based on its current trajectory it would take a fairly sharp turnaround for average values to finish the year ahead of where they started.

"That's not the case across much of the South Island, of course, where home values in most markets are already pulling ahead."

World.title: Labuschagne axed from Aussie squad for New Zealand Tests
World.content:
Marnus Labuschagne has been axed from Australia's Test squad.

Chairman of selectors George Bailey confirmed on Monday that Labuschagne would be omitted from Australia's yet-to-be-named squad for the first Test against New Zealand.

Australia's next Test begins on December 9 in Perth, but Bailey and his panel have made an early call to put Labuschagne out of his misery.

Khawaja says one state was best at ball tampering in Sheffield Shield Usman Khawaja says players went as far as using super glue to tamper with the ball in the Sheffield Shield.

Bailey told reporters the out-of-form star wouldn't be considered for the entire four-Test series against New Zealand.

However, the door remains open for a recall on ensuing tours to India and England.

"This gives him a little bit of space and clears up a bit of conjecture … and we'll pick the rest of that squad at the end of round four of Sheffield Shield," Bailey said.

"It's [a Test recall] still possible, absolutely.

"He's always been an incredible performer at first-class level. So I expect that'll be the case.

"There's no message to go back and do anything in particular, the currency is pretty obvious."

Labuschagne averaged just 21.83 in six innings during the South Africa series. (Getty Images: Gallo Images/Richard Huggard)

Labuschagne burst onto the scene with 10 centuries from his first 33 Tests, when he averaged 59.43 and at one stage was the world's top-ranked batter.

But a tortured tour of South Africa, where he logged scores of zero, four, 14, 39, 37 and 37, extended a miserable run of 49 innings without a Test century.

Labuschagne was briefly dropped for last year's tour of the West Indies, but batted his way straight back into the side for the home Ashes with two centuries for Queensland in the Sheffield Shield.

The 32-year-old, once touted as a future national captain by some pundits, will return to leading Queensland in the Shield as he bids to restore confidence and form.

"We all know how good and how effective Marnus can be at his best, but that performance hasn't been there," Bailey said.

"He's pragmatic, he knows that the fundamental nature of being a batter in the top six is to score runs and that just hasn't happened."

AAP

World.title: Khawaja says one state was best at ball tampering in Sheffield Shield
World.content:
Usman Khawaja says ball tampering was common at Sheffield Shield level and the Victorians were the best at it.

Following his explosive claims that all Australian players and staff knew about the ball tampering during the South Africa tour of 2018, Khawaja has made a further claim about tampering in the domestic first-class competition.

"The Victorians were probably the best at it. The MCG used to be dead and flat. Reverse swing and a bit of spin was the only way you could win a game there," Khawaja wrote in his new book Sabr, which is to be released to the public tomorrow.

"I personally never tampered with a ball — in terms of scratching it or anything — but I knew everything that was going on and I wasn't against it which made me complicit.

"The Victorians of that 2000s and 2010s era were genius at it. Throwing it into the wicket and doing other dark arts to rough it up and make the shiny side relatively shinier. It was all fair game."

Khawaja named former Australian ODI fast bowler Mick Lewis as someone who was caught out changing the state of the ball.

Mick Lewis was caught raking the ball across concrete in 2016. (Supplied)

"It was no surprise when, years later, Victoria's bowling coach, Micky Lewis, was caught on cameras scraping the ball in the gutter when it got hit for a boundary. This kind of stuff was very normal," Khawaja wrote.

"There were plenty of times we hoped a spinner got hit for a six so someone could fetch the ball and scrub it while no one was watching and we could reverse swing it.

"To be honest, everyone knew what was going on in those teams I played in growing up. So whether you did it personally or not we were all complicit. The world game was the same. Reverse swing on those older, flatter Test wickets was how you won the matches, come day four and five.''

The former Australian Test batter also claimed an unnamed player had used super glue to tamper with the ball.

Loading...

"One of the players had super glue on his towel,'' Khawaja wrote about his first year in Sheffield Shield.

"He'd get the ball on the rough side and scrub it against the dried-up super glue. It worked a treat and the ball would always reverse."

Khawaja's claim about the prevalence of ball tampering matches comments made by former Australian coach Darren Lehmann on ABC Sport's Summer Grandstand on Saturday.

Lehmann, who has joined the ABC's Cricket Podcast as co-host this season, said ball tampering had been a "big part of the game" until the Australians were caught in South Africa.

"You do know ball tampering is going on because it's been happening for 150 years," Lehmann said.

"I can only speak to what I know, and I know ball tampering was a big part of the game of cricket. Now it is obsolete.

Darren Lehmann (left) stood down as Australian coach after Cape Town. (AP: Halden Krog)

"That doesn't make it right either, but that's the case, and we paid a heavy price for that."

Khawaja has been on the media trail promoting his book for the past two weeks, but the chapter about ball tampering had been redacted until Saturday morning.

The batter has been criticised for sitting on the information for eight years, however Khawaja defended the timing in a social media post while saying he felt he had not thrown anyone "under the bus" with his revelations.

Cricket Australia has continuously denied all players and staff knew about the South African ball tampering.

World.title: Wallabies' woes mount after terrible Twickenham outing
World.content:
When Max Jorgensen sprinted away to score the Wallabies' first try on the stroke of half time, supporters may have felt a faint stirring of half-remembered joy.

Just two years earlier, Jorgensen raced down that same touchline, albeit running in the other direction, to snatch a thrilling victory at the death.

That the try came at the end of a magnificent move of swift ball movement and rapid running imbibed a justified sense of hope in where the national team was heading.

The possibilities that victory seemed to promise were endless.

Two years ago, it felt like the Wallabies were building.

Back in the present and Jorgensen's solo score, via an intercept pass against the run of play, meant that the Wallabies only trailed England by 9 points at half time, sugar-coating a desperate first half in which that was the Wallabies' only line break.

Max Jorgensen scored a superb try at the end of the first half to keep the Wallabies in touch. (Getty Images: David Rogers)

And it would only get worse.

The Wallabies came away from Twickenham having lost a third-straight match by a big score, conceding a record total against an England team that has now won 12 of their past 14 matches against them.

Incredibly, coming into the game, England were the team under pressure.

Steve Borthwick's team won just a single game in the Six Nations, and that was only against the basket case Welsh, to finish fifth on the ladder.

In fact, England, the richest and best-equipped nation in world rugby, had only won three of their eight matches in 2026.

A report in The Times on match week suggested a deepening rift between the head coach and his players that put further pressure on Borthwick, although senior players angrily denied those claims in the lead-up to the game.

The Wallabies had hoped they could use that distraction to put England to the sword, build on the sensational victory against South Africa in Perth and prove that the All Black thrashings were merely aberrations built on the kryptonite qualities Eden Park holds over the side.

Rob Valetini should start against Scotland next week. (Getty Images: PA Images/Ben Whitley)

Instead, it is the Wallabies who leave south west London in even deeper trouble than before, with time running out to effect reasonable change.

England hammer Wallabies The Wallabies's spring tour started in the worst possible way, as England ran rampant at Twickenham to pile the pressure on coach Les Kiss.

Despite the closeness of the half time score, in truth the Wallabies barely featured in the opening 40 minutes.

England, rampaging forward with impunity, had dominated.

In fact, it was only the hosts' errors that had kept the Wallabies in touch at all — Jorgensen's intercept score included.

England's speed at the breakdown had the Wallabies on the back foot.

Their bravery with the ball in hand contrasted dramatically with the Wallabies' insipid defence, forced too narrow by the pace of England's outside backs.

Les Kiss appeared to grow increasingly angry in the coaching box throughout the first half and well into the second.

Les Kiss appeared to be seething at times in the contest. (Getty Images: CameraSport/Bob Bradford)

But heading into the break within touching distance, despite the way they had played, could have given the Wallabies a boost.

Sadly, the Wallabies came out for the second half just as insipidly as they started the first.

Within 15 minutes of the restart, England were 38-10 up and the game was well and truly over, with all but one of the Wallabies' tries essentially a gift from England errors.

"I am disappointed, there is frustration," Kiss told the BBC after the match.

"A credit to England, they kept us in our third in the first half and made their way into our tryline area. They were very good and clinical.

"This wasn't a true reflection of us but that is what happened."

If Wallabies fans want to look for positives, they will have to spend a long time searching.

Ben Donaldson and Filipo Daugunu did OK off the bench: In the short time they were together on the field they had a combined total of four clean breaks, while the rest of the team had just three in total.

But those are thin straws to clutch at.

Henry Slade crashed into Max Jorgensen to deny him a second try in the second half. (Getty Images: PA Images/Ben Whitley)

The worry for the Wallabies now is how to arrest this slide.

Maro Itoje said pre-game that this match would be crucial ahead of any potential meeting at the World Cup, which could occur at the quarterfinal stage if projections bare out.

"Each game is new but there's no doubt that against teams you're going to play down the line, you want them to know that you've got their number," Itoje said.

"We want to win this weekend for this weekend's sake, but we also want to win because we don't want to give the opposition an inch.

"We want to show ourselves and show England fans that we've turned a corner.

"For that reason, this game is huge."

Henry Pollock scored two tries as a flanker playing on the wing. (Getty Images: Patrick Khachfe)

One match does not change an entire mindset, but if Itoje believes England may use it to turn a corner, what direction are the Wallabies now heading in?

"We need to be better," Kiss said simply.

"Losses like that make you sit back and make you take an internal look into a few things.

"It is important to not look too far and too wide, we need to narrow down a few things that we can work on together.

"It is a disappointment tonight but we have seven days to turn that around."

The problem is that seven days may not be anywhere near enough.

World.title: Norris suffers champagne mishap as Mercedes spins to world title
World.content:
Lando Norris was near perfect to claim victory in Brazil, but the McLaren driver was left to celebrate his win with a shattered champagne bottle.

Norris recovered from a poor start from pole, where he dropped to third, to claim his third grand prix win of the season in a São Paulo Grand Prix that went from wet to dry, and back to wet.

Max Verstappen finished second after starting from 21st on the grid, while his Red Bull teammate Isack Hadjar was third.

McLaren teammate Oscar Piastri bounced back from a disappointing qualifying to place sixth.

One week after watching Mercedes driver Kimi Antonelli be crowned world champion, taking the title off him, Norris responded like a champion should in very tough conditions.

But if the Briton wanted to celebrate his 14th career win in style, his champagne bottle had other ideas.

Norris jumped from the top step and slammed the bottle on the ground, trying to produce the spray of wine that signifies victory.

But the bottle exploded on impact into shards of glass, leaving Norris defenceless as Verstappen and Hadjar soaked the race-winner with French bubbles.

But for the two hours prior to the exploding champagne bottle, Norris was excellent.

He suffered a poor start in the wet and dropped from first to third as Antonelli established a nice lead.

Once the track dried out and all drivers went onto slick tyres, Norris charged while Antonelli struggled.

The Italian, who had spun on his way to the grid, then spun out of the lead on lap 20 of 71.

Antonelli would continue to struggle, while Norris never looked like losing.

"It was a very tough race, obviously not the best of launches off the line," Norris said.

"A lot of challenges today … going onto slicks in the wet is tough.

"This weekend, we had an opportunity to get a pole yesterday, an opportunity to win and this year when I've had an opportunity, I've mostly taken it."

Two years after winning from 17th, and earning a podium from the pit lane last year, Verstappen again produced a stunning drive from the back in Brazil.

From 21st on the grid, he roared up the order in the opening laps, picking off drivers one by one in wet conditions.

Once up to second, he could not catch Norris, with Red Bull reportedly believing Verstappen's car had mysteriously lost rear downforce.

"It was a challenging race. The first few laps were very important; I overtook a lot of cars,' Verstappen said.

"The first stint on the inters was very, very strong. After that, I don't know if I picked up some damage ... The balance went off."

Hadjar was third, followed by the Mercedes duo of George Russell and Antonelli.

Oscar Piastri was sixth, while Charles Leclerc (Ferrari), Liam Lawson (Racing Bulls), Lewis Hamilton (Ferrari) and Nico Hülkenberg (Audi) rounded out the top 10.

Antonelli and Russell spin as Mercedes seal constructors' title

Mercedes would have loved to seal the Formula 1 constructors' championship with their drivers on the podium, but both were caught out by Brazil's wet weather.

Kimi Antonelli, one week after becoming drivers' world champion, looked destined for victory when he took the lead off the start.

He held the lead for 19 laps, but on soft tyres in conditions that were still slippery, the young Italian spun and handed the race lead, and victory, to Lando Norris.

That was not the first incident Antonelli had on Monday morning (AEDT). On a wet track, he slid his Mercedes off the circuit and onto muddy ground on his way to the grid.

He was able to find an escape road and take his place at the front of the grid.

George Russell also suffered a race-ruining spin. The Briton, exiting the pit lane after putting on slick tyres, spun his Mercedes before returning to the track.

He was facing back towards the garages as several rivals passed him on the narrow slip lane, costing him any chance of a podium.

But the duo still managed to finish in the top five, and ahead of both Ferraris to seal the F1 constructors' championship.

It is Mercedes's ninth constructors' title, equalling Williams for the third-most all time.

"It is amazing; it was a very strong beginning of the season, and that got us across the line," team principal Toto Wolff said.

"Overall I'm so proud of the organisation; we have taken a few years to get back to the top spot."

Wolff has been team principal for all nine of Mercedes's constructors' championships, and now equals the record with the late Sir Frank Williams for most ever.

Wolff was once a shareholder in the Williams team, and had a relationship with Frank.

"Frank [Williams] is such an unbelievable icon of the sport, to be tied on constructors' championships, I never thought it would be possible."

There are three rounds remaining in the 2026 season, with the Las Vegas Grand Prix to be held on Sunday, November 22, AEDT.
